title: Falcons' Slow Starts Have Created a Problem They Can't Escape
full_text:
FLOWERY BRANCH – The Atlanta Falcons are constantly playing from behind, and, more often than not, it's buried them.
They struggle to find consistency and have trailed by at least 10 points on 35.9% of their offensive snaps through 10 weeks (the league's highest rate). The results have been three consecutive double-digit losses, with slow starts repeatedly forcing the offense to play catch-up.
“When you're down, it's hard for the coaches, because the playbook gets limited and you have to get some points and stuff like that, get big chunk plays,” left guard Matthew Bergeron said. “It's hard to get the offense rolling when you're trying to get back (in games). We call it G-Bot when you're trying to get back on track. It's not easy. Those guys (the defense), they want to rush the passer, and it makes their life easier. So we just gotta keep working on it.”
Self-inflicted errors have crushed the Falcons through their first 10 games , but Bergeron was adamant that the bye week's priority would be to “clean up” the offensive operation ahead of the season's final stretch. He said that the “leadership” on the roster gives him confidence that they can get there.
“The guys we have in the locker room, I think we have some great guys, some great leaders, on our team,” the left guard said. “I feel like we're going to fight until the end, and we proved that (against the Chiefs). We were down, and we just kept fighting. That's just who we are, and if we hadn't made those mistakes early in the game, we would have been in it.”
But nothing will matter unless this offense can find its legs.
The Falcons' offense looked dramatically different after Michael Penix Jr. returned from injury. Atlanta averaged 31.0 points per game from Weeks 3 through 7, leading the NFL during that stretch. Opposing defenses have since adjusted, and the Falcons have averaged just 10 points over their last three games, all losses.
The rushing attack, in particular, has taken a hit. Despite rostering one of the league’s premier skill players in Bijan Robinson, the Falcons have been outrushed in five of their last six games. The star back has reached the 100-yard rushing mark only once in that stretch and has had at least 20 carries in only one game (their only win).
The slow starts have a lot to do with that, but so does not getting the ball to their star player earlier in games – Robinson only had one carry over the first four possessions against the Chiefs (all three-and-outs).
This inability to establish the offense has drawn scrutiny on the coaching staff. Stefanski confirmed this week that offensive coordinator Tommy Rees will continue calling plays, but the head coach acknowledged that the execution hasn't been good enough.
For an offense that has so much invested in it, this is particularly worrying.
They feature several first-rounders and big-contract players – the five largest contracts are offensive players – but that investment hasn't produced the return the Falcons need so far. That group is averaging just 20.1 points per game and -0.16 EPA per play.
Since Week 5, the numbers are particularly concerning.
According to NextGenStats , the Falcons are 30th in third-down conversion rate and have produced -0.12 EPA per rush. Penix has posted -0.13 EPA per dropback with six interceptions during that stretch, while the offense has averaged just 2.2 points in the first quarter.
Rees was moved from the box to the sideline to improve communication and produce better results, but that change didn’t move the needle against the Chiefs. It remains to be seen whether that move will be permanent.
“The responsibility falls on me,” head coach Kevin Stefanski said about the poor offensive play. “Everything falls on me. We all have to be better. That’s the truth. We are all going to learn from it. We’re not going to hide from it; we’re going to learn from it.”
Stefanski will pull everything apart during the week off to “get under the hood” to see how this team can get back on track, but it starts with these players.
“It’s definitely a mentality, and it’s habits,” Jahan Dotson said. “It’s what you do every day in practice. It doesn’t just happen on game day. It’s what you do every single day. If you are going to say you want to be (a good offense), then you have to be about it every day, and you have to create those habits.”
Frustration is high in the locker room over how the games have gone, but the Falcons still have time to get back on track. Atlanta is still within striking distance in a struggling NFC South and still has games against all three division opponents before the end of the year.
The key now is to keep the team together, despite the 3-7 start. Players have maintained that they still have the right guys in the locker room and the right mindset heading into the final seven games.
“I think the way our team is wired, and the way we were brought on this year – it's not pretty, but we're gonna keep fighting,” Bergeron said. “You just gotta turn that frustration into motivation. And listen, we have a week to fix the bumps and bruises and get back to work.”
“We have a lot of guys that care,” Dotson added. “We have a lot of guys that love this game, a lot of guys that love winning. Obviously, we have not been on that path, so the guys want to fix that.”
Center Corey Levin said the offense is “one guy away” from finding explosive plays. But after 10 games of inconsistent execution, the Falcons need to find out how to turn that optimism into points during this week off.
Otherwise, this season will keep spiraling.
Garrett Chapman is a sports broadcaster, writer, and content creator based in Atlanta. He has several years of experience covering the Atlanta sports scene, college football, Georgia high school football, recruiting for 24/7 Sports, and the NFL. You can also hear him on Sports Radio 92.9 The Game.

title: Mark Andrews' Last 20 Games Have Been Nothing Short Of Disastrous For The Ravens
full_text:
In Week 10, with the Ravens playing on Monday night, out of nowhere during the broadcast came a report about Mark Andrews and a broken hand.
The tight end, who was leading all players at his position in false start penalties and had the highest drop rate as well, went on to have his first productive game, honestly, since September 2025, his first game over 50 yards receiving since then, and the hand, so the story went, has now good to go. Of course, Andrews has not shown up on an injury report and he hasn’t been wearing anything protective on his hand.
Maybe he was feeling better and maybe he wasn’t going to just go on being one of the most overpaid players in the NFL. Maybe, with each passing week, the ridiculous decision to extend his contract last December would look like an utterly foolish decision by a general manager, Eric DeCosta who has made such failures his brand .. Surely, Andrews was never going to look like half the player ex-Ravens tight end Isaiah Likely is week after week for the Giants, but at this point merely string together two 40-yard games would amount to significant progress.
… And nothing close to that came to pass..
Sunday’s debacle in Carolina was simply more of what ever week is for Andrews. A confounding display where he is asked do more than rookie tight ends Matthew Hibner and Josh Cuevas , and he offers precious little. It was another game where he simply did not show up in the passing game at all, he cannot do anything downfield, and he finished with two catches for two catches for 14 yards. The eight grabs for 82 yards vs the Chargers was the outlier, and it may prove to be for quite some time.
Andrews continues to exude rampant positivity in the face of a disaster season, but thinking he has the answers and can actually influence this offense would be silly at this point.
"I'm just fired up, man," he said after Sunday's setback." I am ready to go. I think for me, just playing with my heart, playing all I can and doing anything I can to help this team win is the main thing. And just being there for everybody. I just want to be able to do that."
This is no slump for Andrews; it’s the end of his tenure as a move tight end in the NFL. It’s been over and it is over, only the Ravens are going to be stuck paying him next year anyway with another $5M guaranteed on his deal (top seven at his position in average salary). He was paid like a top 10 tight end, but those days are long gone.
Andrews is going to end his career without every registering a playoff touchdown. Certainly his Ravens' career, with this team not sniffing the postseason anytime soon. And even with back-up quarterback Jacoby Brissett funneling the ball to tight ends, Andrews can’t do anything after the catch and he moves the chains on check downs and short passes and that’s about it.
Over his last 20 games, he's averaged three catches for 26 yards. Gulp.
He has just two touchdowns in his last 20 games.
He averages 2.1 yards after the catch in that span, and for the last two seasons , which is hard to fathom. He has caught just 63 of 91 targets in those games, despite his routes being pedestrian and high percentage by and large. He is averaging just 8.3 yards per reception.
He'll probably play more snaps and run more routes than anyone else at his position again Sunday. Nothing much ever changes in Owings Mills, and they refuse to get real about who they really are and how deep their personnel issues and coaching issues run.

title: Trey Hendrickson Isn't The Only Ravens Offseason Addition Failing To Deliver. He Has Company
full_text:
The Ravens are stuck with Trey Hendrickson.
They missed any chance to pawn him off before the trade deadline, and they will regret it , and they are stuck with another $30M fully guaranteed coming his way next season after getting nothing out of the $30M invested in him during this lost season. General manager Eric DeCosta has a failure offseason continuing a three-year debacle that should have cost him job in January when head coach John Harbaugh was fired.
He got nothing right, his offseason was doomed from the moment he pulled out of a Maxx Crosby trade and The Football Gods or karma have been kicking up every week since (or, well, it’s mostly just that he isn’t very good at this whole evaluating, negotiating, leadership thing). And no one, from an on-field standpoint, is going to embody this 2026 disaster as much as Hendrickson, who should honestly be doing far more standing on the sidelines as he gets attacked in the ground game with the weather turning.
They called him a $60M closer, and he hasn’t shown up in a fourth quarter all season and after six straight loses with rookie head coach looking overmatched all along, nothing Hendrickson does this season even really matters, now. Sad. But true.
With Hendrickson’s malaise getting more and more attention around the NFL, it’s as good a time as any to reflect on all the players brought in from outside the organization by DeCosta for this much-hyped defense and evaluate the evaluator. Hint: This ain’t pretty.
The defense is the biggest failure in the franchise and Minter can’t seem to do anything about it. His side of the ball was handed the preponderance of resources in free agency, and Minter is an alleged mastermind. so this should be keeping owner Steve Bisciotti up at night, and jobs should be on the line.
Key Stats : 2 sacks, 5 pressures in the fourth quarter, 12.7% pressure rate late five weeks
Verdict – F: He was supposed to be the guy who ended the fourth-quarter rot and turned this defense around and stopped all the blowing of fourth quarter leads. Doesn’t have a signature moment or game and has been increasingly invisible lately, except when getting exposed in the ground game. His "revenge" game vs. Bengals could not have been more of a dud.
Key Stats: 1 sack, 1 batted pass, 6 solo tackle, 28 snaps/game
Verdict – D: Hard to see him play out his age 40 season on a joke of a defense in a franchise hardwired to lose. Going to post close to 500 snaps if they keep this pace up, but with so few playmakers around him, the impact has been muted. He is an all-time great leader and exemplary human, but this DL has not been strong and now they are getting run on.
Key Stats : 6 GP, 1 Pressure, 16 tackles, 137.5 Passer Rating
Verdict – F: Will probably be out until the bye. Has not connected with any of the fellow safeties and communication issues are rampant. Showed up against the run and pass game with the Patriots but this has been brutal. Picked on when they do throw his way. Part of one of the worst secondaries in the NFL.
Key Stats: 103 Coverage Snaps. 97.9 Passer Rating
Verdict – D: Compared to last year, where he provided excellent bang for the buck, it’s an F. But, hey, he hasn’t been picked on as much as $19M corner Marlon Humphrey and he hasn’t needed Mayor Brandon Scott to rebuke him for offensive remarks about Baltimore, so we have to grade on a curve here. Even with Humphrey getting carved up, Minter hasn’t wanted to play him much and he’s fallen behind TJ Tampa now, too.
This was a total joke by the front office. Across the board. Every level. They got absolutely nothing out of the draft on defense – Zion Young (second round) has no pass rush and barely plays; Chandler Rivers hasn’t’ seen the field on defense in weeks – and you won’t find a bigger collective bust of new defensive coordinator plus lack of production from the players brought in during the offseason.

title: The Ravens' 5 Biggest Needs For 2027 (Excluding QB, Fingers Crossed)
full_text:
The Ravens refuse to acknowledge the depth of their problems.
Whether it’s failing general manager making silly buy-side trades at the deadline (and some that thankfully didn’t happen) and failing to unload contract of players who have no meaningful future here, or an overmatched rookie head coach dismissing calls to stop calling plays on defense in hopes he can grow into being an NFL head coach. Whether it’s refusing to bench underachieving veterans on bloated contracts who are hurting their product ($60M closer Trey Hendrickson, for instance) or choosing to make rookies healthy scratches every week despite the need to start seeing what they can.
It’s a woefully misguided organization and with six-straight losses and counting, it’s only getting worse. The biggest issue, of course, will be convincing two-time MVP quarterback Lamar Jackson to stick around in 2027, and given what Lamar Jackson Entertainment has put on social media lately, that’s an uphill climb to say the least . It’s daunting all around, the head coach keeps talking and acting like someone who should be one-and-done, and this roster is in decay and needs an overhaul.
Even if you take quarterback out of the equation – which is impossible, but let’s do it anyway – there are glaring and massive needs facing this team in 2027. As it stands right now, here are their five biggest needs outside of QB, in reverse order:
Trading for Cam Jurgens was a failed stopgap measure . Thinking he is going to hold up for 2027 and play well while doing it would be based on pure folly; not game film here or in Philadelphia and not based on his medical history. Paying him $17M next year is a self-inflicted error but that’s GM Eric DeCosta’s brand, and this trade will haunt them.
They played a comp pick game picking up veteran center Ryan Neuzil, who has been riding the bench. Finding a long-term solution is vital; offensive coordinator Declan Doyle has been undermined by the rotating guards and shuffling offensive lines. Rookie guard Vega Ioane is still the best center on the roster, but they want him to focus on guard.
You can find plug-and-play starters on the second day of the draft.
Malaki Starks cannot handle deep duties in Minter’s defense and if he is married to split safety concepts , he better find a few guys who can do it. Free agent Jaylinn Hawkins has been a bust. Kyle Hamilton is a SAM linebacker.
It’s a pass-happy league and the Ravens have not been able to defend the middle of the field - short, intermediate or deep – since coordinator Mike Macdonald left after the 2023 season. This needs desperate attention and probably needs to be a proven veteran type if at all possible; this franchise stopped drafting or developing defensive backs with ball skills a long time ago.
Finally, Marlon Humphrey will be gone next season, along with a bunch of other cooked veterans on ridiculous contracts. But he’ll leave behind a $12M cap hit. Nate Wiggins has zero ball skills, Chidobe Awuzie won’t be back, and rookie slot corner Chandler Rivers never sees the field on defense despite Baltimore having the worst slot defense in the NFL … So yeah, this might be low because they need a handful.
Nice to see TJ Tampa finallly get to play and come up with their first pick by a corner all season, but this staff has shown no conviction in him.
This was allegedly a superpower for the Ravens and their wunderkind head coach . Oh well. More folly.
They tried to patch it up by keeping run-stuffer Broderick Washington around on a team-friendly deal and bringing back Calais Campbell for a second stint, despite being 40. They crossed their fingers that Nnamdi Madubuike would return to All Pro form after a neck injury negated almost all of his 2025 campaign.
And, worst of all, despite this being a lingering need DeCosta completely ignored it in any meaningful way in consecutive drafts that were loaded with DTs – one of which will go down as potentially generational. Madubuike as this point is a good player but might not be consistently great anymore, and he is only signed for one more year. Travis Jones is a nice rotational player but nothing more. This defense has lacked a spine for years, we already covered free safety, and Roquan Smith has been a marginal-at-best middle linebacker for years.
Better fortify the middle in a big way at the point of attack if this defense is ever not going to stink. (at least some youngsters are emerging on the edge).
Ronnie Stanley had a great career but he’s not going to be here by June 1 if this franchise has a clue. They should have drafted his successor by now and he is on borrowed time physically and is committing penalties in droves and the pass protection is going south. It’s time to move and this needs to a substantial commitment in terms of assets.
Not some hope-and-pray late round pick. If they don’t think enough of Carson Vinson to give him a run in a garbage season with journeyman Jacoby Brissett back there, don’t start selling parables about his potential and upside in the offseason. And the idea that Roger Rosengarten is a two-contract right tackle is in doubt; he can’t help on the blind side.
Jason has covered sports professionally for newspapers, websites and broadcast networks since 1996 and have covered the NFL extensively for The Washington Post, CBS Sports and The NFL Network from 2004-2025.

title: Ravens Snap Count Analysis: Biggest Winners, Losers and Role Changes From Week 11
full_text:
The Ravens results do not change.
They lose, week after week, as questions mount about just how overmatched this front office and coaching staff appear to be . It’s six straight games and counting and given the piercing issues in all three aspects of play there is no reason to expect that to change anytime soon. This franchise refuses to embrace its obvious rebuild and continues to keep players like Adam Randall and Elijah Sarratt inactive, while abstaining from letting youngsters like Carson Vinson and rookie tight ends Josh Cuevas or Matthew Hibner play as much as they should .
There were definitely some noteworthy trends with the snap counts however – that always tells the story of what coaches really think beyond what they say – and hopefully a thorough youth movement is unleashed amid this lost season in which the job simply appears too big for Jesse Minter; well, both jobs: head coach and defensive coordinator .
The questions are coming regularly now about Minter relinquishing play calling duties and, around the league, the chatter about him perhaps not being cut out to be a head coach is mounting. The Ravens faced some new personnel scenarios on defense with corner Marlon Humphrey suspended by the team for the game and top defensive tackle Nnamdi Madubuike out with injury.
TJ Tampa : Minter has been slow to embrace this former mid-round pick despite his body type seemingly a better fit in his zone-heavy schemes than other boundary options. Minter barely played him in the first half (six snaps), preferring veteran Chidobe Awuzie, but with the secondary starting to get lit up in the second quarter he made the switch to the youngster.
Tampa played 39 snaps on defense, by far his most under Minter and his most, period, since Week 5 of 2025. Tampa responded by getting into excellent train coverage on Tet McMillan and picking off a pass in the back of the endzone for the first interception by a Ravens corner all season. Even with Humphrey coming back, it would take a truly cowardly organization to sit him for Humphrey, but with Eric DeCosta in charge, well, don’t hold your breath .
“I thought T.J. took advantage of the opportunity to play more,” Minter said.” I thought, man, the play two plays before the interception, great play as well, particularly where they're at and just trying to throw like the run-pass option slant there. Great play by him there.”
Mike Green: The pass rusher is having a true breakthrough in Year Two, he’s headed for double-digit sacks, and he is out-performing $60M alleged “closer” Trey Hendrickson in a big way against the run and getting to the QB. Green out-snapped the big-ticket free agent again and v astly outperformed him.
Green played 50 snaps – tied for second-most of his career and most since Minter took over. He produced five tackles and two sacks and two QB hits and will continue to pace this edge group in snaps. He and Tavius Robinson should be the starters next season, but good luck dumping Hendrickson’s contract.
“He gives you everything he's got from a physical standpoint,” Minter said. “He strikes people in the run game. There are times where he's taking on a lot bigger bodies, and he's holding his own, and then he does things in the pass rush game where he works well with other guys. He works well within games.”
Ja’Kobi Lane: Receivers DeCosta drafts almost always stink, and the learning curves tend to be steep . The heady days of rookie offensive coordinator Declan Doyle being called a genius this summer and Lane being a preseason superstar seem long ago. After a very rough game against the Chargers Lane’s passing snaps were slashed from 36 to just 23 against the Panthers, he continues to struggle to find his way in this offense and we suspect the shift to more 12 and 13 personnel is on (more tight end emphasis). He did not have a target in the game.
Matthew Hibne r: The rookie tight end was the big beneficiary of Lane’s slashed role; but it didn’t turn into much. Hibner went from 22 snaps against the Chargers to 33 against the Panthers, but he isn’t really separating and the big-play potential hasn’t shown up since before Lamar Jackson got hurt in Week 4. He had two receptions for 12 yards and unlocking his YAC is a must. Jacoby Brissett loves throwing to TEs and the have to get this cooking.
Jason has covered sports professionally for newspapers, websites and broadcast networks since 1996 and have covered the NFL extensively for The Washington Post, CBS Sports and The NFL Network from 2004-2025.

title: Ravens Rookie Head Coach Jesse Minter Still Resisting Calls To Divest Play Calling Duties
full_text:
Ravens rookie head coach Jesse Minter, struggling mightily to manage games and on-field situations, while also suffering as a defensive play caller, nudged a bit on Monday when probed about his failures as a coordinator.
For the second time in his 12 regular-season weeks on the job Minter was asked at a Monday press conference about his willingness to relinquish play calling duties of what’s becoming one of the worst defenses in franchise history. And unlike the first time, he offered an actual response.
Two weeks ago, he blurted out, “No,” when the topic was first broached and now, with his team holding the worst second-half scoring differential in the NFL (-98) and his defense giving up 33 points or more in four of the last five games, Minter (4-7) deigned to show some understanding of why he was being questioned about Anthony Weaver potentially taking over play calling for him.
“Everything crosses my mind,” Minter said when asked about considering a change on the headset, “but I’m always going to try to do what I think is best for where we are right now.”
So, that was still a no, but not quite as resounding. And with a lot less sass.
And if the Texans smash Minter’s defense on Sunday for a seventh-straight loss – and there is every reason to expect that to be the case – he will invariably be asked about this again before Baltimore takes its Week 13 bye. His highest-paid players continue to fail at their jobs and players now speak openly about the lack of “trust” and “execution,” while Minter himself was already begging for “leaders” to emerge in his locker room by October.
Minter’s tone changed when asked about having arguably both the NFL’s worst second half offense and defense (30-year-old offensive coordinator Declan Doyle suffers mightily once off his early-game script). "clearly everything,” was his response in terms of what needs to change in that regard.
In general, Mnter has been short of specifics and devoid of corrections but heavy on trite colloquialisms about “sticking together” and everyone “in it together,” that are straight from the John Harbaugh/Jim Harbaugh playbook.
Now that teams aren’t just throwing the ball all over the field on an overmatched secondary that was supposed to be one of the best in the NFL, the run defense has become a significant issue. Minter’s alleged $60M “closer” Trey Hendrickson not only offers no late pass rush but is getting attacked in the ground game. Expect that to continue, with Minter unwilling to bench overpaid veterans to this point (struggling $19M corner Marlon Humphrey will return to practice to this week, Minter said, after being deactivated Sunday for disparaging remarks about Baltimore on his podcast).
The Ravens entered the season boasting about a defense that should be among the best in the NFL, propelling the team to its self-purported Super Bowl expectations, but the best Minter could muster Monday about where that standard is now was:
“We can be a serviceable, productive defense, but right now it’s too inconsistent." Good luck sending out those season-ticket renewals off that.
Minter did take blame, in a more straightforward sense, for botching a two-minute drill at the end of the game, keeping two timeouts in his pocket with back-up quarterback Jacoby Brissett under assault and wasting close to a minute of precious time.
In hindsight “banging” a timeout after a QB sneak would have been the better decision, Minter offered, as he weighed the need to save a timeout for a potential sack or negative play later in the drive. “You always want to try to keep one for that,” he explained.
The Ravens have lost seven straight games in a season just once before, 2007, when Super Bowl head coach Brian Billick was fired. Minter’s defense has a lot in common with that one , and he continued to carry the look of someone who might not be cut out for a second year on the job.
“We haven’t played the level of defense I think we’re capable of,” Minter said.
Jason has covered sports professionally for newspapers, websites and broadcast networks since 1996 and have covered the NFL extensively for The Washington Post, CBS Sports and The NFL Network from 2004-2025.

title: The Ravens Created A $60M Problem With Trey Hendrickson They Won't Be Able To Fix
full_text:
The Ravens have a $60M problem on defense.
Well, in full candor, they have a $160M problem on defense.
Their team-record payroll on that side of the ball is producing almost no results – Sunday was another debacle – calling the job security of rookie head coach Jesse Minter already into question. They have no discernable strengths as a defense, getting gutted on the ground now that teams have finally started running the ball on them after being content to merely pick apart Minter’s dime coverages for most of the season .
Trey Hendrickson was the handpicked solution to years of defensive rot. Failing general manager Eric DeCosta – after bailing on an agreed to trade for Raiders elite run stuffer/pass rusher Maxx Crosby for alleged medical concerns  – then pretended he was planning to land Crosby and Hendrickson . In reality, he thought Hendrickson was a value-play, with his age, injury history and inability to stop the run leaving him with a shallow free-agent market.
And it turns out the market was right, and DeCosta was wrong (he has been consistently wrong for years on end in a way that should have had him fired when head coach John Harbaugh was let go ), And Hendrickson, about to turn 32, is a $60M (fully guaranteed) waste. He’s nothing close to the “closer” he was anointed to be by DeCosta and Minter. He has added nothing at all – no juice and no jam and damn sure no sacks – to their atrocious fourth-quarter defense and his ineffectiveness is a hallmark of their six-game losing streak.
Signed to put the team’s Super Bowl pursuits over the top, he is already a bust. These Ravens will "compete" to be possibly the worst defense in franchise history in 2026 , and won’t be contending for anything in 2027, either, with a rebuild imminent. This is a sunk cost, already. (Oh and the Bengals defense and pass rush is markedly better without him and hold-ins, as evidenced when they crushed the Ravens).
Literally nothing about how Hendrickson was billed has showed up. Thankfully, Mike Green is taking a leap in year two, but Hendrickson should be making way for him.
Hendrickson was somehow more effective while playing through a painful finger injury than he’s been since the surgery to repair it . He is the face of Minter’s shortcomings – nearly as much as Minter himself – and his recent suspect play would call for his benching if this was a meritocracy (but it’s a fiefdom for the front office where their litany of egregiously overpaid “stars” - Hendrickson, Roquan Smith, Marlon Humphrey, Mark Andrews – get unfettered opportunities to play because anything else would make an overmatched front office look even more so).
As bad as the Hendrickson signing has looked since around Week 3, it’s truly starting to tug at whatever fabric of this defense remains; opponents will be running 30 times or more on this failing front, and Hendrickson will be further exposed and the defense will suffer even more because of it.
“Going against him when he was with the Bengals I think he is a very good pass rusher, and that's it,” former Ravens coordinator Wink Martindale told me on “The Daily Flock Show” a few weeks back. “That's what he is. I think he's a third down, second-and-long type guy because he wants to get to the quarterback.
“The problem is … They're not getting leads where people have to throw the ball to get back in the game (with Lamar Jackson hurt). And when you get selfish, and you're rushing a passer on a run play, it exposes players. And that's what I'm seeing. That's what I'm seeing with him.”
Quite a rebuke, but a truthful one. And it’s really showing up now.
What Have You Done For Me Lately?
In the last five games, no longer wearing an apparatus and without his hand heavily bandaged in recent weeks, Hendrickson has three total pressures in the second half of games. That is a putrid 6.7% pressure rate for “the closer” who is being paid to be in the 18% and up stratosphere. Consider the following:
Last 5 Games (2nd Half): 3 Press/45 Rush (6.7% Pressure Rate)
Season (4th Quarter): 0 Sacks, 2 QBH, 3 Hurry, 6 Press (10.7% rate)
Since Surgery (6 Games): 1 Sack, 5 QBH, 11 Hurry (12.4%)
But that’s only half the problem.
Baltimore has allowed 300 yards rushing the last two weeks, and Minter has been unable to curb any issues thus far. With Hendrickson on the field the last two weeks, opponents have rushed 43 times for 234 yards and two TDs. He can’t set the edge; he is getting stiff-armed and cast aside and that 5.5 yards/carry average is going to go up. Watch.
On Sunday Baltimore had a pathetic 45.5% run defense success rate with Hendrickson on the field. He will be targeted on the ground - like Humphrey is through the air - by speed and power backs. And with Kyle Hamilton playing more deep safety (and struggling), he’s offering less thump around the line of scrimmage; Hamilton missed four tackles Sunday and Hendrickson will get picked on even more.
Baltimore’s best all-around edge – Tavius Robinson on a bargain-basement rookie deal – is on season-ending IR. Hendrickson not only isn’t a strength; he’s a liability. A franchise even somewhat serious about curbing its rot and beginning an obvious rebuild  would have peddled Hendrickson’s contract for anything possible at the deadline as we pointed out , but instead DeCosta bought older players and gutted future drafts .
More Zion Young – a second-round edge project DeCosta took over a bevy of starting center options – might help against the run, but he has limitations and he’s actually been playing less lately, despite facing run-heavy teams. Young shows up in short-yardage packages but it’s worth noting teams can pick on those personnel groups on the air, as a 128.4 opposing passer rating (vs. mostly weak QBs) with Young on the field speaks to. Jeepers.
Quite a quandary, and one this coaching staff and front office will be ill-equipped to solve. They create problems; they don’t fix them.
Jason has covered sports professionally for newspapers, websites and broadcast networks since 1996 and have covered the NFL extensively for The Washington Post, CBS Sports and The NFL Network from 2004-2025.

title: Ravens Unprecedented Second-Half Failures Call Jesse Miner's Job Security Into Question
full_text:
If only NFL games were a half-hour long, the Ravens’ novice coaching staff might have a fighting chance.
Of the many reasons why neophyte head coach Jesse Minter looks overwhelmed and overmatched every week – devoid of cogent defensive adjustments as a play caller let alone understanding game- management, timeouts, two-minute drills and obvious benchings/substitutions – the second-half failings stand tall. It’s part of why longtime Raiders team president and NFL analyst Amy Trask called for swift changes to the coaching staff – including potentially both coordinators  – and it’s a big reason why the Ravens have been so non-competitive for much of their six-game losing streak that should have Minter’s job security under immediate review .
The Ravens (4-7) are doing to finish with consecutive losing seasons for the first time since their first three years after moving from Cleveland and no team they ever hyped this much immediately fell flat on its face like this one. They are fallacy propped up only by Lamar Jackson’s singular brilliance, and Minter set about blowing 10-to-13-point leads with regularity even before Jackson got hurt the first time (they have taken a double-digit lead six times and handed it back five times and lost four of those games).
Minter’s defense is the biggest issue with the franchise ( historically bad ), despite a team-record $160M sunk into that side of the ball after the anointing of $60M “closer” Trey Hendrickson in March (two sacks) – even bigger than the loss of two-time MVP quarterback Lamar Jackson. Journeyman Jacoby Brissett has revived a moribund pass attack, but Minter got outclassed by the previously winless Chargers at home on a Monday night – by the worst offense in the NFL – and then gave up 35 points to the tepid Panthers despite being staked to a quick 12-point lead .
Choking leads is his brand, having no in-game solutions has defined Minter and 30-year-old offensive coordinator Delan Doyle (worst second-half offense in the NFL), and it’s all only getting worse with a schedule ahead in which even the Buccaneers are likely to be favored over the Ravens despite Baltimore being at home and coming off a bye before that Week 14 game.
They may not win another game, there should be sweeping changes from team president and general manager all the way down , and the inability to put out any fires through the course of a game means Minter likely does not merit another season at the helm for a team that crowed about “competing for championships” starting immediately upon hiring Minter according to team president Sashi Brown (who was arguably the worst GM in NFL history running the Cleveland Browns).
Minter not calling a timeout with Brissett under assault on a two-minute drill was bizarre – “Obviously, in hindsight, I could have banged a timeout there and calmed it down a little bit," he offered after the game. But his lack of defensive awareness and acumen is the biggest problem. As to blowing another late lead: “It was just a poor job by me, and that's what it was.”
Been that way all year, and the brutal second-half splits must make everyone question everything inside The Castle. That is why Minter is perceived by execs around the NFL as having to be on the hot seat. That is why his job security is already rightfully being questioned. This is a total mess, and the Ravens need a total rebuild, and Lamar quite reasonably may not want to stick around for it .
This staff can only show up for half a game, on both sides of the ball. That will get you exposed every week and will likely send the Ravens to the bye off seven straight losses (only happened once before here; 2007, which got Super Bowl winning head coach Brian Billick fired).
Here are the Ravens’ rankings in the second half:
169 Points Allowed : 2nd Most NFL (DAL)
71 Points Scored: 2nd Fewest NFL (PHI)
-98 Points Differential: Worst in NFL
Held 6 10+ Leads : Blow 5 (2-4)
The offense has plenty of excuses – no Jackson, a terrible offensive line that changes by the week, other injuries. Not the defense. All the major assets were put into that side of the ball – despite Minter (supposedly) being able to do more with less (he did with Chargers as simply a play caller under a strong-willed head coach with very streamlined duties).
Minter’s unit has been healthy, he proclaimed Hendrickson’s early-season finger surgery to be a springboard to dominance ( failing pressure rate since ) and he got elite defensive tackle Nnamdi Madubuike back for major neck surgery; turns out former DC Zach Orr did an infinitely better job with a lesser roster without Madubuike last season than Minter could dream of doing this season.
Here are the second -half defensive rankings:
Net Yards/Pass: 7.8/att. (28th)
Opposing Passer Rating : 112.9 (30th)
Completion %: 72.1% (31st)
Pass Yards: 1405 yds (30th)
Plays Allowed 20+ yds : 21 (25th)
Pressure Rate : 35.3% press (21st)
And in the last two weeks, with teams finally seeking volume on the ground against Minter’s defense, the Chargers and Panthers rolled up over 300 yards rushing. Expect more of the same as the weather turns and teams find more and more ways to exploit this coaching staff, and certainly not fewer.
Jason has covered sports professionally for newspapers, websites and broadcast networks since 1996 and have covered the NFL extensively for The Washington Post, CBS Sports and The NFL Network from 2004-2025.

title: By Ravens' Standards, Jesse Minter's Defense Is Historically Bad. Bottom 3 And Sinking
full_text:
Part of what made Jesse Minter such an irresistible choice for Ravens general manager and team president Sashi Brown, besides him being a newbie and incredibly malleable and willing to work cheap, was his deep ties to this organization.
He had worked here as a very young assistant on defense, under Wink Martindale (who isn’t shy about detailing DeCosta’s role in this franchise’s collapse ), and understood the loftiest of standards set for Baltimore on defense. Minter had mastered the fabric and schemes of the past that would allow him to erase the many mistakes of former coordinator Zach Orr (who, what do you know, was a superior coach of this defense than Minter has proven to be).
DeCosta and Brown and owner Steve Bisciotti bathed themselves in their past and claimed Minter as one of their own and anointed him capable of leading the franchise to the Super Bowl in his first year here – despite a staff of relatives, neophytes and college buddies – because it was potential Hall of Fame head coach John Harbaugh and his expensive staff there holding this roster and this franchise back. That's the parable they pushed.
So, one can assume, nothing laid out in this article could surprise Minter, an expert on the Ravens’ defensive history who already has a uniquely bleak place in it and is making a strong case to be fired after one year on the job, with Sunday’s debacle to the Panthers the latest example of how ill-equipped he appears to run an NFL defense at this point, let alone an entire team. He can’t manage personnel on special teams, he can’t manage timeouts and he is commanding one of the most embarrassing defenses in the history of this franchise.
The Panthers created explosive plays against Minter like everyone else does, and when they needed a late drive for a field goal to take a 35-33 lead, of course they got it. It's time for Anthony Weaver, or someone else, to call plays.
"I'm the head coach, and I'm calling the plays on defense," Minter said in asking for blame (though also deflected plenty to the offense and special teams when his D is the culprit. Here’s who bad this defense, through its first 11 games, ranks with every other in Ravens history.
Minter has already allowed 294 points. Only two teams in franchise history have allowed more in 11 games; the 1996 team that had just relocated from Cleveland, was scrambling and had most of the resources in the offensive side of the ball. The other was 2007, a team that totally fell apart, looked a lot like this one, and got Brian Billick, the first Super Bowl winning coach in franchise history, fired.
That 2007 team also lost six straight games, with Minter’s team becoming just the third in franchise history to do so a mere 11 games in. That 2007 team – a coach killer, forcing Bisciotti into action for the first time – lost nine in a row, a franchise low. Minter’s outfit, overseen by a front office that is becoming a laughingstock (the Daniel Jones pursuit is a chef’s kiss ), seems quite capable of that and might not win again.
Minter’s Ravens have the third-worst point differential (-52) through 11 games in franchise history.
Minter’s defense is truly horrific and broken in the second half, where the lack of adjustments and tactical shifts have utterly undermined any chance to win and led them to blow a double-digit lead for the fifth time this season (they lost four of those games, continuing the nastiest of trades that dates back to DeCosta taking over for legendary GM Ozzie Newsome). But in its totality, this pass defense has been a joke.
Minter is supposed to have the secret sauce like former Ravens coordinator Mike Macdonald to win up front with light boxes and flood the quadrants of the field where the QB is most likely to pass with willing defenders. Worked with the Chargers; been a disaster here. he has a team-record $160M defensive payroll and none of his big-money players is having a strong season.
The Ravens, despite facing pedestrian-or-worse QBs (like Bryce Young Sunday), have allowed an opposing QB rating of 96.6 – that’s third worst through 11 games in franchise history. They not only do not get any plays on the ball – TJ Tampa registered their first interception by a corner all season on Sunday – but they can’t even prevent big plays despite teams pushing the ball downfield on them.
Opposing QBs are completing 66% of their passes (third worst through 11 games). They have just 22 sacks – a grand total of two from alleged season-changing “closer” Trey Hendrickson HYPR EX – which is fifth lowest in Ravens history through this point in the season. Ten total takeaways for a mastermind coordinator who was going to put players in pristine position is damning.
Sunday was the same typical garbage – middle of field wide open, no one defending the slot – and Minter had no answers for it. He tried putting Kyle Hamilton back deeper in coverage and he gave up a 35-yard pass and did nothing on the football.
Young was 14/18 for 143 yds with a TD (118.3 rating) throwing to the middle of the field and 12/14 for 146 yds (110.1 rating) throwing to the slot. It’s no coincidence that Minter’s operation has so much in common with the 1996 edition that was just trying to get through the relocation and the one that cost Billick his job.
It merits a similar outcome.
Jason has covered sports professionally for newspapers, websites and broadcast networks since 1996 and have covered the NFL extensively for The Washington Post, CBS Sports and The NFL Network from 2004-2025.

title: Jesse Minter Exposed Again In Ravens' Sixth-Straight Loss: Key Takeaways From Another Debacle
full_text:
The Ravens season was summed up in one stretch of the first half of this game.
Their inability to seize the moment, their predilection for undermining their own success, and the utter cluelessness of this novice coaching staff far too often (in this case not making obvious adjustments on defense and special teams) dooms them week after week, and their failure to take a commanding lead caught up to them again.
The Ravens lost their sixth straight game – something that’s happened in one season only twice prior in franchise history – despite a fast start in a 35-33 defeat to the Panthers in Carolina. Rookie head coach Jesse Minter is making a compelling case for his staff being fired after one season on the job , general manager Eric DeCosta is getting ridiculed around the NFL (with a failed attempt to land broken QB Daniel Jones the latest head scratcher - and this team (4-7) might not win another game.
Lamar Jackson is not coming back to save them, this season or maybe ever again , and one sequence in this game summed up the Jesse Minter Experience (he's allowed 33 points or more in four of the last five games):
In the span of around three minutes of play, with the Ravens holding an early 12-7 lead after getting a safety early and an explosive touchdown off a flea flicker, things got weird, the Panthers were able to keep this a close game, and that did not bode well for the worst second-half team in the NFL.
Justice Hill was about to finish a long run for a touchdown when the ball was punched out of his hands at the two and rolled out of the endzone for a touchback and a turnover. The defense forced a rare three-and-out, and then struggling return man LaJohntay Wester muffed the punt for another turnover. Carolina scored almost immediately, then Devontez Walker returned the ensuing kickoff for a TD, and a 19-14 lead, but the defense would get rolled the rest of the way in another embarrassing outing for that horrible unit.
Back-up quarterback Jacoby Brissett (276 passing yards with a TD) was once again better than anyone could have expected, but it wasn’t enough to buck this season collapsing, with another Derrick Henry fourth-down fumble contributing to this latest debacle (he scored a late TD and hit the back of his head hard, checked for a concussion).
When Minter needed a stop late, his unit gave up a field goal, same as it ever was. He should be running out of time for a team that billed itself as a top Lombardi Trophy contender.
"At the end of the day we're on the field with the lead and we didn't hold it," Minter said. "So I take responsibility for that."
Minter sells out to take away big plays yet still gets exposed and unmask every week – mostly be pedestrian offenses – despite all his efforts. The Panthers' attack was fueled by big plays. Their first scoring drive featured consecutive big plays, Carolina had 10 plays of 10 yards or more through three quarters and four of 25 yards or more – it’s been obvious for weeks Minter needs to relinquish defensive play calling duties and perhaps this will cement it.
Receiver Jalen Coker beat Kyle Hamilton in coverage on an underthrown ball for 35 yards and flea flicker for 25 yards on the next play produced a TD and cut Baltimore’s lead to 12-7. Bryce Young came out firing in the second half with big shots to Tet McMillan and Darren Waller and only an interception by TJ Tampa (first by a Ravens corner all season) in the endzone, with excellent job trailing McMillan, kept this from getting out of hand sooner. It was bad on the ground too (more on that below).
"I'm the head coach and I'm calling the plays on defense," Minter said, repeatedly putting the onus on himself in his post-game remarks.
"I really don't know what to say at this point, honestly," said linebacker/safety Hamilton, who played more coverage in this game with little positive impact.
On the bright side, Mike Green continues to flash breakout pass-rush impact.
Every unit has been bad for long stretches of this season and special teams was brutal Sunday, even with Devontez Walker taking a kick return back for a touchdown.
If this coaching staff had a clue, Wester would have been benched after muffing a punt early in the game. He had made no impact since being drafted and doesn’t field the ball cleanly often enough and even after swinging the game in that regard, with a turnover, he wasn’t done. Wester totally misplayed another punt at the end of the first half; it bounced off his helmet and was nearly a scoop-and-score for Carolina.
Baltimore recovered at the 2, but it cost precious field position and the Ravens ended up stalling at midfield.
But the rot went beyond that. The Ravens kept giving up big returns on kick coverage units. Rookie Ethan Burke had a bad penalty on teams late in the first half. And their specialists have been an issue on and off all season.
The one thing this defense clung to was that it looked okay against the run. Of course, they haven’t faced many teams all season that can run the ball. And they entered Week 10 having been among the least run on defenses in the NFL. OF course, that changed with the Chargers churning them up and down the field for 160 yards and the Panthers picked up where LA left off.
Without top defensive tackle Nnamdi Madubuike, and with $60M “closer” Trey Hendrickson (two sacks all season; just three pressures Sunday) bad against the run the Panthers believed they could run the ball off the edge and up the middle and they were correct, especially as they shifted in not more 12 personnel (multiple tight ends) in the second quarter. They were able to key both Chuba Hubbard and Travis Etienne sprung for big runs in critical spots, and this is yet another hole Minter – totally overmatched to this point – is going to have to try to fix on the fly.
Hubbard came out of the half with a seven-yard burst and then again gutted Baltimore up the middle for 26 yards and he finished the drive with an easy, two-yard touchdown to cap the drive and five the Panthers a 29-26 lead.
Teams will absolutely be attacking Baltimore on the ground as weather becomes a factor and the Ravens do not have any more dome games or warm-weather road games, so buckle up. Carolina’s backs ran 14 times for 79 yards in the first half; Hubbard had a 19-yard TD blast off left tackle and Etienne took a carry inside the tackles for 18.
Carolina finished with 149 rushing yards and Hubbard had 120 himself.
The Ravens offensive line was embarrassed Monday night in every aspect of play. And no rushing yards in the first half and 15 carries for 16 yards in that game led to quite the inquiry leading up to this game.
The run blocking was much improved, the Ravens got Henry going on outside for the first time in weeks and struggling offensive coordinator Declan Doyle leaned into many of the tweaks we suggested – more Zay Flowers deception behind the line of scrimmage, more inside sprint plays for Hill, and more screens all around.
The Ravens had 12 carries for 116 yards in the first half, Brissett was able to crank up the play-action passing off of those looks and this was a truly balanced offense for the first time since Jackson was injured at the end of the first half in Week 4.
Henry finished with 94 rushing yards (7.2 yards/carry) and Hill added 90 scrimmage yards.
Doyle has no answers in the second half of games, once he gets beyond his early scripts.
The razzle-dazzle that worked early in the game fell flat after the half, he didn’t lean into the run game enough that had established itself in the early going and this team didn’t register a first down in the third quarter until just before it expired.
Baltimore hadn’t led at all in three games entering this, and the lack of adjustments in-game have been staggering. The Ravens entered this game having scored the second fewest points in the NFL after the half (64) and during the five-game slide their second-half scoring amounted to: 10, 7, 3, 0, 0. They managed seven points Sunday after…

title: Four Pivotal Ravens Matchups to Watch vs. Panthers
full_text:
The Baltimore Ravens' Week 11 bout against the Carolina Panthers could ultimately be decided by battles between specific position groups or individual players outperforming their counterparts on the other side of the ball.
In the team's second game with journeyman veteran Jacoby Brissett at center after he nearly led them to a comeback win in his first, they're entering this matchup as understandable underdogs following last week's inexcusable loss to the previously winless Los Angeles Chargers .
If the Ravens prevail, they will improve to 5-6 and will still be in last place in the AFC North standings since they're the only team without a division win. Here are the four matchups that can either make or break this game:
With four-time Pro Bowler Marlon Humphrey deactivated for this game , the Ravens will be going up against the talented wideout tandem of Tetairoa McMillan and Jalen Coker without one of their top playmaking corners. They still have their No. 1 player at the position in third-year pro Nate Wiggins, and playing opposite him on the perimeter will be a two-man rotation of 10-year veteran Chidobe Awuzie and third-year pro T.J. Tampa , a young player who fans and pundits have been clamoring to see more of for weeks.
The Ravens' third-year pro and starting right tackle will go up against the reigning NFC Defensive Player of the Week, who primarily lines up at SAM. In his first game back from injury since Week 6, Phillips was an absolute menace off the edge for the Panthers, recording five total tackles, including four solos and three for a loss, a strip-sack, and a fumble recovery. Rosengarten is coming off a rough game in pass protection in which he allowed a team-high six pressures, according to Pro Football Focus , so he'll have his hands full again and will need to step his game up to help keep Brissett upright more often than not.
While the Ravens aren't going up against one of the top overall rushing attacks in the league in this game, they are tasked with trying to limit one of its best and most dynamic running backs. Hubbard leads the Panthers and ranks eighth in the NFL with 711 rushing yards and ranks ninth among all players in both scrimmage yards (958) and touchdowns (nine). This means the Ravens' off-ball linebacker trio of Roquan Smith, Trenton Simpson and Teddye Buchanan could find themselves matched up with the six-year veteran in the hole at the line of scrimmage, in coverage out in space, or in the backfield on a blitz pickup, and will need to make plays in all three instances to excel in this game.
Carolina has been Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde when it comes to defending the opposing team's rushing attacks this year. Against poor running games, they are stout and have held five of their nine opponents to under 100 rushing yards, but in the other four games when they've faced more potent rushing offenses, they've allowed over 250 yards on the ground twice and an average of 209.5.
The Ravens' ground game without Lamar Jackson has been anything but prolific in all but one of the six games he's missed, especially during this current skid, when they've averaged just 86.8 rushing yards a game. However, if offensive coordinator Declan Doyle and his much-maligned offensive line can find a way to establish the run with any sort of consistency, five-time Pro Bowl running back Derrick Henry could do some serious damage and take a lot of the onus from Brissett to have to put the entire offense on his back again in just his second start for the team.

title: How Has Bills' Defensive Coordinator Jim Leonhard Fared vs. Patrick Mahomes, Chiefs?
full_text:
The 9-1 Buffalo Bills face a huge test on Thanksgiving as they host the 8-2 Kansas City Chiefs. The Week 12 matchup looms large over the AFC playoff picture as the Bills look to hold onto the No. 1 seed while Kansas City aims to knock them down a peg.
Buffalo is coming in on a hot streak, especially on defense. First-year defensive coordinator Jim Leonhard had some growing pains early in the season, but his unit has not allowed a touchdown in three weeks. That's somewhat misleading since the Bills have been facing backup quarterbacks and struggling teams, making this game a major measuring stick for Leonhard.
One advantage Buffalo could have in this one is the familiarity that Leonhard has against Patrick Mahomes and the Chiefs after spending two years as a divisional rival with the Denver Broncos.
Leonhard, who was the defensive backs coach and pass game coordinator in Denver, first faced Mahomes and the Chiefs in Week 10 of the 2024 season. They held the Chiefs to just 16 points, with Mahomes going 28-of-42 for 266 yards with one touchdown and no interception.
That's the type of performance any team would take from its defense, but it wasn't enough to get the win. Denver managed just 14 points with rookie Bo Nix under center. The Chiefs improved to 9-0 with that win, and ironically, the Bills handed them their first loss the following week.
The second time that Leonhard faced the Chiefs, the Broncos won easily 38-0. Kansas City was held to 71 net passing yards, but they weren't exactly trying. The Chiefs already had 15 wins and were starting Carson Wentz, who was just 10-of-17 for 98 yards and was sacked four times.
In his second season with Denver, Leonhard helped lead his team to two victories. The first was against Mahomes in Week 11. The Broncos won 22-19 as Mahomes went 29-of-45 for 276 yards with one touchdown and one interception. They played again in Week 17, with Denver winning once again, this time 20-13. Mahomes missed that game after tearing his ACL in Week 15, and Leonhard and the Denver defense (led by defensive coordinator Vance Joseph) shut down Chris Oladokun, who had 66 passing yards.
So while Leonhard's sample size against Mahomes is minimal, he helped keep him from lighting up the scoreboard. Kansas City never hit 20 points against Leonhard, and had just 35 in two games with Mahomes. Overall, Leonhard was 3-1 against the Chiefs and 1-1 against Mahomes, which should give Buffalo hope that he can find success on Thanksgiving Day.

title: Bills Defense Catches Break as Chiefs Rule Out Super Bowl MVP in Week 12
full_text:
For the first time ever, the Buffalo Bills will be at home for a Thanksgiving Day game . Not only will all eyes be on them this weekend because they’re playing on a holiday, but also because of the importance of this matchup.
The 9-1 Bills will host the 8-2 Kansas City Chiefs as two AFC juggernauts square off in Week 12. Both teams have been playing well over the past few weeks, even if the recent level of competition for both franchises has left something to be desired.
Of course, no team can control who is on the schedule. All they can do is take care of their opponents, and both have done that. The Bills have been especially impressive, as their defense hasn’t surrendered a touchdown in three games. While the Chiefs have the talent to end that streak, they will have to do so without one of their best players.
On Wednesday, the Chiefs officially ruled out running back Kenneth Walker III , who has been dealing with a groin injury and missed the past two games as well.
That means Buffalo’s defense, led by first-year defensive coordinator Jim Leonhard, won’t have to deal with the reigning Super Bowl MVP. Walker, who won the award last year while helping the Seattle Seahawks capture a Super Bowl title, signed a three-year $43.05 million deal with the Chiefs.
That’s a rich contract for any running back, but Walker has lived up to the deal. Walker has 1,044 yards from scrimmage and 11 total touchdowns in eight games for the Chiefs. He’s an explosive back, and his absence will be felt, especially in a game where the weather will be a factor and both teams might lean heavily on the ground game.
While Walker being out will make a difference, the Bills can’t breathe too easy. With Walker sidelined for the past two games, rookie Emmett Johnson has become a breakout star.
A fifth-round pick out of Nebraska, Johnson has started the past two games and topped 100 rushing yards in each. In all, he has 206 yards and one touchdown on 45 carries. He’s also proven to be a weapon as a pass-catcher with 10 receptions for 108 yards and two more touchdowns.
Buffalo will need to be worried about Johnson, but the good news is that they won’t have to worry about Johnson and Walker on Thursday night.

title: Three Bills' Emergency QB Options Currently Available on NFL Free-Agent Market
full_text:
The Buffalo Bills have no third-quarterback option standing by this week.
With the Indianapolis Colts signing Shane Buechele off the Bills' practice squad and onto their active roster on Tuesday, the QB room is down to two members in Orchard Park.
While the Bills seemingly prefer to roll with only two field generals on their 53-man roster, one would think they'll look to add some company for starter Josh Allen and backup Kyle Allen over the mini bye that follows Thursday night's holiday home game against the Kansas City Chiefs.
After the November 26 primetime appearance, Buffalo is off until December 6 against the New England Patriots.
With a highly-important game to prepare for on a short week, the Bills will have to settle for an emergency QB option such as tight end Dawson Knox or third-down running back Ty Johnson. Punter Tommy Doman showed his ability to sling the rock in Week 11.
As for who Buffalo could bring in next Monday, here are three available options. Note that with the Bills presumably unwilling to dedicate a third roster spot to an emergency QB, their option are limited to current street free agents. One can only permissibly claim a player off another team's practice squad by subsequently guaranteeing an active roster contract for said player.
Adding a former first-round pick with playoff experience to the quarterbacks room can't be a bad thing, right?
Jones, who won a 2022 playoff game with the New York Giants under then-head coach Brian Daboll, may want to go to a team where he can play right away as opposed to sitting on the Bills' practice squad, but it's worth a call.
In his second season with the Indianapolis Colts, Jones made 11 starts before being released after last Thursday's 26-3 loss to the Houston Texans.
After going 8-5 as Indy's starter in 2025, he was 3-8 this year. Completing fewer than 60 percent of passes, Jones accounted for only seven touchdown passes while being intercepted 13 times.
What's better than two Allens? Well, three obviously.
While the Bills shouldn't make a move based upon the potential of marketing three quarterbacks with the same last name, adding Allen to the practice squad seems to have some merit. After all, the 34-year-old has started games for three different franchises since entering the NFL as a 2016 sixth-round pick.
Allen elected free agency after spending the 2025 season with the Tennessee Titans, subsequently signing with the New York Giants in April. Over three preseason appearances, he went 26-of-38 passing for 224 yards and two interceptions.
The Giants released him on cutdown day. He played one game for Tennessee in 2025.
Zappe last played a NFL regular season game in 2024 for Cleveland Browns, but he's another free agent with starting experience. He spent the 2025 campaign on Cleveland's practice squad before landing with the New York Jets this past offseason.
The Jets released Zappe after training camp. He landed on their practice squad before being cut loose on September 22. Over three preseason appearances for Gang Green, the 2022 fourth-round pick went 14-of-23 passing for 135 yards and two interceptions.
The 27-year-old Zappe, who was drafted by the New England Patriots, has also spent time with the Kansas City Chiefs.

title: Three Key Areas Where Bills-Chiefs Outcome May Be Decided on Thanksgiving
full_text:
Although the NFL schedule is chock-full of quality holiday games on Thursday, there may be no other matchup more intriguing than the primetime meeting between the Buffalo Bills and Kansas City Chiefs at Highmark Stadium in Orchard Park.
With the Bills sitting atop the NFL at 9-1, and the Chiefs nipping at their heels with a record of 8-2, a lot is hinging on the results of the intraconference matchup . . . particularly when it pertains to Buffalo’s hopes of finally obtaining the No. 1 seed in the AFC, which is something that has eluded quarterback Josh Allen his entire professional career .
But, even though history indicates that Allen and Co. should fare well during the Thanksgiving matchup against Kansas City, coming away with a victory will likely be easier said than done as the AFC West squad will present plenty of roadblocks for Buffalo along the way .
Keeping that in mind, here are three key areas that will likely play a role in determining the final outcome between the two powerhouses.
During this past Sunday’s CBS broadcast, it was mentioned more than once how Bills’ first-year head coach Joe Brady was adamant about sticking with the run game even before the weather starts turning for the worse in December and January.
And, so far it’s proven to be a quality recipe for success for Brady and Co. through 10 games, but whether or not it will remain that way Thursday night against Kansas City is a big question mark.
The Chiefs currently boast the league’s eighth-best defense overall in terms of yards allowed per game (314.8 ), and they’re also ranked 11th against the run at 97.8 yards allowed per game.
So, although Buffalo will undoubtedly hope to get things going on the ground with James Cook III against Kansas City, especially if the less-than-ideal weather report turns out to be true, it will take yet another valiant effort from Cook and the Bills’ offensive line up front in order to persevere in primetime.
Ultimately, this is the toughest test Buffalo’s rushing attack has faced since Week 8 when the team squared off against the Baltimore Ravens (13th, 105.9 YPG), as the Miami Dolphins (18th, 118.4 YPG), New York Jets (30th, 135.3 YPG), and Minnesota Vikings (17th, 111.9 YPG) are all ranked in the bottom half of the NFL when it comes to defending the run.
Since coming out of the bye week against Baltimore, Buffalo’s offense has converted on just 37.3% of its third-down attempts in its last four outings despite facing a couple teams that have bottom-half-of-league defenses statistically in that critical category like the Jets (18th, 40.5%) and Dolphins (28th, 45.8%) over the last two weeks.
And, keeping that in mind, the Bills can’t always rely on Josh Allen’s legs or brute strength in short-yardage situations, especially if he refuses to run at all like he did against Miami last Sunday. They'll need to be more efficient in the passing game.
At the moment, Buffalo is living dangerously in terms of counting too much on fourth-down conversions throughout the course of a game, and it could eventually come back to bite them . . . if not now, then maybe in the playoffs.
With that said, the team from Western New York will be presented with quite the challenge against Kansas City on Thursday as defensive coordinator Steve Spagnuolo’s unit is ranked 10th in the NFL for third-down conversions allowed at a rate of just 36% through 10 games.
This will undoubtedly be a huge factor in the matchup for the “Brady Bunch” of Buffalo.
At least from afar, Kansas City’s longtime veteran tight end Travis Kelce seemed to be at a bit of a crossroads this offseason regarding whether or not he would return for another ride around the NFL carousel in 2026.
Now, however, it’s looking as if Kelce might want to think about returning once again next year as he’s currently leading the Chiefs in receiving entering Thursday’s matchup.
In fact, through November this fall, the 14th-year veteran is on pace to top his single-season outputs (984 yds in ‘23; 823 yds in ‘24; 851 yds in ‘25) from each of previous three years as Kelce has recorded 41 receptions for 586 yards and four touchdowns in 10 games so far this year.
And, it appears he’s only heating up, as the 37-year-old has recorded at least four receptions in five of the last six games while also eclipsing the 50-yard mark in four of those matchups.
Last week, Kelce tallied six catches on seven targets for 74 yards and two touchdowns in Kansas City’s 34-7 victory over the Arizona Cardinals.
So, with that in mind, there’s no denying that the Bills’ linebackers and safeties—like recently-acquired defensive back Amani Hooker —must be aware of where the 6-foot-5, 250-pound playmaker is at all times.
“I mean, yeah, he’s one of the greatest of all time, right? You know . . . he’ll have a gold jacket whenever he’s done playing. So, I mean, he’s revolutionized the tight-end position. Like, everybody studies him—the way that he runs routes, the feel for the game—the comparisons forever (from anywhere) is going to be compared to Travis Kelce,” Bills’ first-year head coach Joe Brady said at One Bills Drive on Tuesday.
“And, he’s not slowing down. . . . So, as always—when you play the Kansas City Chiefs—you’ve got to know where Travis Kelce is at all times.”

title: Bills' Updated Injury Report (Chiefs Week): Greg Rousseau, Two More Starters Upgraded
full_text:
The Buffalo Bills are slowly regaining full health in Week 12.
The Bills listed 14 players on the initial official injury report , but there's a scenario where all of them are available to face the Kansas City Chiefs in a Thanksgiving night special on November 26 in Orchard Park.
During Tuesday's walkthrough practice, nine of the 14 injured parties were designated as full participants. The five others were all present, but limited.
"I know it's walkthrough today, but everybody will be out there today. We'll kind of just continue to evaluate it through Thursday. Obviously, not practicing today, but everybody seems like they're in as good of a place as we can be right now," said Bills' head coach Joe Brady .
There are three recently-added starters and three key holdovers who warrant close watching with their availability for Thursday somewhat in question.
Right tackle Spencer Brown, right guard O'Cyrus Torrence and outside linebacker Greg Rousseau popped up on the injury report this week coming out of the November 22 win over the Miami Dolphins.
Brown and Rousseau took a leap forward on Tuesday, progressing from limited to full participation. Torrence, however, remained limited.
Brown, who appeared in the clear last week, is back on the injury report due to another back flare-up. The right tackle was forced out of the October 12 road game after 16 snaps due to the issue. He returned for the October 18 game against the Las Vegas Raiders, only to sit again on November 1 coming out of the Week 7 bye.
On Sunday against the Dolphins, Brown played every snap except the final kneel down. He spoke to reporters from the podium after Tuesday's practice, and he didn't give any indication that his Thursday availability could be in question.
Rousseau, who apparently tweaked his back, reached double-digits sack during the November 22 win, matching Bradley Chubb for most defensive snaps (34) by a Bills' edge rushers. He addressed reporters in the locker room postgame, and didn't appear to be in any noticeable discomfort.
Torrence also played all but the final snap on Sunday against Miami. It's not known exactly when his ankle injury occurred, but it doesn't seem to be of great severity. It's also worth mentioning that Torrence has never missed a start.
Cornerback Christian Benford, inside linebacker Dorian Williams and tight end Dalton Kincaid were all scratched from the November 22 game day lineup due to injuries that occurred during the Week 10 win over the Jets.
All three were deemed limited participants on Tuesday.
For Benford, who is dealing with a groin issue, the designation represents an important upgrade. After not practicing in Week 11, the starting outside cornerback was listed as a non-participant again on Monday.
While his return to the practice field is encouraging, the Bills and Benford are taking a day-by-day approach. It may be overly optimistic, however, to expect him ready to go only 11 days after going down.
Williams is dealing with a calf injury that sidelined him for the fourth quarter against the Jets on November 15. Fourth-round rookie Kaleb Elarms-Orr started in his place in Week 11 . He seems to be a little further along than Benford at this point.
Kincaid's major issue is the thumb that got tangled up when the tight end briefly engaged with Jets' linebacker Demario Davis on a third-quarter red zone play in Week 10. He did not practice in Week 11, earning a doubtful tag for the Dolphins game .
Back-to-back limited statuses are encouraging that Kincaid will be able to play through the injury on Thursday. On Tuesday, he told reporters that he should be out there on Thanksgiving.

title: What is Buffalo Bills' All-Time Thanksgiving Record With Next Chapter vs. Chiefs?
full_text:
Thanksgiving and football go hand in hand, and the Buffalo Bills are set to close out this year's holiday triple-header.
Thursday won't be the first time the Bills have played on Thanksgiving, but it will make some history for the franchise. Buffalo has appeared in 11 Thanksgiving Day games, but they have always been the road team. That changes this week when they host the Kansas City Chiefs on Thursday night in Week 12 .
Both teams enter this game with exceptional records as they fight for position in the AFC playoff race . The 9-1 Bills have had a rather easy schedule as of late, facing multiple backup quarterbacks in recent weeks.
While that's gotten a lot of attention, the 7-2 Chiefs haven't been tested since their two-game losing streak in Week 7 and Week 8 to the Denver Broncos and Seattle Seahawks. Since those losses, they have defeated the New York Jets, Atlanta Falcons, and Arizona Cardinals. It's going to be a massive showdown that will have postseason implications.
The upcoming game itself will be broken down plenty of times ahead of Thursday, but for now, let's take a trip down memory lane and see how Buffalo has fared during its previous appearances on Thanksgiving.
Thursday will be the 12th time the Bills have been featured on Turkey Day and they've fared well overall. Their record on the holiday is 6-4-1, but more importantly, they've had a lot of success as of late.
Buffalo has won their past three games on Thanksgiving, giving them a 3-0 record with Josh Allen. That includes a 28-25 victory in 2022 against the Detroit Lions, which went down to the wire as Tyler Bass hit a 45-yard field goal with two seconds remaining to seal the win. Before that, they knocked off the New Orleans Saints in a lopsided 31-6 win in 2021 and defeated the Dallas Cowboys 26-15 in 2019.
That game was interesting as well with Cole Beasley making life miserable for his former team. The always trustworthy slot receiver had six receptions for 110 yards and a touchdown against the Cowboys.
Another game of note was back in 1976 when the Bills lost to the Lions, but O.J. Simpson set an NFL single-game rushing record with 273 yards. That total has since been surpassed, but it was incredibly significant at the time and remains the most in franchise history.
Here's a full list of every Thanksgiving game the Bills have played in:
2022 vs. Detroit Lions: Win, 28-25 2021 vs. New Orleans Saints: Win, 31-6 2019 vs. Dallas Cowboys: Win, 26-15 1994 vs. Detroit Lions: Loss, 21-35 1976 vs. Detroit Lions: Loss, 14-27 1975 vs. St. Louis Cardinals: Win, 32-14 1968 vs. Oakland Raiders: Loss, 10-13 1966 vs. Oakland Raiders: Win, 31-10 1965 vs. San Diego Chargers: Tie, 20-20 1964 vs. San Diego Chargers: Win, 27-24 1961 vs. New York Titans: Loss, 14-21
Before the victory over Dallas, the Bills had not been featured on Thanksgiving since the 1994 season. Prior to that, it had been since the 1970s. Now, they've become more of a fixture with this being their fourth appearance since 2019.
