title: Jaguars Week 11 Snap Count Analysis: Bhayshul Tuten's Injury Demands Solutions
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The Jacksonville Jaguars have some questions to answer after arguably their worst loss of the season.
The Jaguars fell to the New York Giants 23-18 in one of the sloppiest games the Jaguars have played in the Liam Coen era, racking up penalties and self-inflicted mistakes at an unsustainable rate. The Jaguars still sit at 7-3, but this game clearly could have, and should have, played out differently.
"Clearly, not prepared well enough as we have been, maybe had too many things in, moving parts," Coen said after the game. "That's a direct reflection of me, and making sure that these guys are prepared well enough. We had been prepared in the majority of our football games, I felt like, and that did not show tonight, especially early on. I put that directly on me."
What could the Jaguars have done differently in the tough road loss? We take a look at some of the Jaguars' snap counts to try to find some of those answers.
It is clear the Jaguars are not getting the same version of Bhayshul Tuten that they were earlier in the season, and it is completely injury related. Tuten was one of the best and most productive running backs in football through the first eight weeks of the 2026 season, but a foot/ankle injury over the last three weeks have hurt his numbers and, as a result, hurt the rest of the offense that in many ways flows through the running game.
Tuten played his second-lowest snap count of the season with 31 snaps (43%), which saw Chris Rodriguez Jr. play 27 snaps (38%). But even with the snaps closer to a true 50/50 split this week than most others, Tuten still got a good bit more touches than Rodriguez, who finished the game with just four carries. Tuten left the game twice after getting stepped on, and it certainly seems like the Jaguars could reevaluate things.
“Yeah, we'll see. The recheck today wasn't too bad. Obviously got stepped on in the game a few times, I think twice on the same play, so that re-aggravated it for sure. So, we're definitely having some of those conversations," Coen said Monday.
"He's tough as nails. He wants to play. He wants to continue to fight and give us the best chance to be able to go. We'll have some more of those conversations and see what he looks like when he gets out there running around or moving around on Wednesday and Thursday. Let it play out throughout the week and knowing that he probably won't be able to do a ton for us like he hasn't been for the last few weeks in practice. So really it'll be a business as usual throughout the week for Tuten, and then we'll just kind of see where we're at towards the end of the week.”
The Jaguars have long leaned on Parker Washington as their punt returner, but there was a bit of a shift in that department on Sunday. Jaguars running back Ameer Abdullah played 10 special teams snaps on Sunday, but four of those snaps were as a punt returner. Abdullah had not returned a single punt for the Jaguars all season long until Sunday when he ended up returning four punts for 23 yards (5.8 yards per attempt), a change-up from Washington as punt returner.
Washington played zero special teams snaps for the first time since Week 17 in the 2024 season, meaning Sunday was the first time during the entire Liam Coen era that he was not a big piece of Heath Farwell's unit. This sure looks like a change that could stick, considering what Coen said when asked about Abdullah at the returner spot on Monday.
“Yeah, I think that obviously, as Parker [Washington] continues to ascend and doing really good things for us, just trying to limit some of the hits that he may take and some of the different game plan and meetings and things that he has to be involved in and have a lot of trust in Ameer," Coen said. "He's done it throughout the course of his career, did a great job last night of fielding them and giving us a chance. We didn't cover great. We didn't block it great. Didn't give him too many opportunities. I thought their punter did a phenomenal job flipping the field on a number of different occasions. I definitely see Ameer being able to do it for us moving forward.”
The Jaguars saw Jordan Davis (35 snaps, 50%) and Jessie Bates III (66 snaps, 94%) make their official Jaguars debuts, and the difference made by Davis at least was clear. The Giants averaged under 2.0 yards per carry when Davis was on the field and did not have a rush longer than five yards, giving him a clear impact made through his first day. Meanwhile, Bates played every snap but the few snaps when the Jaguars were in a goal line defense and had their heavy personnel on the field.
Davis played 52% of the snaps for the Eagles this year before the trade and his career-high was the 61% of snaps he played during the 2025 season, so him playing 50% of the snaps snaps in his debut made plenty of sense. Jaguars starting nose tackle Davon Hamilton played over 50% of the snaps just twice in six full games his season, and he hit the number just seven times in 17 games in 2025.
“Yeah, I thought both guys did their jobs well. I thought specifically Jordan and [DT] Davon Godchaux did some really good things up front in terms of allowing our second level guys to play freely. Our linebackers were free a lot in the run game. They disrupted some things," Coen said.
"I think Jessie just didn't have a ton of ops. Like there wasn't a lot of balls his way. He got kind of moved on the double move there that they ended up not hitting. But, nothing really stood out in terms of glaring negatives and nothing really stood out as like obviously big-time playmaking or anything that way. But fully anticipate those guys to be able to continue to help us, and they're going to make some plays for our team. I don’t doubt that whatsoever”

title: Jaguars' No. 1 Seed Hopes Just Took a Major Hit After Costly Giants Loss
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- There is still plenty of football left to be played in the 2026 season, but there is a good chance we look back at Week 11 as a missed oppurtunity by the Jaguars.
The Jaguars are still one of the AFC's top teams after a 23-18 loss to the New York Giants on Sunday, but the 7-3 Jaguars have bigger goals than winning the AFC South and simply being an above-.500 team.
But for the Jaguars to hit those goals, they will have to respond after their mistake-filled loss to the Giants . That response would have been needed regardless, but the pressure is up even more considering their current road toward a No. 1 seed in the AFC has had a few hurdles thrown up.
Week 11 was always set to be a tough week for the Jaguars when it came to how the AFC could shake out over the course of the second-half. Not only were the Jaguars set to play a division leader with a winning record on the road, but the Houston Texans had already won on Thursday Night Football and the Denver Broncos, Buffalo Bills, Kansas City Chiefs, and Cincinnati Bengals were all set to play teams with losing records.
The Bengals have not played the Washington Commanders as of this writing, but the other teams fighting for the No. 1 seed went 3-0 without breaking much of a sweat. If the season ended today, the Jaguars would be the No. 4 seed. According to The Athletic's playoff simulator, the Jaguars now have a 44% of being the No. 4 seed, a 29% of being the No. 3 seed, a 17% chance of being the No. 2 seed, and just a 5% chance of being the No. 1 seed.
As things stand today, the Bills (42%), Broncos (23%), Chiefs (15%), and Bengals (15%) all have better chances of the No. 1 seed. This all can change with the matter of a few results here and there, but the Jaguars have three losses through 10 games. With seven games remaining, it stands to reason the Jaguars might have to win out to keep pace with the 9-1 Buffalo Bills and 8-2 Broncos, who own a tiebreaker over the Jaguars.
Considering the Jaguars still have to play the 8-2 Chicago Bears on the road, the Texans in Houston, and Dak Prescott in Dallas, that is a tall task. The Jaguars had a limited margin of error before the Giants loss, and that margin has now expired. That starts with the Jaguars finding a way to bounceback at home in Week 12 against the 1-9 Tennessee Titans.
"So a lot of this, in my opinion, for us is going to be about just settling back down, regathering, coming back with our play style, getting back to being physical in all three phases. You know, we got outplayed and outcoached in all three phases, and so when that occurs, well, you go back to basics" Liam Coen said on Monday.
"You go back to fundamentals, you go back to the simplicity of things to allow the players to go play freely, to go be able to communicate everything that they're seeing. And so much of that goes back to keep it simple and let the guys go play."
Jacksonville has plenty to play for and can go far places. The loss to the Giants doesn't change that, and it doesn't change the fact they are one of the teams in the AFC from top to bottom. But the Jaguars can not afford many more hiccups if they truly want to be the AFC's top team come January.

title: Shipley's Dozen: How Jaguars, Liam Coen Must Take Stock After Miserable Giants Loss
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- Few teams get into as many weird games as the Jacksonville Jaguars, and buddy was Sunday's game weird.
The Jaguars were not the better team in Week 11's 23-18 loss to the New York Giants, with the loss coming on the heels of the Jaguars losing at the line of scrimmage on offense and simply looking out of sorts compared to the Jaguars team we have gotten used to.
We break down all of our thoughts on the Jaguars' loss below in this week's Shipley's Dozen. A reminder that this column is released the day after each Jaguars contest.
Liam Coen has drawn some flak for two different decisions he made in the fourth-quarter: his decision to go for two while down eight points, and his decision to kick a field goal at the end of the game instead of going for it on 4th-and-8. The decisions will be panned in the wake of the loss, but the Jaguars and Coen made the right calls, I think. They just didn't get the other outcomes they needed.
The "Go for Two When Down 8" strategy seems like it happens every single week, and it always seems to also break the brains of half of the population. But the simple truth is Coen always goes for it in those scenarios, and he would have went for two later if he had even kicked the PAT. I would have made the same call, and this didn't impact the game's final result.
As for kicking it late, most models seem to have the call as a true coin flip in terms of winning probability, but it was 4th-and-8 with a third-string left tackle and Abdul Carter looking like Lawrence Taylor. If Foyesade Oluokun's finger reaches a half an inch higher on JJ McCarthy's second down pass on the following drive, this decision looks right. Trusting the defense, and not trusting the offense, made sense there.
There is not much to say about this that we haven't already said, but we will let Jevon Holland say it too:
Giants safety Jevon Holland on this play: "The game's over — that might have been a catch. That was a hell of a play. I thought he got his foot down, I was like, 'Damn.' But then they called it out and I was like, 'Shit, all right.' Shout-out Vegas. I don't know." https://t.co/Eid1ANMGOp
Jacksonville entered the season with seemingly an embarassment of riches at the offensive tackle spot, but they are hurting there right now. Anton Harrison is out for the year, Walker Little got hurt on Sunday and didn't return, and Cole Van Lanen had arguably his worst game of the last two seasons against the Giants' impressive group of pass-rushers. The Jaguars had to put Wyatt Milum at left tackle after Little's injury, which is not an ideal spot.
It remains to be seen how long Little will be out, but the offensive tackle depth is a big issue depending on the timeline. Patrick Mekari and Daniel Faalele are likely next up as potential options at left tackle, which does not seem like a spot the Jaguars will want to be in for games against the Bears and Texans next month.
The Jaguars were 1-for-6 when it came to converting red-zone trips into touchdowns, a number that is just not going to be able to deliver wins on a constant basis. The Jaguars saw the Giants go 2-for-3 in their own right, and this was the biggest difference in the game. If the Jaguars were able to make just two of these red-zone trips go their way on offense, then they would have been a much different ball game.
Why has the red-zone offense been so hit-and-miss? That remains to be seen. There are some issues ranging from penalties, to protection issues, to not converting on enough rushing attempts when near the goal-line. The Jaguars need to figure out these red-zone issues quickly, or else it will keep showing up in bigger and more important games that the Jaguars play down the road.
I think the Jaguars' defense was good on Sunday! I know they gave up 20 first-half points, but seven of those came on a ... questionable Montaric Brown DPI and then saw the Giants take four tries to score from inches away. Six more points were due to Trevor Lawrence interceptions. I knock the Jaguars' defense for allowing the other 10 points, but the numbers and tape show that, outside of a few J.J. McCarthy scrambles, the Jaguars shut down the running game and forced McCarthy to try to win the game with his arm. If the Jaguars' offense was even average on Sunday, this defensive effort would have led to a win. There is not much more to say about the defense other than the offense let them down.
"Yeah, I didn't think we played great early on. I thought they came out of the half. They got a drive. But after that, I mean, you get the fumble, I mean they gave us plenty of opportunities," Coen said after the game. "We didn't play complementary football, right? We turned it over, they scored points. We get turnovers, we didn't score points. I felt like you hold a team to 23 points in the National Football League, you should win some of those games."
Do the Jaguars have a Bhayshul Tuten problem? From my view, it is starting to look like it. Giving him 26 carries against the Tennessee Titans in a game they could have won without him a week ago makes little sense after seeing how bruised and battered he was by the end of Sunday's game, leaving it twice due to his injuries. The Jaguars have been going against the grain a bit when it comes to playing Tuten, but it is starting to feel like they have pushed the envelope too far.
Now that the Jaguars are entering the pivotal second-half stretch of their season, it is too late to change much. They need Tuten to get healthy, but the time to put him on ice was in Baltimore and Nashville. Now, the Jaguars are entering some important games with a pivotal player set to be at less than 100%.
The Jaguars had Jordan Davis play 35 snaps (50%) and Jessie Bates III play 66 snaps (94%) in their Jaguars debuts. Neither made a very big impact in terms of splash plays, which has since led to some hand-wringing about how aggressive the Jaguars were at the deadline. When you lose a game, that is what happens. But when going back to watch the tape, it sure seemed like Davis did his job against the run. He did a good job of freeing up other defenders, and the Jaguars' run defense was largely top-notch with him on the field. He provided nothing as a pass-rusher, but that is likely who he is going to be this season.
The lone spot of improvement for #Jaguars on Sunday was the run defense. After back-to-back poor weeks by their standards, they got back on track outside of a few McCarthy scrambles. With Jordan Davis on the field, Giants rushed 14 times for 23 yards. Jacksonville will need him
Bates seems like he is still working through some things on the back end of the defense, which makes sense considering his position. This was also a game where he wasn't tested much since J.J. McCarthy was incapable of hitting any deep passes, though. I see Bates making an impact much sooner rather than later.
Trevor Lawrence. We have seen Lawrence press when the offensive line struggles before, such as in Week 2 against the Denver Broncos. But Lawrence was straight-up irresponsible with the ball on Sunday, and with himself on one hit out of bounds while running. Lawrence holds the fate of the offense, and the team, in his hands each time he takes the snap, but Sunday saw him revert to too many pre-Coen era Lawrence tendencies. It is likely a blip, but it was a bad blip for certain. Sunday was Lawrence's fourth-worst game of the last two seasons in terms of EPA/Play, and there is no real excuse for some of the throws he made.
Abdul Carter taking this game over. The Jaguars have had issues against blue-chip pass-rushers time after time, and it is clearly a talent issue. I was not surprised in the least by Carter having the impact he had, even if I was a bit surprised that the Jaguars did not say screw it and start chipping him with tight ends and running backs from the jump. Carter has elite talent, and the Jaguars have not yet proven they can handle that.
There are a few different ways to go…

title: The NFL Won't Admit It Got Parker Washington's Touchdown Wrong, and That's the Problem
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The Jacksonville Jaguars lost to the New York Giants in Week 11 for a variety of reasons, but there is one play that has already struck the cord as the catalyst.
For the Jaguars, the Parker Washington non-touchdown call, both on the field and on review, was one of several key turning points of a tough, physical, and frankly weird game against the Giants. For most, it was the controversial call of the weekend.
But touchdown or not aside , there are bigger issues for the Jaguars after this loss. For the NFL, the issue has already become a moot point, which is the entire root of the problem.
When the officials first ruled Washington's catch incomplete, there was 12:26 left in the game and the Jaguars were trailing 20-6. Washington appeared to have gotten both feet down in bounds in the left corner of the end-zone before going out of the back of the end zone, but the play was ruled incomplete on the field after the officials discussed it on the field.
"I did not think he lost possession of the football... I think it's a touchdown, fellas." CBS rules analyst Gene Steratore disagreed with this being ruled incomplete after review on a potential Parker Washington TD for the Jaguars. 🏈🦓🎙️ pic.twitter.com/4RdlPYAYXQ
Jaguars head coach Liam Coen challenged the play, but the ruling was upheld on review and the Jaguars had to settle for a 31-yard Cam Little field goal and a 20-9 deficit. "I was told that the ball switched hands, so that was what it came down to," Coen said after the game.
NFL Vice President of Replay Mark Butterworth spoke to Pro Football Writers Association pool reporter Pat Leonard after the game, and here is what he had to say.
"The ruling on the field was an incomplete pass. First, to overturn a call, we need clear and obvious video evidence to overturn the on-field ruling. It was determined that the receiver did not gain full control of the ball until he was out of bounds. ... He needs to maintain control of the ball throughout the process of the catch."
It is clear when reviewing the play that, no matter how you slice it, Washington caught the pass. Just a few hours later there was a Mike Evans touchdown agains the Minnesota Vikings that defied everything Butterworth just said. There is no clear pattern on how the NFL rules catches, and it seems here they simply went with the original call on the field despite having the evidence to change it.
That is the NFL's motto when it comes to officiating issues, though. Catch or no catch has become as traditional in the NFL as tailgates and touchdown cellys. If the gut reaction to a clear catch is "let's see if they actually call it one," then the NFL has a problem with how they are ruling plays on a game-to-game basis.
But the NFL will not ever flat-out say they got it wrong. It is not the reason the Jaguars lost on Sunday; they have themselves to blame for that. And the NFL finally becoming accountable would not go back in time and give the Jaguars the points. But the fact they can not admit fault has become the biggest issue with such plays.
"Yeah, I mean, it's a close play, obviously. They called it and said it wasn't. I thought it was incredible that he gave us a shot there and he caught it. It looked like he had two feet down, but it was close, and you can't leave it in the ref's hands," Trevor Lawrence said post-game.
"I think it's a tough call for them. Even though that didn't go our way, we had so many opportunities that we just didn't capitalize on. So, we’ve got to keep playing the next play.
That wasn't the Jaguars' only odd sequence with the officials Sunday. There was also the replay assist debacle in the first-half, with the Jaguars having to use one of their challenges to overrule a Chris Rodriguez Jr. rush on third-down. Rodriguez was originally given the first down, but replay assist overruled it and changed it to fourth-and-short. Coen won the challenge, but the fact he had to use one of his limited challenges to correct a replay assist.
"For the first part, the ruling on the field was a first down. It was an improper replay assist to short of the line to gain. They thought the knee was down," Butterworth said. "The key here is even when we replay assist, that still allows teams to challenge in most circumstances if they don't agree with the replay assist. And when we went to challenge, it was clear and obvious that the runner's knee was up and he was, therefore, he made a first down and we awarded a successful challenge to the team."
That ... does not make much sense. Butterworth saying it was "an impropert replay assist," is as close as the NFL will likely ever get to saying they were wrong about a ruling. But he then goes on to defend replay assist by noting that teams can still challenge the play and, well, fix the wrong call made. The issue is that the Jaguars had to use one of their only challenges, and Coen doesn't just get that challenge back.
Head coaches are afforded two challenges each game. If they get both correct, then they get a third. Coen used all three during the game, winning the first two (including on a Malik Nabers catch in the first-half), before losing the Washington one. But what if there was a play worth challenging before the Washington catch? If Coen had challenged it, win or lose, he would not have been able to challenge the Washington play.
Even with the hindsight of Coen losing the Washington challenge, there is no coach in football who would not have thrown the red flag there. There are a number of scenarios where the Jaguars could have gotten burned by the league because of the replay assist challenge, and it never should have happened.
Will the NFL ever concede that? No, not likely. But that is the NFL's mode of operation when it comes to officiating. Right, wrong, or in between, they toe their company line and do not offer up accountability. This is not the first time a team has seen their games impacted by such mistakes, and the NFL's attitude means it also will not be the last.

title: Kenneth Walker Ruled Out for Thanksgiving Game: What It Means for the Chiefs
full_text:
For the third consecutive game, the Kansas City Chiefs will be rolling with a fifth-round rookie to lead the backfield. Star running back Kenneth Walker III was officially ruled out for Kansas City's Thanksgiving Day game vs. the Bills this morning due to a lingering groin injury . He has now missed three consecutive contests without a clear timetable for his recovery.
#Chiefs RB Kenneth Walker (groin) will be OUT for Thursday night’s game vs the Bills, per @Schultz_Report pic.twitter.com/rezzlryEp2
When Walker initially missed last week's game against the Cardinals, the expectation was that the team was holding him out to get some extra rest before Thanksgiving. However, it appears the turnaround was too quick to overcome. KC must lean on Johnson heavily once again.
In Walker's absence, Johnson has been nothing short of spectacular . The Nebraska product rushed for over 100 yards in both of his starts and found the end zone on three different occasions. Tomorrow's showdown will be a lot different, though, since the Bills have a much more formidable defense than Atlanta or Arizona. ESPN's Jeffri Chadiha revealed that Walker is dealing with a Grade 2 groin injury, which typically requires two to three weeks of rest. Since he first felt the symptoms two Fridays ago, it will have been nearly 21 days since the discomfort began.
It's uncertain whether the Chiefs are keeping Walker out as a precautionary measure or if he's still seriously injured. He was moving pretty gingerly in clips that surfaced online from yesterday's practice session, despite being listed as a limited participant. Additionally, he missed the team's walkthrough on Monday.
The :17 seconds of the open portion of practice where Kenneth Walker was doing something other than standing/stretching. #Chiefs pic.twitter.com/96VDcrxLhi
Offensive coordinator Eric Bieniemy made it known earlier this week that if Walker were to return, he would retain his job as the Chiefs' starting running back . Regardless, the coaching staff must wait at least one more game before getting the two tailbacks on the field together.
This development shouldn't massively impact the outcome of Thursday's matchup. The weather in Buffalo tomorrow is expected to be cold and rainy, which would create less-than-ideal conditions for a hampered Walker to return to action. The real concern is that a seemingly minor injury has turned into a near IR-length absence. The Chiefs have the utmost confidence in Johnson to hold down the fort while Walker recovers. Johnson has a chance to become a Thanksgiving Day legend if he can continue to produce at a high level.

title: Chiefs Rookie and Sophomore Power Rankings: Youthful Secondary Starring After Week 11
full_text:
As Thanksgiving NFL action approaches on the horizon, the Kansas City Chiefs are turning the page to their upcoming showdown against the Buffalo Bills. Before that, however, let's dive into the events of Sunday's triumph over the Arizona Cardinals and analyze how the club's young talents are faring.
With Week 11's win in the books, here's an updated look at the Chiefs' rookies and sophomores by ranking each member of the 53-man roster in tiers. Check back each week to see who's moving and shaking on the list.
This week's edition doesn't include running back Brashard Smith or left tackle Josh Simmons , both of whom remain on the injured reserve list.
With Kenneth Walker III out for the second game in a row, it was once again the Emmett Johnson show. The fifth-round pick averaged 5.3 yards per touch on Sunday, going off for 143 scrimmage yards and a touchdown to bring his season total to five. He's becoming quite the force on offense for Kansas City, although he credits his teammates for helping him get and stay ready.
In the secondary, the duo of Nohl Williams and Mansoor Delane continues to be one of the best young cornerback tandems the sport has to offer. The only thing that could knock the latter down a rung would be more issues with his shoulder, but he seems to be managing it fine for the time being.
Wideout Cyrus Allen's progression rolled on in Week 11, seeing him get targeted four times and log a pair of receptions for the second outing in a row. The Cincinnati product had 41 yards, one of them being a nice sideline snag, and is coming into his own as a potentially formidable boundary option for a passing game that has plenty of slot-oriented pieces already.
Cyrus Allen season vs. the last 2 weeks, per @FantasyPtsData : Week 1-9 + 16.6% route share + 0.17 TPRR + 1.35 YPRR Week 10-11 + 36.7% route share + 0.24 TPRR + 2.93 YPRR
Sunday was quiet for defensive ends Ashton Gillotte and R Mason Thomas, but sometimes the box score simply doesn't show your impact like it should. Fellow lineman George Karlaftis made it a point to shout out Thomas in his postgame media availability on Sunday, so those within the building still recognize his talent. Gillotte's been a steady contributor since figuring out how to work through his plantar fascia ailment .
In our stock watch column in the aftermath of Week 11, we signaled that Jalen Royals could be the one to have his targets and production limited now that Josh Downs is in the fold at receiver. Royals' lone target on Sunday fell incomplete, so his participation will be worth keeping an eye on moving forward.
Speaking of which, it'll also be interesting to see what plans the Chiefs have for veteran lineman Fred Johnson . He was signed outright to the active roster from the practice squad on Tuesday, which coincides with Jaylon Moore still nursing a lower-body injury. It remains unclear whether it'd be Johnson or Joshua Ezeudu manning the post in a fill-in scenario on Thursday night.
There have been rumblings that an ideal starting tackle duo could eventually be Moore in at right tackle and Johnson on the left, which would throw undrafted rookie Kahlil Benson back to the bench. It'd be hard to argue with that hypothetical, but Benson appears safe for another week.
Offensive tackle efficiency: As if this wasn't already obvious, the Colton McKivitz injury is going to be a huge loss for the 49ers pic.twitter.com/YZ3C65GrwO
Defensive tackle Peter Woods was inactive for another weekend due to a neck injury, but he's been a full participant in practice this week. His return could be on the horizon.
Elsewhere, it was a run-of-the-mill Week 11 for the trio of wideout Andrew Armstrong, tight end Jake Briningstool and defensive tackle Bryson Eason. Noah Gray's rib injury did open the door for more Briningstool snaps; his workload jumped to 27 reps after being 17 the week prior.
The nature of a blowout victory allowed the likes of linebacker Jeffrey Bassa (16 more snaps than Week 10) to get in the lineup more, which is exactly what some have clamored for all the way from the onset of the season. The same couldn't be said for rookie cornerback Jadon Canady, who had a nice special teams tackle but lost two reps versus wideout Harrison Wallace III on only five defensive snaps.
After logging three rushes for 19 yards against the New York Jets in Week 9 and getting Week 10 off, former Oklahoma running back Jaydn Ott had a career-high five carries in 12 offensive snaps versus the Cardinals. Until the aforementioned Smith is back, Ott could carve out an end-of-roster role as a supporting piece.
Linebacker Cooper McDonald and safety Xavier Nwankpa received minimal work — their value is certainly felt more on teams than for Steve Spagnuolo's unit.
For the second game in a row, August trade pickup Diego Pounds got a taste of life as a pro with a handful of live opportunities. The former Baltimore Ravens tackle had six snaps on offense late in Sunday's victory, good for 8.3% of those available.
Nothing going on here. Smith was once again inactive, and Nussmeier will be the club's emergency third quarterback for as long as he's healthy this season.
It is worth noting that players like offensive lineman Pete Nygra and running back Nate Carter, who are on the practice squad, did get elevated and see the field on Sunday.

title: Chiefs Stock Watch: Separation Sunday in Week 11's Big Win vs. Cardinals?
full_text:
With 10 games in the books, the Kansas City Chiefs find themselves sitting pretty in the AFC with an 8-2 record. An upcoming tilt against the Buffalo Bills has everyone's attention, but the club should also be thankful for a Week 11 victory over the Arizona Cardinals .
Plenty of players showed out in front of the home crowd on Sunday, although others struggled a bit. Who deserves a shoutout as the page turns to Week 12's slate?
Let's dive into the good and bad from the Chiefs' Week 11 triumph against Arizona and single out three players whose stock is going up, as well as three who could stand to improve in Week 12 and beyond.
These players stood out for good reasons in Week 11, potentially setting themselves up for increased roles or sustained excellence.
Since leaving Week 4's contest against the Las Vegas Raiders with a hamstring injury , Rashee Rice has quietly been a solid performer and a reliable contributor for the Chiefs' offense. In Weeks 8-10, the former second-round pick posted an 81% catch rate and averaged 8.8 yards per target and 61.3 yards per game.
Those numbers extrapolate out to over 1,000 yards in a full season, so while the pre-injury Rice from 2024 isn't back, this version is just fine.
He then converted on all six of his targets on Sunday, going for 53 yards on just 32 offensive snaps. Ironically, that comes out precisely to the aforementioned 8.8-yard threshold on a per-target basis. Given how willing Kansas City is to spread the love on this side of the ball, it's good for Rice that he's capitalizing and making plays, especially on multiple late downs.
The Chiefs' Week 11 target split: Travis Kelce 7 Rashee Rice 6 Josh Downs 5 Noah Gray 5 Xavier Worthy 4 Emmett Johnson 4 Cyrus Allen 4 Seven players with 4+ targets. Nobody with more than 7. Since 1999, that's happened in fewer than 15 of nearly 15,000 team games. Xavier… pic.twitter.com/EFcypQlNjB
The Chiefs have played a grand total of zero games with the starting offensive line they envisioned coming into the season. Most of that is due to the continued absence of left tackle Josh Simmons , but a multitude of other issues have also crept up in recent weeks.
From left guard Kingsley Suamataia's random benchings to right guard Trey Smith entering concussion protocol and right tackle Jaylon Moore's lower-body injury, it's been a wild ride up front for Kansas City. In Week 11, another wrench was thrown into everyone's plans when Hunter Nourzad stepped in for Mike Caliendo in relief of Smith. This time, the move worked out in the team's favor.
Nourzad fared well in the second start of his professional career, looking comfortable as a run blocker and finishing with just one pressure surrendered, per Pro Football Focus . It was a quality outing for the 2024 NFL Draft Day 3 pickup, which could boost the confidence of both him and the coaching staff down the stretch of his third campaign in town.
Given that Nourzad has another year of club control beyond 2026, perhaps he can now truly be counted on to assume the Caliendo role moving forward.
Speaking of potential expectations prior to Week 1, I'm not sure anyone could've guessed exactly what the Chiefs would do with veteran cornerback Kristian Fulton.
Was he relegated to serve merely as organizational depth following an underwhelming first season in KC? Could injuries see him become a critical part of the cornerback rotation? What about being a trade piece for a corner-needy team out there? The real answer, through 10 games, is a bit of everything.
Fulton's workload is down; he logged 60 and 62 snaps in Weeks 8 and 9 compared to 31 and 28 in Weeks 10 and 11. With that said, his output remains quality. The former Los Angeles Chargers standout surrendered a 57.3 passer rating when thrown at against the Cardinals, keeping his season figure mostly still at a new personal record of 43.1.
After ceding 16.9 yards per reception a year ago, Fulton's down to 10.5 in 2026. That's the lowest bar of his time in the NFL dating back to 2020, so whatever role Kansas City trots out for him each week seems to be working.
Cornerback target rate vs catch rate over expected: JPJ as advertised for the Cowboys pic.twitter.com/TQzc4HtS0y
The following players would benefit from rounding back into form in the coming days and weeks.
Just over a month ago, I wrote about how Nick Bolton was the Chiefs highest-paid linebacker but also was outplayed by Drue Tranquill to that point in the season. While the overall sentiment of general contract value remains valid, Bolton's fulfilled the duty of a steady rock in the middle of the Kansas City defense. Tranquill's contributions have fluctuated — Week 11 wasn't great.
In addition to missing a tackle, the 31-year-old 'backer was credited with giving up a reception each time he was targeted. After not yielding a passer rating in the triple digits in his first seven contests, Tranquill's done so in each of his last three. He's being asked to do a ton on that side of the ball and is far from a liability overall, but it'd be good for Kansas City if he found more of a middle ground in the final part of the regular season.
At one stage of this campaign, it appeared that 2025 fourth-round pick Jalen Royals was settling into a bit of a groove as a rotational receiver option for KC. From Weeks 4-9, the former Utah State prospect averaged 32.4 offensive snaps and 2.2 targets per game. Since then, he's combined for 43 snaps, good for a per-game ledger of 21.5.
That span's accompanied by just one lonely target in blowout wins over the Cardinals and Atlanta Falcons. Quarterback Patrick Mahomes missed Royals on his only opportunity in Week 11, underscoring the possibility that the sophomore wideout may be the odd man out in the aftermath of the Josh Downs trade .
In consecutive contests, rookie defensive back Jadon Canady saw his defensive snap share increase from seven to 11 and 26. This past weekend marked a huge decline all the way down to five, which borders on remarkable considering how many times his No. 22 jersey was caught by the in-game broadcast.
Canady lost to Cardinals wideout Harrison Wallace III on a 25-yard conversion in the second quarter, then got beat by him again on a third-and-5 on the opening drive of the second half. In fairness to the 109th pick in this year's draft , he did log a big-time hit on Devin Duvernay on punt coverage in the final frame. Maybe that's something to build on.

title: Eric Bieniemy Reveals Chiefs’ Plan for Emmett Johnson if Kenneth Walker Returns vs. Bills
full_text:
While Kenneth Walker III has been one of the best running backs in the NFL in his first year as a Chief, rookie Emmett Johnson has emerged as a revelation throughout the two weeks he has filled in as the starter. In wins over the Falcons and Cardinals, the Nebraska product eclipsed the century mark in rushing yards and found the end zone three times.
Fresh off being named Super Bowl LX MVP in Seattle, Walker signed a three-year, $43.05 million contract with Kansas City in the offseason. But two days before the Chiefs squared off against Atlanta in Week 10, Walker told Andy Reid he had pulled his groin and needed to sit out, forcing him to miss the past two contests. Johnson, the Chiefs' fifth-round draft selection , has looked equally as impressive in his own right, albeit against less formidable opponents. Even so, Walker is still the fifth-leading rusher in the NFL even after missing a pair of games and already having gone through a bye week.
With Walker potentially returning this week for a Thanksgiving showdown vs. the Bills , offensive coordinator Eric Bieniemy was asked how the team expects to divvy up the carries between the two standout running backs when they are both healthy. Bieniemy provided about as straightforward a response as there could be.
"Kenneth is the starter, and if Kenneth was to play, he'll remain the starter," Bieniemy confirmed. "That's how this deal rolls. It's been great having an opportunity to watch Emmett do his thing, because that's what he's supposed to do. The next man should always have that mentality."
These comments make it abundantly clear that when Walker is active, he will remain the Chiefs' RB1. That isn't likely to change because of two impressive performances by a rookie.
"We're coaching the starter to be the starter, but we're also coaching that next man to be prepared to be the man," he continued. "I think Emmett has done a great job, but we also understand the value that Kenneth brings as well."
As a fan, it's easy to get caught up in Johnson's production, but Walker's impact has been massive. His presence has opened up the play-action game for Patrick Mahomes, and he's bailed an often stagnant Chiefs offense more times than not. Walker has earned the right to retain his title as the starter for the remainder of the season. Where Johnson has actually separated himself is the passing game. Over the last four weeks, he has reeled in 15 of his 16 targets for 236 receiving yards and three touchdowns, including a 73-yard catch-and-run score against the Broncos. Johnson could be featured as more of a third-down back in passing situations moving forward.
It's still far from a sure thing that Walker is available on Thursday. The Chiefs are facing a short week just two days removed from their victory over Arizona, and Walker wasn't present during the team's walkthrough yesterday. It sounds like the coaching staff is using today's session to feel out how Walker may look in an actual game setting.
Andy Reid says RB Kenneth Walker (groin) will return to practice today Reid adds: “We’ll just see how he does. I’m not anticipating a ton of work there.” pic.twitter.com/ZmBCy2EvMM
Although there are understandable concerns about Walker coming back from a groin ailment in cold, potentially snowy conditions in Buffalo, his game status should be determined soon. There wouldn't be much of a drop-off if Johnson had to start his third consecutive game in the backfield, but his role will be reduced significantly should Walker suit up.

title: ESPN Matchup Predictor Analyzes Chiefs vs. Bills Showdown on Thanksgiving
full_text:
The Chiefs and Bills have built one of the best non-divisional rivalries in the current decade. For the first time in either team's history, they will meet on Thanksgiving Day when Buffalo hosts Kansas City at Highmark Stadium.
Last year, Andy Reid's squad fell to the Cowboys on Thanksgiving two weeks before Patrick Mahomes went down with a torn ACL and LCL . Kansas City is hoping for a better result this time around as it battles with the Bills for the top seed in the AFC. Fans have circled this matchup on their calendars since the schedule came out. Mahomes and Josh Allen have produced some instant classics over the years, though Mahomes has prevailed when it mattered most. The Bills are looking to finally get over the hump against KC.
Heading into this marquee showdown, what does the ESPN Matchup Predictor forecast? Here's what the computer model projects two days before kickoff.
For the first time in the entire 2026 NFL campaign, the Chiefs enter Thursday's matchup as underdogs in ESPN's computer model.
ESPN Matchup Predictor Chances at Victory: Bills 53.1, Chiefs 46.6%
While the Chiefs have been betting underdogs twice this season, the matchup predictor has viewed them as favorites every game until now.
It's hard to argue that the Chiefs aren't favored over a one-loss team on its home field. Buffalo's only loss came in an outlier performance against the Patriots, who have since lost Drake Maye and may miss the postseason. They boast a 9-1 record with strong wins over the Lions, Rams, and Texans.
The issue with the Bills has not been in regular-season matchups against KC. Allen currently holds an all-time 5-1 record over Mahomes in the regular season — the Chiefs seemingly become Allen's kryptonite in the playoffs, where Buffalo has lost all four contests during his tenure. Buffalo's defense has had a massive impact on its recent winning streak, as it has not allowed a touchdown for 15 consecutive quarters. It has faced a few terrible offenses during that stretch, but it is still an impressive feat to watch out for nonetheless.
The Chiefs are optimistic they will get Kenneth Walker back this week, which makes things interesting given the emergence of rookie running back Emmett Johnson . They could form a dangerous two-headed monster against this strong Bills defensive unit.
Regardless of who is favored by oddsmakers, it should be a memorable matchup between two of the top contenders in the AFC.

title: Chiefs On SI Mailbag: What If Kenneth Walker Doesn't Play in Buffalo?
full_text:
It's a short week, and the Kansas City Chiefs are preparing for the biggest game of their season so far, set to take on the Buffalo Bills in Orchard Park, New York, on Thanksgiving night.
In this edition of the Chiefs On SI mailbag, all eyes are on Thursday night's AFC showdown, starting with a player who hasn't suited up for the Chiefs in the last two weeks.
Should we be concerned if Ken Walker can't go in a HUGE game on Thursday? Would the groin injury knocking K9 out for at least three straight games affect your hopes for him going into January? - @EthanCo67716681
Well, it wouldn't be ideal! It certainly felt like the Chiefs were being cautious with Walker for the sake of getting him back to 100% for Thanksgiving night in Buffalo, but now we're left to monitor the injury reports with very little time for Walker to physically improve from however he felt before the Arizona Cardinals game. Add in the forecast of cold, wet, sloppy conditions expected on Thursday, and you have another element to be concerned about. That environment sounds like a recipe for a heavy workload for the game's running backs, but it's not ideal for a runner nursing a leg ailment.
Just told by our @WGRZ weather folks that conditions for #Bills and Chiefs on Thanksgiving night are going to be about as poor as it gets. Steady rain and upper 30s before, during, and after the game.
To fully wade into a hypothetical that might be irrelevant by the time Tuesday's injury report comes out: If Walker doesn't play in Buffalo, I think you have to have some level of concern about his timeline and expectations for the rest of the year, simply due to the possibility that a short-term injury, downplayed by the team, could be lingering much longer than the player and team expected. That's always alarming until the player returns and looks like their pre-injury self.
There's also a possibility that we're overreacting to a Monday walkthrough "DNP" designation while Walker and the team could fully intend on having him suit up against the Bills. But in this moment of uncertainty, it's not what you'd want to see from the first estimated injury report of a short week.
Meanwhile, to ask myself the next question: Is Walker still as important to the Chiefs' offense as he was a few weeks ago, before rookie running back Emmett Johnson put up back-to-back 100-yard rushing performances?
I've been hugely impressed by Johnson's performances throughout the first half of his rookie season, and I think it's legitimate. No smoke and mirrors here; he's a quality NFL back. Still, Walker is obviously the more accomplished player, the more complete player, and he was an absolute revelation through the first act of the Chiefs' season. He also allows Johnson to become an overqualified No. 2 back when they're both healthy.
Even with Johnson's excellent performances now on film, the offense would be hurt if it's without Walker for another week.
How do you like the Chiefs-Bills matchup for Thursday night’s game? - @MrEd315
From an entertainment and storyline perspective? I love it! From an individual matchup perspective? ...Yeah, I still love it, but I'm not overconfident on the Chiefs' behalf!
This should be a tremendous battle between two of the best teams in the AFC who, obviously, have played high-profile thrillers on the game's biggest stages. They're also both flawed and have some things to prove regarding this season's iteration of their teams.
To pick one specific matchup, I'm excited (if not nervous) to see how the Chiefs' offensive line holds up against a somewhat rejuvinated Bills pass rush. Gregory Rousseau has 10 sacks this season, good for the second-most in the league behind only Will Anderson. Amidst recent struggles , how will the Chiefs' tackles (and particularly rookie Kahlil Benson) manage? Can Kansas City execute its desired game plan while protecting Benson in the way they have at other times this season, or will this be a do-or-die game for KC's line?
The Chiefs' offense will have the advantage over the Bills' often-struggling defense as long as the line can give Mahomes time to work. If they can't hold their own, Mahomes may need a masterclass to keep the offense in rhythm.
Going into the gauntlet 8-2. Best case scenario we could hope for. Do you think we go at least 3-2 over the next five-game stretch? I think we can. - @zandersahlia.bsky.social
To refresh, the Chiefs' next five games go as follows: at Bills, at Rams, at Bengals, vs. Patriots, vs. 49ers. The road got a bit less daunting with the injuries to Patriots quarterback Drake Maye and Rams wide receiver Puka Nacua , which will likely hobble the 5-5 Patriots and limit the already-battered 6-4 Rams. (Los Angeles won't have tight end Terrance Ferguson and former Chiefs cornerback Jaylen Watson, among others, while wide receiver Davante Adams seems like a longshot to suit up against the Chiefs .)
On paper, the Chiefs "should" beat the Rams and Patriots. Considering how good the Niners have looked, they appear to be the most daunting opponent of this stretch.
That leads us back to the Bills and Bengals, Kansas City's most noteworthy non-AFC West rivals in recent years. Even with Cincinnati coming off of a surprising loss to the Commanders on Monday night, ending their five-game winning streak, traveling to Cincy is still a serious test.
I certainly think the Chiefs are capable of going 3-2 in this upcoming gauntlet, and they might need to go 4-1 to win the AFC—or even just to secure the AFC West. I'd be more than happy to trade a loss to the Niners for wins over Buffalo and Cincinnati for the sake of getting KC closer to the ever-precious first-round bye. They have such a small margin for error, and, for better or for worse, we'll be talking about the next few games very differently after Thursday's showdown in Buffalo.

title: The Chiefs Did Everything They Could in Three-Game Winning Streak; Now, the Gauntlet Begins
full_text:
Sometimes, football looks pretty simple. It takes a lot of work and a significant talent gap for one professional team to look enormously better-suited for the sport than the other , but it happens on rare occasions.
Over the last three weeks, the Kansas City Chiefs accomplished that feat three consecutive times.
Yes, the same Chiefs who went to overtime against the Colts in Week 2 , who beat the Raiders by a field goal in Week 4, and who have received plenty of criticism for "playing down to their opponents" in recent years just won a trio of games by final scores of 35-12, 35-13, and 34-7. If it seems like it's been a long time since the Chiefs have won three straight games by 20 or more points, it's because it has been. Nearly 30 years, in fact !
The last time the Chiefs won three consecutive games by 20 or more points was late in the 1997 regular season. https://t.co/gU6TsHTpKl
Against the struggling Jets, Falcons and Cardinals, the Chiefs did exactly what they needed to do . After some mild issues in the first half against New York, KC's offense and defense both played very good football, even when they were without key players due to injury. So, what did the Chiefs earn with their excellent three-game winning streak?
Nothing. Not really, anyway. Of course, losing any of those three games would've obliterated any hope and goodwill that was accumulating before Thanksgiving, but that's the cruel thing about the Chiefs' late-season slate. They did everything you could ask for in those early-November wins, but it will be swept away into the deep recesses of our collective memories if they stumble in the next act of the season. With the weeks of smooth sailing now in the rearview mirror, it's time to look ahead to the gauntlet that begins on Thanksgiving.
The Chiefs just checked off a feat with their win over the Cardinals that they hadn't achieved SINCE 1997 😳 pic.twitter.com/qVJzM3Zolp
On Thursday night, the Chiefs will round out the NFL's Thanksgiving Day slate with one of the league's most anticipated regular season games: Chiefs at Bills. The AFC's defining rivalry of the era has been lopsided, depending on when the games have been played. The Bills have won five consecutive regular season showdowns against Kansas City, while the Chiefs have dominated Buffalo in the postseason, 4-0. Of course, the Chiefs would take that deal every season if they could, but if there was ever a year for KC to buck the regular season trend, this would be a good time for it. With a win in Buffalo, the Chiefs would become the narrative favorites in the AFC while being neck and neck with the Denver Broncos in the AFC West, with an eye on the No. 1 seed.
But even if the Chiefs do leave Buffalo with a win on Thanksgiving night, their schedule doesn't ease up in December. Next week, the Chiefs play on Thursday again, this time traveling to Los Angeles to face the Rams. This version of LA isn't the preseason superteam many expected , but in a loaded AFC playoff picture, stumbling against an NFC squad is no excuse.
After that, Kansas City gets a few extra days to prepare for the Bengals in Cincinnati on Sunday, December 13. The 7-2 Bengals haven't lost since October 4 and certainly should be 9-2 by the time the Chiefs come to town after Cincy's upcoming games at the Washington Commanders and home against the New Orleans Saints.
The Chiefs then round out December by hosting the New England Patriots and San Francisco 49ers at Arrowhead Stadium. The Patriots are a much less daunting team without Drake Maye, but the 49ers have to be considered the best team in football so far this season.
This is the unfortunate reality of the second half of the Chiefs' schedule. They successfully began their season with an impressive 8-2 record, only blemished by two road losses against two good teams. The Chiefs' reward for that accomplishment? The hardest three-game stretch the NFL has to offer.
The Chiefs are about to begin the league’s most difficult 3-game road trip of this season: Thursday: at Bills Week 13 TNF: at Rams Week 14: at Bengals Major ramifications for how the top of the AFC playoff field ends up.

title: Chiefs' Week 11 Winners and Losers in Win Over the Cardinals
full_text:
Say what you will about beating the Jets, Falcons, and Cardinals in a row, three teams with a combined 9-23 record, but good teams beat up on bad ones. According to research from our KCSN colleague Tucker Franklin, the Chiefs have not won three straight games by three touchdowns or more since 1997. No matter how you slice it, that is an impressive stretch of football, and 8-2 is nothing to scoff at in the NFL.
The game was effectively settled in the first 15 minutes: Kansas City ran 27 plays for 152 yards, while Arizona managed three plays for three yards, putting Kansas City up 14-0. The most notable performances may shape the end-of-year award conversations, along with a couple of roster questions that could get louder as the schedule gets harder, mainly along the offensive line.
Here are the biggest winners and losers from Week 11.
Quarterback Patrick Mahomes is the ultimate winner here, and not only because of his numbers. He was protected better than in recent weeks, and his weapons played as well as they have all season. He was pressured only seven times, and he wasn't as reliant on running backs and tight ends as he had been before Week 10.
He attempted 31 passes in the first half alone, completing about two-thirds of them for 233 yards and two touchdowns. He then watched a Justin Fields and Jaydn Ott-led offense from the sideline after Xavier Worthy scored on the first play of the fourth quarter.
He finished 27-for-39 for 324 yards, three touchdowns, and no interceptions, with a 7.5 average depth of target. The latter is his third-highest mark of the season, all while posting his quickest time to throw, at 2.33 seconds.
Rashee Rice caught all six of his first-half targets for 53 yards and made several third-down grabs, including one where he took a big hit and held on. Newcomer Josh Downs had four catches for 59 yards, including a 26-yard gain, and Cyrus Allen added 41 yards on two catches. Worthy bounced back with 38 yards and a score. Travis Kelce caught two touchdowns and also led the team with 74 yards.
Over his last four games, Mahomes has thrown 13 touchdowns, thrown no interceptions, and averaged more than 300 yards per game, further establishing his name in the MVP conversation. His two head-to-head matchups with MVP candidates Josh Allen and Joe Burrow, in two of the next three weeks, will be the ultimate barometer.
Not enough can be said about George Karlaftis' season, and Chiefs Kingdom may even be underrating it a bit. Box scores and analytics show he has been one of the best pass rushers in the NFL.
He is tied for seventh in the NFL in sacks, leads the league in batted passes, and is third among defensive ends in total pressures. All eight of his sacks have come since the bye week, meaning eight in the last six games, with seven contests left.
Sunday was his best day yet, with 2.5 sacks, a season high. He shared a half-sack with Chris Jones, then added a sack and a strip-sack in the second half, plus a quarterback hit. His six pressures led the team according to PFF, and only Felix Anudike-Uzomah had more than one.
He has at least one sack in each of his last four games, with multiple sacks in two of them, and he has the most sacks in the NFL since Week 8, with seven. Karlaftis is also 2.5 sacks shy of the 10.5 he posted in 2023.
The Defensive Player of the Year award is narrative-based, like the MVP, so if he performs the same against high-flying offenses like the Bills, Rams, Bengals, and 49ers, there is a non-zero percent chance that he can enter DPOY conversations.
The awards theme continues with rookie running back Emmett Johnson , who has entered the Offensive Rookie of the Year discussion, at least in Chiefs circles. That may have something to do with how many first-year offensive players are underperforming, but it does not mean his production in limited opportunities is unwarranted.
Receivers KC Concepcion, Carnell Tate, and Denzel Boston, along with running back Jonah Coleman, are all having solid seasons, but after another strong day filling in for Kenneth Walker, Johnson is on pace for more than 1,000 yards from scrimmage and eight touchdowns. That is remarkable considering that his running mate already has 1,044 yards from scrimmage and 11 touchdowns.
Kenneth Walker missed his second straight game with a groin injury, and Johnson carried the ball 23 times for 105 yards and caught four passes for 38 yards. He scored for the fourth straight game and forced seven missed tackles.
It is not too often you take an Offensive Player of the Year Candidate out of the offense and said offense doesn’t skip a beat, but that is exactly what has happened. We’ll see if Walker is good enough for Buffalo, but Johnson is worthy of another start if not.
How can a left tackle who has started all 10 games and a right tackle who has missed the past two weeks be losers in a 34-7 win? It is because of what is happening around them and what they are not doing.
Kahlil Benson's work this season has been both impressive and admirable. An undrafted rookie filling in for Josh Simmons without derailing the offense is an accomplishment in itself. That said, he did allow a team-high four pressures, and nobody else on the line allowed more than one. As much as he has stabilized the offensive line this season, he ranks second-to-last in the NFL in pressures given up, with 34, according to PFF.
Who knows how safe Benson’s starting spot really is, but Jaylon Moore may be in the same boat. He wasn't exactly a world-beater before his ankle injury, and the Chiefs recently signed Fred Johnson , a 6-foot-7, 326-pound tackle from the Eagles. Johnson, with 833 career snaps at left tackle and 893 at right tackle, could compete with both Benson and Moore.
Not only that, but swing tackle Josh Ezeudu is also making a case. Over parts of the last three games, including two starts, he has allowed just three total pressures. These are good problems for a team to have, but neither tackle has ideal job security heading into the part of the season that really counts.
I am lumping these two together because they are in the same situation on opposite sides of the ball. Royals is getting snaps but not targets, and Canady is only getting opportunities in a pinch. Canady is a rookie, and Royals may as well be one given his 2025 season.
Neither had a horrible game, but both did little with their chances compared to their counterparts. Royals was third among receivers in snaps again but had no catches on one target. Downs and Allen played fewer snaps and combined for nine targets, six catches, and 100 yards. That doesn't help the Royals' long-term outlook.
Canady played just five snaps in a decided game, and those five snaps really could not have gone much worse. He was targeted three times and allowed two catches for 35 yards, all against Harrison Wallace III. The Ole Miss rookie came in with one catch for nine yards. Wallace led Arizona with four catches for 57 yards, and Canady played a big role.

title: Another Great Emmett Johnson Start May Have Been Thanks to His Chiefs Teammates
full_text:
Most of the time, being down one of the very best running backs in the sport borders on disaster for an NFL offense. For the second weekend in a row, though, that didn't apply to the Kansas City Chiefs even a bit.
As prized free agent signing Kenneth Walker III continued to deal with a groin injury , the club sat him once again. Not only was that a wise call given the magnitude of the upcoming schedule, but it also signaled belief that rookie Emmett Johnson could still get the job done in relief.
Some 34 points and 435 total net yards later, it's clear that Kansas City made the right call. Johnson turned in his second tremendous start in a row and didn't allow the offense to experience any dip in performance, asserting himself as an Offensive Rookie of the Year candidate in the process.
After Week 10's win over the Atlanta Falcons, the message from the Chiefs was that Johnson simply had his meticulous preparation meet the right opportunity . On Sunday versus the Atlanta Falcons, the fifth-round pick said his levels of comfort and output were influenced by his teammates.
“Very comfortable,” Johnson said. “I feel like just the guys trusting me up front, Pat (Mahomes) and all those guys having trust in me, I think it just makes my job a lot easier to go out there and be myself.”
“Yeah that’s cool, but I just wanna win a Super Bowl.” Emmett Johnson when asked how he feels about being mentioned in Rookie of the Year talks. pic.twitter.com/ISfhQvPIuh
He also tips his cap to Walker, who's seen and done everything ranging from being in a committee of sorts to winning Super Bowl MVP, for bringing out the best of him and being a perfect on-field role model.
“He’s done a lot, man,” Johnson said. “I think just how we practice [and] how we push each other every single day, we get the most out of each other. I think that’s the biggest thing about me and Kenneth — we’re both hungry guys. We go out there and work our butts off. We both want to help the team to win, so him just being there in practice really pushes me to be the best version of myself when I’m on the field.”
Johnson led the way right out of the gate for the Chiefs in Week 11 and never truly looked back. The Nebraska product toted the ball 23 times for 105 yards on the ground and also hauled in four passes for 38 yards. In all, he's the first player this century ( and the first since 1994 Marshall Faulk ) to log at least 100 rushing yards and 30 receiving yards in each of his first two professional starts.
Of course, it wouldn't have been a Johnson game without some elusiveness and wiggle showcased on the gridiron. Per NFL Pro , the first-year man forced eight missed tackles by Arizona defenders, further supporting his league-leading 41.1% clip on the season. Johnson's blend of contact balance, short-area burst, leverage, durability and conditioning has him thriving.
A year or two ago, Kansas City would've dreamed for one player that was even 80% of Walker or Johnson's caliber. Now, Mahomes and company are benefitting from the luxury of perhaps football's best one-two punch at the halfback spot.
The scariest thing of all? There's likely still a final evolution coming in which the Chiefs can find the most optimal way to use both players once Walker's back.

title: Chargers Still Hoping Quentin Johnston Shakes Bust Label is Another Big Problem in LA
full_text:
It took a series of big missteps and overall mismanagement to put the Los Angeles Chargers in their current hole.
The weird misalignment between a thrifty front office and a poor coaching staff is a big part of it.
Look at former first-round pick Quentin Johnston.
The Chargers took Johnston in the first round back in 2023 and drop issues have been the major defining thing about his tenure, even overshadowing the fact he scored eight touchdowns apiece in 2024 and 2025.
Despite this, the Chargers and general manager Joe Hortiz took the obvious “bargain” by picking up Johnston’s fifth-year option.
Now 1-9, the Chargers have 15 catches for 275 yards and one touchdown from Johnston.
Let Chargers head coach Jim Harbaugh tell it, the offense just needs to get Johnston the ball more.
“We’ve got to get the ball to Quentin,” Harbaugh said . “I’d like to see the ball in Quentin’s hands. Blocked extremely well, but more targets, more opportunities, I think, would really help us. … You can’t force (targets) … but yeah, I’d like to see the ball in his hands more.”
It’s a pretty wild idea, considering Johnston has caught just 15 of his 32 targets. A Mike McDaniel offense that seems to need speedier options doesn’t really feel like it has a place for what Johnston brings to the table.
Making matters all the worse is that pesky fifth-year option. The Chargers are on the hook for a fully guaranteed $18 million salary next year. Nobody is walking through that door to trade for Johnston based on what he’s put on film.
So, looking ahead to 2027, what’s the play? Keep McDaniel and the bad fit? Start over with a coordinator who better fits a wideout who has caught 159 of 275 career targets from a quarterback like Justin Herbert? Let the $18 million player ride the bench?
The Chargers’ cheap front office isn’t helping. Johnston should be on an expiring contract right now, opening up their offseason options. It’s a problem that extends throughout the roster. They cheaped out on guards yet again and it shows. Not paying Odafe Oweh led to using a first-round pick on Akheem Mesidor when the answer was already on the roster. Don’t forget the “can’t-miss offer” for Daiyan Henley at the trade deadline to a rival after proclaiming they wouldn’t trade anyone, then failing that trade anyway.
Four seasons in now, Johnston’s time with the Chargers is pretty much up. Except, of course, for that pesky front office that values good deals more over actual production and winning. Until that front office proves otherwise, anyway.

title: Omarion Hampton is Perfect Example of Everything Wrong With Chargers
full_text:
Los Angeles Chargers running back Omarion Hampton is a fantastic football player.
The problem is, he plays for the Chargers.
Amid the 1-9 disaster, the Chargers boast emerging players to watch . Yet somehow, Hampton isn’t one of them, not really, because of a coaching and organizational approach that borders on malpractice.
Look right at the top with the listless Jim Harbaugh , who had some pretty shocking quotes about Hampton this week.
“Yeah, in hindsight, we should have done that sooner,” Harbaugh said . “I’m glad we’re doing it now, glad he’s certainly responded like the really good player that he is.”
Harbaugh was talking about making Hampton the workhorse back. He rushed for 105 yards and a score on 22 carries in a Week 10 win over Baltimore. He averaged 6.4 yards per carry on 14 chances in the loss to the New York Jets last week.
Before those games? Hampton was lost in a three-back rotation and he played fewer snaps than Kimani Vidal and Keaton Mitchell in weeks 4, 5 and 8. They went 0-8 over that span and are only just figuring out that Hampton might be the key.
How the heck did the Chargers get here?
Start back in 2025, when the Chargers decided that a running back was a good value in the first round at No. 22 overall. A wild decision, given the value debate around taking that position so early. And that’s to say nothing of the many premium spots on the offensive line, at wideout or across the defense they could have filled instead.
Hampton then struggled as a rookie at times due to injuries. He ended his rookie year with 124 carries, 545 yards and four scores on a 4.4 average over nine games. But the vision and obvious first-round stuff were there. The future was bright.
Then arrived Mike McDaniel this year and his weird insistence on running three-back looks. Keeping everyone fresh for the entire season is a nice idea, but when the record hits 0-5 or 0-6, maybe it’s time to step back and admit that making Hampton the workhorse everyone knows he can be might be the only way to pick up some wins.
That’s to say nothing of Joe Hortiz’s mediocre roster building. They knew the guard positions were an issue and signed an obvious dud in Cole Strange and had five guys competing for the other guard spot, including a second-round center Jake Slaughter asked to learn a new position in the pros.
It’s really just Chargering the whole thing. It was questionable to draft Hampton at all, they then failed to build the trenches in front of him properly, brought in a “good” coordinator who decided not to use him and are only just realizing near December that maybe the first-round running back should be playing more.
It would be funny if it weren’t so predictable and bordering on malpractice, really. Now, they’ll use Hampton as a workhorse in meaningless games, risk injury and top draft slotting the rest of the way, too.

title: Don’t Overlook These 3 Chargers Emerging Through Jets Loss
full_text:
The Los Angeles Chargers are 1-9 and coming off a loss at home to the New York Jets. The loss significantly moved the Chargers towards locking down a top-three pick in the 2027 draft but several players stood out in their efforts.
The Chargers are finally starting to get some consistency and players have carved out roles amidst injuries and the volatility associated with a 1-9 season. The Chargers will face significant questions heading into 2027 regarding roster construction and depth. Let's discuss three players who played or have been playing well enough to enter into 2027 considerations.
The Chargers have been featuring a heavy rotation of three edge rushers throughout most of the season with a fourth occasionally joining the mix. Veteran Bud Dupree has not played a snap on defense since week five with Caleb Murphy, now back with the Chargers for his second stint, taking over the role behind Khalil Mack, Tuli Tuipulotu and rookie Akheem Mesidor.
Murphy's role has slowly grown over the past few weeks and he had a monster sack negated by a penalty Sunday against the Jets. The play that was called back featured Murphy bull rushing the left tackle Olu Fashanu into Jets quarterback Geno Smith and Murphy reached through Fashanu to ensnare Smith and drag him to the ground along with the blocker.
Khalil Mack may not be back in 2027, and the Chargers and Tuli Tuipulotu have yet to come to terms on an extension leaving the edge rusher room thin heading into the offseason. Murphy, since returning to the Chargers, has shown significant development as an edge rusher as both a pass rusher and run defender. Paired with his effective play on special teams he should at the very least be considered a lock to be edge number four heading into next year.
Logan Taylor earned the starting left guard role, head coach Jim Harbaugh confirmed it during the week leading up to the Jets game. Taylor still has plenty of rookie wrinkles to smooth out but he has improved every week in the starting lineup. Taylor's ascension makes the rotation at left guard throughout training camp all the more confusing and frustrating in how that process played out only for it to naturally get figured out months later.
If Taylor can continue developing and head to the offseason with a solid foundation in the NFL, a full offseason of position-focused training, as opposed to combine preparation, should set him up to challenge for the starting job going forward.
Cole Strange: Unnecessary roughness Kayode Awosika: Very acceptable and necessary roughness pic.twitter.com/vUjTDZ9ovx
The Chargers signed Kayode Awosika this past offseason as a low-cost veteran guard to potentially compete for playing time in the reworked offensive line. He became the frontrunner for the starting left guard job almost instantly and despite the frustrating efforts of the coaching staff with questionable rotations, Awosika eventually won the starting job but was hurt with what was described as a fibula injury in week two against the Raiders, his only unopposed start before this past Sunday against the Jets.
Awosika was finally off the injury report following the Chargers victory over the Ravens and the Chargers plugged him into the starting lineup over Cole Strange who has been struggling. Inserting Awosika into the starting lineup immediately raised the floor of the unit and Awosika's physical presence helped rookie center Jake Slaughter and rookie tackle Travis Burke.
The Chargers will need to address their interior offensive line in the offseason and search for upgrades, but Awosika's presence should be strongly considered as an option to return to compete if he can stay healthy and keep performing down the stretch. The free agent guard class in 2027 may be light again and as history has shown, the Chargers need capable depth.

title: Justin Herbert Injury Updates: Latest on Chargers QB for Week 12 vs. Patriots
full_text:
Los Angeles Chargers quarterback Justin Herbert has a new injury to manage , this time ahead of his team’s Week 12 game against the New England Patriots.
After dealing with a finger issue in prior weeks, Herbert is now in concussion protocol.
Chargers head coach Jim Harbaugh told reporters early this week that Herbert “reported symptoms to the trainers and the doctors” after the loss to the New York Jets.
Here’s a look at Herbert injury updates before the Chargers play the Patriots in Week 12.
This story will be updated with more information as it becomes available .
At 1-9, the Chargers don’t have much hope without Herbert on the field. Primary backup Trey Lance is on injured reserve with an issue of his own.
Harbaugh provided a course of action if Herbert needs to miss Week 12: "Uiagalelei would be the next man up, and then we would bring Jake Browning up as well," Harbaugh said.
That’s DJ Uiagalelei, who has attempted seven passes this year, his only regular-season reps since entering the league. The Chargers also have Jake Browning on the practice squad, a journeyman backup who hasn’t attempted a regular-season pass since 2025.
At this point it should go without saying, but the Chargers and Mike McDaniel are a fantasy football disaster no matter who is out there. Herbert has completed 62.4 percent of his passes with eight touchdowns and 11 interceptions. His leading receiver has just 28 catches (Tre Harris) and lead back Omarion Hampton only just crept past the four-yards-per-carry mark on the season behind an offensive line battling various injuries.
With how things have gone, it’s now worth questioning whether the Chargers simply shut Herbert down for the season. But they certainly won’t rush him out there against the Patriots.

title: Jim Harbaugh’s Latest Stunning Moment Says It All About Chargers Future
full_text:
The Jim Harbaugh era sure feels like it’s over for the Los Angeles Chargers .
Before things hit 1-9 and the latest reason for Harbaugh’s firing went viral, it was easier to handwave this year as a fluke. It was even easy to argue that derailing Justin Herbert with yet another coaching staff would cause more problems when continuity might win the day.
But to say there are long-term concerns around the Chargers and Herbert now would be underselling things at this point.
And Harbaugh’s latest viral moment sort of points to where this whole thing is headed, for better or worse.
There are plenty of moments where outsiders could say “this is the one” in terms of the signs that things between Harbaugh and the Chargers had fully run their course.
But a rambling Harbaugh during a presser who didn't know what was going on with his own team just days prior is probably top of the list now.
Asked early this week which defensive player had the “green dot” on his helmet during the weekend’s loss to the New York Jets, Harbaugh stammered through a response and went as far as asking a background staffer for help with the question:
Reporter: “Who was wearing the green dot on Sunday” Jim Harbaugh: “I don’t know” then asks a staffer “Who had the green dot” Seems like something a head coach should know pic.twitter.com/POuXG8oHnw
First of all, it was a fair question. The failed Daiyan Henley trade and then an injury meant the starting linebacker didn’t have the green dot. Whether the communication duties went to another linebacker like Del’Shawn Phillips or Marlowe Wax is a very good question to ask.
The fact Harbaugh didn’t know? It’s concerning. After all, Harbaugh is a head coach, for starters. He’s also a “CEO” style coach who oversees the whole thing but really lets his coordinators do their thing.
Given this overarching responsibility, never mind the whole, you know, “head coach” thing, it’s eye-opening that Harbaugh doesn’t know which player was handling the communications to the sideline for one of his three units.
And considering we’ve been wondering if Harbaugh has lost the locker room already, it’s not a good sign for his usual “details matter” messaging in public to straight-up not know a detail like this.
Were the Chargers floating near even .500 before a sudden green dot change, this might not register as such a big deal. But adding it to the pile of a mess that is a 1-9 team and the fact this is another weird “checked out Harbaugh" moment and it looks terrible.
