title: How Raiders Crossing Goals Off Checklist Despite Losses
full_text:
Like most teams, the Las Vegas Raiders entered the 2026 season with several goals. A productive offseason led to Las Vegas improving its roster from the league's worst, worthy of the No. 1 overall draft pick, but one of the league's toughest schedules followed.
The Raiders are 4-7 and are currently on their second different three-game losing streak of the season. Yet the first year under Klint Kubiak was always more about the future than the 2026 season itself. The Raiders began the season with several starters who are rookies or in their second season.
It was a gamble Las Vegas' front office took primarily to find long-term answers at those positions. The gamble came with its fair share of growing pains, but the past two weeks have made it reasonable to believe that starting so many young players will eventually pay off.
Despite the losses, the past two weeks also made it fair to believe it could pay off sooner rather than later. Las Vegas has lost seven of its last eight games, but the past two weeks have arguably been its best two losses of the season.
Las Vegas' young players have battled two of the best teams in the league down to the wire in consecutive weeks. Furthermore, they have put up a legitimate fight in each of the past two weeks, losing in much more respectable fashion than their first five losses this season.
More importantly, Las Vegas has improved over the past two weeks, largely because of those young players, and not in spite of them. This being the case has allowed the Raiders to legitimately compete while gaining valuable experience. It could be argued one was sacrificed for the other much of the season.
“It's a really good question. It's a really fair question. You want to win right now. You want to win every game, but you know that part of the future is those guys having success. So, obviously you go into every game, and you put a game plan together to go win, and you know that some young guys are going to make mistakes," Kubiak said.
"That's part of their growth. So, that's just part of it. But you need to give them the reps they need to see it live for us to have success moving forward."
Those mistakes have decreased, especially in the defensive backfield, over the past two weeks. It may not result in wins right away, as Las Vegas continues working through a challenging schedule. However, Week 11 was huge for Kubiak's Raiders for several reasons.
Not only have the significant mistakes decreased for Las Vegas' young roster over the past two weeks, but it is also clear that their confidence has grown, even through the losses. This is how rebuilds work. This is how rebuilds feel. More losses are sure to come, but so is more progress.
The past two losses have undeniably been better than the previous five. Las Vegas had a much more legitimate shot at beating the Seattle Seahawks and Denver Broncos with Mendoza under center than they had at winning most of their other losses.
Yet the progress the Raiders have shown in recent weeks go far beyond Mendoza or solely Week 11.
Over the past two weeks, the Raiders have competed at a level they hadn't in their other five losses. Players like Mendoza and Jermod McCoy, finally joining the youth movement, have helped the Raiders take the next step on the field and as an organization.
It is only a matter of time before they go from consistently competing at a high level to consistently winning games. That time will come, but for now, the Las Vegas Raiders look to keep gradually improving on the backs of the many young players they knew months ago would be vital to their success.
Soon, all the losses the Raiders have racked up this season, and over the past three, will be worth it. If Las Vegas can be productive in Week 12 against the Cleveland Browns, with their Bye Week right after, there is no more denying these young Raiders are on the right track.
They are on the right track and may be closer than they appear.
Ezekiel is a former Sports Editor from the Western Herald and former Atlanta Falcons beat writer.

title: How Week 11 Confirmed Fernando Mendoza Is Raiders' Missing Piece
full_text:
There are no moral victories, but the light bulb may have finally gone on for the Las Vegas Raiders' offense on Sunday against the Denver Broncos. The Raiders offense had struggled for weeks, including much of the first half of Week 11. Then the unit woke up and went on an unforeseen run.
Sunday was Fernando Mendoza's first time starting a road game as a professional. The game almost got away from Mendoza and the Raiders until two drives shortly before halftime quickly changed the game's momentum. The Raiders have longed for a quality quarterback that fits today's NFL.
Their Week 11 loss to the Broncos confirmed they have the missing piece they have been searching for. It will take time to complete, but Sunday was a glimpse of what the Raiders can become if they surround Mendoza with a solid supporting cast.
Three of the Raiders' four wins this season have come on the road. All four of those wins were against teams with a losing record. In Week 11, Mendoza and the Raiders nearly beat one of the league's best teams on the road, without Brock Bowers. It was Mendoza's first career road start.
Las Vegas walked into a hostile environment and nearly won with a rookie quarterback and a shorthanded roster. Sunday's results solidified that they still have a long way to go, but how the game unfolded was the bigger story for a Raiders team that entered Sunday missing multiple players.
"Well, number one is just the environment. That is a very hostile environment, and I thought overall, I thought he did a good job of getting everybody on the same page. I thought he used his legs extremely well, extended some plays for his second start in the NFL against two elite defenses, I've seen improvement,” Kubiak said.
"I think that's who he is. That's what he's made of. I think back to us being backed up, taking a sack and then him making a really big third-and-long throw to Jack Bech. That's what you need from your quarterback."
The Raiders spent the offseason and first half of the season looking to improve in as many areas as possible. It has been difficult at times, but the past two weeks have confirmed their improvement on both sides of the ball. The past two weeks have also confirmed Mendoza's improvement.
A rookie quarterback with two starts under his belt is far from a finished product, as Mendoza's crucial turnover proved. However, from his play-fakes to his actual passes, the rookie quarterback looked much better in his second start than in his first.
"Yes, that's something that he definitely works on with Coach [Mike] Sullivan and Coach Andrew [Janocko]. But I think plays like that are successful when there's the threat of the run. Then on third-and-two, when there's a threat of the run, that's when you can get the edge like that,” Kubiak said.
“Play fake or no play fake, early in the game, when you're running the football, that's when those play actions and those keepers really come to life. But you've got to be able to run the ball first."
The Raiders lost to the Broncos, but the Raiders are their biggest competition this season. With Mendoza under center in Week 11, Las Vegas improved on both sides of the ball, especially once Mendoza and the Raiders' offense got going.
Las Vegas entered Week 11 with the second-fewest rushing yards in the league, but ran for over 140 against the Broncos. Tough completions and mobility from Mendoza helped open things up for the Raiders' offense, as Denver could not simply blitz Mendoza and throw the entire offense off.
Mendoza's skill set helped keep the Broncos off balance through the air, which helped open things up on the ground. Once the completions came, so did the rushing yards. Completed passes and a strong ground game led to sustained drives and eventually points.
In turn, Las Vegas' defense had one of its best overall performances in Week 11. It could be argued that Las Vegas' defense played better in their loss to the Broncos than in their win against the New York Jets, proving that wins and losses don't always tell the whole story.
Ezekiel is a former Sports Editor from the Western Herald and former Atlanta Falcons beat writer.

title: Raiders Report Card: The Good, Bad & Ugly From Denver
full_text:
HENDERSON, Nev.—The Las Vegas Raiders (4-7) head to Cleveland this weekend to face the Browns (6-4).
The Raiders are overachieving when viewed through the prism of the preseason expectations, and the future is bright, despite losing seven of the last eight. The winners and losers from the Broncos game were clear, but this is more than that.
Today, like every Tuesday, we break down the critical factions of the team and grade them accordingly.
Each Tuesday, I offer you my report card on the game after talking to people in and outside the building, and watching the film multiple times. So, without further ado, here is my latest report card.
The Raiders offense reached its goal of 24 points against a legitimate Super Bowl-caliber defense, despite Fernando Mendoza’s five sacks (mostly his fault), six batted-down throws (all his fault), and veterans like Jalen Nailor, Tre Tucker, and Michael Mayer playing poorly.
The offensive line, however, had a good outing; the Raiders' rushing game returned, and sophomore WR Jack Bech and TE Ian Thomas did well.
Mendoza, the number one overall pick that NFL executives raved about when coming out of college, made his expected rookie mistakes. Still, he also made some franchise QB plays—leaving Raider Nation with the disappointment of a loss and the jubilation of a bright future.
It had been seven weeks since the Raiders had run the ball with their offensive line performing as it did, and Kubiak was thrilled to talk about how his rushing attack found a push up front.
"I just think over the season, as it's gone on, our guys are getting more familiar and comfortable with the scheme, and the more time on task that you have, you anticipate improvement, and it was a step in the right direction."
Rushing the football is the foundation of Klint Kubiak’s offense, and it is vital for the overall success of this team. "Oh yeah, absolutely. Obviously, you get to shorter third downs. In the fourth quarter is when you normally get bigger runs. So, when you're able to run the ball in the fourth quarter, that has a big effect on the outcome of the game. It helps the defense. It helps the whole organization when you're running the football well."
Free agent prize IOL Tyler Linderbaum discussed how the team can build off of this moving forward: “Obviously, there’s a lot of stuff to clean up and just got to keep working, keep working, keep working until we’re on the other side of things and that’s got to be our mentality. We can’t have, you know, moral victories in this locker room. There’s obviously things we can take away that are good, but there’s also reasons why we’re losing football games, so it’s understanding that, you know, building off the good and then correcting the stuff that we need.”
The Raiders defense gave up 38 points, but when you look at the fact that they came in down one of their two starting defensive tackles before the game, and then lost the other starter in Adam Butler and two additional players. The Silver and Black need help at DT; we have known that since last season ended, and that is a blatantly obvious fact. This defense can’t get an interior push, and it is brutal. Kubiak addressed that.
"Well, we got guys on the practice squad that are going to have to step up. We're going to have to take a look outside and probably bring some guys in, but that's where we're at right now. So, we got to make sure that the guys that are coming in from the practice squad are ready to roll."
I called for GM John Spytek to sign Eric Stokes; he should have, and he did. Stokes is struggling, as badly as the DL, but he hasn’t quit, and he's fighting. Do I still believe in him? I do, but the reality is that the Broncos, like others, are targeting him, and he has to turn it around quickly. The Raiders signed him because he is a star, but he isn’t playing like it right now.
That said, multiple rookies and young players are getting valuable reps and improving, including Jermod McCoy, who Kubiak assessed.
"That was just our decision as coaches, and I thought Jermod [McCoy] did some good things yesterday. Obviously, he had a high snap count. There's plenty of things he's got to continue to improve on, but I like where he's headed, his trajectory. It doesn't mean that we're down on Zeke [Hezekiah Masses]. Doesn't mean we're down on DP [Darien Porter]. We got a room full of really solid players. But yesterday, we wanted to get a bigger look at Jermod."
STC Joe DeCamillis is an exceptional leader, but after multiple weeks of A grades, the unit was not the feared, stellar performer at Mile High Stadium we have come to expect. Breaking to own is simple.
The usually terrific punt protection broke down and set the negative tone early. The Broncos impacted two of AJ Cole’s Raiders punts. There was a mind-boggling full block by Sai'voin Jones and a partial block. Those two protection issues gift-wrapped Denver early momentum and set up points during the Broncos' opening push.
Coming into the game, there were questions about whether Matt Gay would even play, but as usual, he was a bright spot. Gay shook off a hip injury and converted all four of his kicks.
The Silver and Black containment was successful. The Raiders limited Denver's return game by keeping kicks away from Marvin Mims.
In a road game where Kubiak was returning home, they fell into an early hole and needed clean execution, but they gave up punt pressure and points off special teams, swinging field position against a contender. It was not the best of performances. The Raiders aren’t good enough to have gone to Denver to beat the Broncos and themselves, and that is how they set themselves up to fail.
Klint Kubiak’s play calling was good; the defense had the right ideas, minus the players, and on special teams, offense, and defense, this loss sat far more on the shoulders of veteran mistakes, an anemic roster, and young player mistakes.
The bottom line is that you could see the game plan and the struggles while understanding the Raiders rebuild; that juxtaposition is why you can love and hate it at the same time.
The point is that, in all reality, rookies Jermod McCoy, Hezekiah Masses, Fernando Mendoza, Treydann Stukes, sophomore Jack Bech, and Trey Zuhn III all had productive games.
"Yes, the expectation is for these young guys to play and these young guys to contribute. And you're right, those guys definitely have stepped up really all season. Fernando [Mendoza] is making his second start, but we have a roster of a lot of young guys, and it's our job as coaches to develop them and make sure they're a huge part of our future."
So how is Kubiak balancing the value of letting young players develop while also keeping true to the mantra of the Silver and Black of, “Just Win, Baby.” "Yeah, it's a really good question. It's a really fair question. You want to win right now. You want to win every game, but you know that part of the future is those guys having success. So, obviously you go into every game and you put a game plan together to go win, and you know that some young guys are going to make mistakes. That's part of their growth. So, that's just part of it. But you need to give them the reps they need to see it live for us to have success moving forward."
While Raider fans were there, it is not like it's been on the road every game this year. Starting down 17-0 certainly didn’t help, but Raider Nation was seen, but not heard much.
Hondo S. Carpenter Sr. is an award-winning sports journalist with decades of experience. He serves as the Senior Writer for NFL and College sports, and is the beat writer covering the Las Vegas Raiders. Additionally, he is the editor and publisher for several sites On SI. Carpenter is a member of the Pro Football Writers Association (PFWA), the Football Writers Association of America (FWAA), and the United States Basketball Writers Association (USBWA).

title: Should Anderson Stay in the Starting Lineup? And Other Players We Want to See
full_text:
Zayne Anderson's remarkable stat line in the Miami Dolphins' Week 11 game was all the more remarkable considering it came after he had played a grand total of 18 defensive snaps the previous five games.
The question now is what that performance could do for Anderson's status with the defense.
Back in the starting lineup because of the injury to Dante Trader Jr., Anderson became the NFL first defensive back since at least 2000 to finish a game with at least 11 tackles, one sack, one interception and three passes defensed.
This was quite remarkable in and of itself, but even more so when you consider the reason Anderson played so little on defense since the beginning of the season was his performance simply wasn't up to par.
So the question is whether his work against Buffalo was an outlier or a sign of more good things to come.
And that's not insignificant considering Anderson, like so many of the offseason free agent pick-ups, signed a one-year contract when he joined the Dolphins.
Now, we're not suggesting that Anderson suddenly is an All-Pro-caliber safety just because he filled the stat sheet against the Bills, but it certainly was a step toward getting himself an extension in Miami.
And in the short term, logic says he should earn him more snaps on defense even if Trader can return to action against the Jets because Trader's performance hasn't necessarily been top notch either.
Beyond Anderson, there are some other young players who we feel should be getting more snaps on offense or defense as we head into the final seven games of the regular season.
RB Kaytron Allen — Allen did some get work, albeit very limited, at running back against the Colts in Week 10, but it says here maybe the Dolphins should give him the backup carries because it's just not happening for Jaylen Wright and it would be nice to see what Allen can do.
TE Justin Joly — The Dolphins claimed him off waivers from the Denver Broncos as a rookie fifth-round pick based mostly on his receiving ability, and the Dolphins could use that at tight end. Now, with Joly and everybody else, we should mention that usually there's a good reason coaches aren't using certain players, whether it be knowledge of the offense or being fundamentally sound enough, so we get it if certain lineup decisions are being made.
TE Will Kacmarek — The rookie third-round pick is playing 38.1 percent of the offensive snaps, which is the exact same percentage as rookie free agent fullback DJ Herman, and quite frankly we'd like to see Kacmarek a bit more involved.
CB Darrell Baker Jr. — Baker definitely was noticeable in his limited action on defense against Buffalo in his Dolphins debut and has earned more playing time from where we sit.

title: Examining the New Complication on the Dolphins Offensive Line
full_text:
Kadyn Proctor will not be moving to right tackle this week for the Miami Dolphins this week, and that might not happen at all this season.
But there still is a question about the status of Austin Jackson, not so much in terms of keeping his starting job but rather an injury issue that has popped up.
Head coach Jeff Hafley indicated before practice Wednesday that Jackson would be limited in practice on this day, though he didn't disclose the nature of his injury.
Hafley did add that Jackson would be at his spot at right tackle barring an injury forcing him out of the game against the New York Jets at Hard Rock Stadium on Sunday.
Jackson played every snap in the 26-9 loss against the Buffalo Bills on Sunday and it's unclear when or how he got injured, but if he ended up being physically compromised for the Jets game, it could give Hafley the opportunity to look at somebody else at right tackle without having to bench Jackson.
Since Hafley made it clear Proctor isn't an option at right tackle right now, the other logical choices if not Jackson would be Chukwuebuka Godrick or Caedan Wallace.
Godrick started three games for the Kansas City Chiefs last season; Wallace has two career starts on his resume, both in 2024 with the New England Patriots but one came at left tackle and the other was as a sixth offensive lineman.
Whoever plays right tackle will face the difficult task of trying to contain rookie pass rusher David Bailey, the second overall pick in the 2026 NFL draft who is tied for third in the NFL with 9.5 sacks.
The Dolphins held Bailey in check in the teams' first meeting in Week 7 as part of their best offensive performance of the season, with Bailey finishing with half a sack and four tackles in 61 snaps.
While there's now a little bit of mystery at right tackle because of Jackson's injury, the Proctor topic appears closed.
And it appears Hafley doesn't care to revisit it.
When he was asked about Proctor and practice time at right tackle, Hafley kind of shut down the discussion by saying, "I respect the question, guys. I'm not going to sit up here and talk about what could happen in hypotheticals. If we get to that, if we ever get to that point, we'll discuss all those things. But I'm not going to live in a world of what if this, what if that. I mean, it's not the time or the place to do that right now because I don't see it (Proctor going to right tackle) happening right now."

title: Why Sieler Returning to the Dolphins Always Figured To Be a (Near) Slam Dunk
full_text:
The Miami Dolphins' rebuilding project will revolve around their young players moving forward, certainly as we head into the 2027 season.
But there also will be a handful of key veterans who will be counted on to lead the way with what they do on and off the field, and one of those always figured to be defensive tackle Zach Sieler.
His agent, Drew Rosenhaus, indicated as much on his most recent appearance on South Florida TV station WSVN.
“I expect Zach to be back with the team next year,” Rosenhaus said. “I don’t think there’s going to be much debate about that. I’m pretty confident in talking to the team that he’s in their plans. I don’t ever speak for the team. I’ll let them say when it comes to announcing whether a player will be back.
"But I’ll just say from my perspective, based on conversations with the team, I’m confident Zach will be back. We don’t have any reason to think otherwise.”
That this would be even be in question is because of the combination of Sieler's age and contract.
Sieler will be 32 at the start of the 2027 regular season and the contract extension he signed in September 2025 has three years remaining with cap numbers between $21 million and $24 million annually.
That's not an egregious figure, but maybe a bit high for what still might be a rebuilding team in 2027.
As it was, Sieler's cap number of $11 million this year is far ahead of that of any other player still on the roster, surpassing the second-place cap number of $6.7 million for tackle Austin Jackson.
There's also the issue of the structure of Sieler's contract, which has no guaranteed salary remaining.
If the Dolphins were so inclined, they could release Sieler and save $8 million off their cap for 2027 or they could make it a post-June 1 release and save $16 million by spreading the dead cap hit over two years instead of one.
But what we would expect is a contract restructure where his base salary could be converted into a signing bonus to lower his cap number — and keep him on the roster.
The Dolphins probably tipped their hand in regards to Sieler when they reportedly refused to entertain trade offers for him around the deadline.
And why would they do that if they weren't planning on having him around for the foreseeable future.
Before he landed on injured reserve with a biceps injury, Sieler was the Dolphins' most productive interior defensive lineman because of his all-around ability against the run and as a pass rusher — and the gap between him and the rest of the position group was not insignificant.
Beyond that, there always is the leadership aspect, with Sieler again serving as a team captain as well as having been selected by his teammates as their representative with the NFL Players Association.
Perhaps more important than anything, the Dolphins do have some cap space available next year, so they don't need to be getting rid of quality players.
And Sieler clearly qualifies.

title: Why the Dolphins Finally Gave Up on a Rookie Draft Pick
full_text:
The Miami Dolphins' churning of the roster is still going, and two end-of-the-roster players were waived Monday.
The day after the 26-9 loss against the Buffalo Bills in Week 11, the team announced it had waived edge defender Max Llewellyn and linebacker Shaka Heyward.
This is the second time Llewellyn has been waived since the Dolphins made him their seventh-round pick in the 2026 NFL draft. He made the initial 53-man roster before being cut when the team added players from other teams after the "final cuts," then was re-signed to the practice squad and re-signed to the 53-man roster after he exhausted his three allowed practice squad elevations.
But in his fourth game, and first on the active roster, Llewellyn again was an afterthought. He played a total of 18 snaps, nine on defense and nine on special teams, in those four games.
He clearly didn't show enough to keep a spot on the 53 in a season where the Dolphins are looking to identify young players to keep around for the future.
Since he can't play for the Dolphins again in 2026 unless he's re-signed to the active roster because he's out of practice squad elevations, it's likely Llewellyn is done with the Dolphins. This isn't a failure because he was a seventh-round pick and the Dolphins still have done very well with their 2026 draft class.
Everybody else is on the roster, though Trey Moore currently is on injured reserve and DJ Campbell is on the practice squad.
As for Heyward, he was strictly a special teams contributor after the Dolphins signed him off the Cincinnati Bengals practice squad.
With Llewellyn and Heyward gone, the Dolphins now have two roster openings, one of which might go to kicker Daniel Carlson after he went 3-for-3 on his field goal attempts against the Bills.
Keeping up with all the roster moves this month:
November 23 — Waived EDGE Max Llewellyn and LB Shaka Heyward
November 21 — Activated Darrell Baker Jr. off Reserve/PUP
November 18 — Signed EDGE Max Llewellyn to the active roster off the practice squad ... signed P Jack Browning to the practice squad
November 17 — Placed DL Zeek Bigger and Jordan Phillips on injured reserve ... signed QB Brady Cook, DL Jordan Jefferson and EDGE Eric Watts to the active roster off the practice squad ... signed WR Brady Boyd, DL Matthew Butler, K Daniel Carlson and DL Chris Smith to the practice squad
November 16 — Waived K Zane Gonzalez and EDGE Jamree Kromah
November 11 — Signed DT Keith Cooper Jr. off the Carolina Panthers practice squad
November 10 — Placed DT Zach Sieler and QB Malik Willis on injured reserve ... waived CB Reese Taylor

title: Dolphins QB Malik Willis Health Update and Why We Should Want Him Back in the Lineup
full_text:
The Miami Dolphins now have played two games without starting quarterback Malik Willis, and the question remains how many more beyond the next two required after he was placed on injured reserve.
The latest update from head coach Jeff Hafley regarding Willis' status remain as positive as they can be, though we might not know until after the Week 13 game against the Denver Broncos when Willis will be ready to return to the lineup.
And, make no mistake, the Dolphins need him back in the lineup.
"I would say right now, as of today," Hafley said Monday, "I would say that he does not need the surgery right now, just to try to clear that up for you. I don't foresee him needing the surgery leading up to that time. Once we get to the four weeks, we'll re-evaluate that to see how he feels and if he's ready to go. But as of today, I would not say that, yeah, he's going to have the surgery before that time period."
Now, this wasn't exactly committing to Willis being ready to return for the Week 14 game against the Chicago Bears, though it beat the alternative of Willis definitely needing surgery, which likely would sideline him for the rest of the 2026 season.
Backup quarterback Kyle McCord had a dreadful statistical performance in the 26-9 loss against the Buffalo Bills, completing only 12 of 33 passes for 102 yards with no touchdowns, one interception and a 32.6 passer rating.
The 36.4 completion percentage was the worst by a Dolphins starting QB since 2022 when Tua Tagovailoa went 10-for-28 (35.7) in a loss against the Los Angeles Chargers and the passer rating was the lowest since Tua's 31.6 against the Cleveland Browns last year.
But as we wrote after the game Sunday, McCord's performance wasn't anywhere near as bad as the numbers when you factor in all the dropped passes, particularly Chris Bell failing to catch a perfectly thrown deep pass down the left sideline.
That said, it's clear there are limitations to Kyle McCord's game, but then again we should have known that given his background (sixth-round pick on his third team before throwing a regular season pass).
It's not like McCord can't have a future in the NFL and maybe he could become a dependable backup on a good team, but let's just say it looks an awful lot when Quinn Ewers was in the game last year.
There certainly wasn't anything terrible about McCord's work, it just was fairly uninspiring and, again, this is what should have been expected, though some fans got carried away by his work at Syracuse and some glowing scouting reports.
Willis, for his part, remains more of an unknown quantity and he showed enough flashes before landing on IR to remain an intriguing player.
No, the results haven't been good enough and there were times when he didn't make the right decisions in the first nine games, but the reality is the number of games when he was totally healthy was very small.
So it would be nice to get more of an evaluation on Willis to maybe determine just how urgent the need to get a quarterback in the 2027 draft will become. In a best-case scenario, Willis performs well down the stretch this season and the Dolphins can be more selective in the draft.
If Willis doesn't come back and doesn't show enough promise, then it could be that the Dolphins' hands will be tied and they'll have to go quarterback if they hope to have success next season.
Regardless of whether Willis or McCord plays quarterback down the stretch, the Dolphins still aren't likely to win many games. It's just better for the player evaluation process that it be Willis running the offense in those final weeks.

title: (Overdue?) Offensive Line Changes Could Be Coming for Dolphins
full_text:
The Miami Dolphins offensive line probably stands at the top of the most disappointing position groups for the team this season, and it might be time for some changes on the underperforming unit.
Head coach Jeff Hafley brought up the possibility during his weekly day-after-the-game media session Monday, one day after backup quarterback Kyle McCord was constantly harassed by the Buffalo Bills pass rush — much the same way Malik Willis was harassed every game before he landed on injured reserve.
Hafley was asked specifically about possibly benching starting right tackle Austin Jackson, who has struggled in pass protection all season, but offered a broader-view answer.
"Yeah, I would say we'll look at the offensive line hard this week," Hafley said. "We sat down this morning. We're going to do more this afternoon, and we'll look at everything to see you what we need to do to help him more, and what we need to do overall. Like I said to you guys yesterday, we'll take a look at what we can do better to help, and then we'll take a look at what we can do overall to play better on offense. So I would say that with all the positions."
While Hafley made it more about the whole group — actually everybody on offense — it's pretty clear to anyone watching Dolphins games this season that the right side of the line has been the weak line, with guard Jonah Savaiinaea's play slipping after he got off to a decent start this season.
And, yes, the Dolphins have issues on offense that extend beyond the offensive line, which is how they rank last in the NFL in scoring and 31st in total offense.
But good offensive line play can mask a lot of deficiencies, and what's happening with the Dolphins is just the opposite.
And that's a major problem.
And it's gone on long enough.
It's why it's high time for a change.
So who could come in and come out of the lineup on the offensive line starting Sunday in the rematch against the New York Jets at Hard Rock Stadium?
Obviously the two players in danger of being benched are Savaiinaea and Jackson, and it's probably easier to bench Jackson considering he's in the last year of his contract and probably won't be back in 2027.
It also would be painful to bench Savaiinaea before the end of his second season as a second-round pick, but at some point the Dolphins might be forced to accept the reality he's just not the answer at right guard.
If the Dolphins do make a move at guard, then the easy solution for a replacement is Jarrett Kingston, who started against Cincinnati when rookie first-round pick Kadyn Proctor was out with a concussion and has taken over from Caedan Wallace as the sixth offensive lineman whenever the Dolphins use the jumbo package.
The right tackle spot is a bit more complicated because of the Proctor factor.
And this is where Hafley's answer Monday whether there have been conversations about moving Proctor to right tackle certainly was interesting.
Remember that Proctor played left tackle at Alabama and the thinking by many folks when the Dolphins selected him 12th overall in the 2026 draft was that his long-term future in Miami was at right tackle on the opposite end of left tackle Patrick Paul.
Neither Hafley nor GM Jon-Eric Sullivan ever have made definitive statements about Proctor's position for the entire season, only saying in the spring that they were going to start him out at guard.
"I would say conversations have been had because there's a lot of conversations, and I say that to be honest with you," Hafley said. "As of right now, I don't see him playing tackle this week. So yeah, that's how it answers your question."
Of course, the "as of right now" means that Hafley could change his mind before the start of practice Wednesday, which is when preparations for the Jets game will begin with the first practice of the week.
If the Dolphins indeed keep Proctor at guard, then the logical choice to replace Jackson if Hafley and his staff decide to do so would be Chukwuebuka Godrick, who they signed as a free agent after the final cuts to 53 after he had been released by the Kansas City Chiefs.
Godrick started three games at right tackle for the Chiefs late last season. He would seem the logical choice even though he's listed as the second-team left tackle on the depth chart and Wallace is listed as the second-team right tackle ... considering Wallace was inactive the last two games.
Of course, it's possible that Hafley ultimately decides to maintain the status quo for the Jets game, but in this season of evaluation there's no reason to keep going with players who don't fit into the long-term plans.
So it says it's time. Let's make a change.

title: Four Losers And Four Winners From Miami's Week 11 Loss
full_text:
Chilly weather, broken tables, and the Miami Dolphins falling to the Buffalo Bills in Orchard Park. It's been a common theme since 2016, the last time the Dolphins won a game in Western New York. They didn't come close to breaking that streak Sunday.
While the Dolphins have lost as many games as they have, a good chunk of them had been by a touchdown or less. That wasn't the case against Buffalo, as after the Bills went up 13-0 with 13:23 to go in the second quarter, the deficit never went back down to less than eight points.
Against a team looking to compete for a spot in Super Bowl LXI, the youth and inexperience of the Dolphins reared their ugly head in a way that hasn't been seen since maybe the San Francisco loss. That said, you can find positives if you look hard enough, and there was especially some good from the defense.
As you'll probably come to find out, the entire offense looked shaky in this game. McCord got no help from his offensive line, and a lot of his wide receivers forgot to wear their extra-sticky gloves. He's playing the Bills in Buffalo, for crying out loud.
He looked like someone who hadn't played many games of professional football, with a generous number of passes that either sailed over receivers or were underthrown. He rarely went for the long ball, and when he was under pressure, he equally struggled with check-downs or anything that required him to scan the field. He only threw one interception, which in itself feels like a win.
At no point in this game did it look like he could take over by himself, which is justified because that was always going to be impossible given the circumstances.
Back-to-back weeks for Chop being one of the biggest winners on these lists. Numbers-wise, his performance doesn't stand out with three tackles, a pass deflection, and a QB hit. If it were any other quarterback, he probably would have also recorded at least two sacks, but Josh Allen did what he does best and escaped an impossible situation.
The one time he couldn't make magic happen, though, was on that Robinson pass deflection, leading to an errant throw that sailed right to Jacob Rodriguez for an interception. He's not a one-dimensional player, as he was also solid in managing the run game, helping the defense limit the Bills to 95 rushing yards, an astronomically low number for a team with Allen and James Cook III.
The rookie sensation had a hard time establishing himself. He was targeted 10 times, and while a fair number of the throws were off the mark, he was only able to haul in two receptions for 30 yards. More than anything, though, this will be the game that showcased perhaps his biggest issue — the drops.
There were four in this game for Douglas, with none bigger than the one on third-and-goal early in the third quarter. It forced their third field goal of the day, and it was the closest they ever got to a touchdown the rest of the game.
Filling in for Dante Trader Jr., Anderson made the most of an extended workload and recorded 12 tackles, a sack, three pass deflections, and an interception. It's easily his best performance of the season, considering how red-hot Buffalo's offense was entering this game. The sack was critical, as it forced a 54-yard field goal attempt from Tyler Bass that sailed wide left in the third quarter.
The interception, meanwhile, was the first of back-to-back picks thrown by Allen and McCord toward the end of the first half. It wasn't all perfect for Anderson, as DJ Moore's touchdown was assisted by both Anderson and Michael Taaffe blowing the coverage, and forcing us all to watch Moore pretend to be a seal for two full seconds.
Just when you thought maybe Jackson was improving after a clean stat sheet with no pressures, sacks or penalties against Indianapolis, things got ugly against Greg Rousseau and Buffalo. He was responsible for two sacks by Rousseau, and every time he didn't pressure McCord, it felt like a small victory.
Jonah Savaiinaea also had a rough game, but it seems clear that one of the positions where Miami needs a fresh face at is right tackle. Jackson's best attribute this season isn't blocking, but rather how he's stayed healthy, and that's not good enough. It doesn't matter who the quarterback is; the right side of the line of scrimmage is always a battleground that they'd better avoid being near.
It sure is great not to have a small panic attack every time a kicker is brought on the field. Carlson set the tone in the second quarter with back-to-back 52-yard field goals, then added a 27-yarder in the third quarter for good measure.
Yes, it's only one game for Carlson, but it's refreshing to see someone provide consistency to Miami's special teams, as it's been anything but that this season. No one will find long-term reasons to remember this game from a Dolphins perspective, but at least it looks like Miami has one less problem to worry about on their roster for the time being.
Here we go again. Wright can't catch a break; the jokes about him being a magnet for defenders in the backfield have unfortunately aged well. He recorded 10 yards on five carries, and this is somehow an improvement from his games against the New York Jets, New England and Indianapolis.
Wright actually was decent on kick returns with 79 yards on three returns. Once he gets a full head of steam, he tends to be hard to bring down, but he never gets that opportunity on offense. That's why it's puzzling that he's been given this many carries up to this point as opposed to anyone else.
In fairness, it would have been hard to beat what Washington was able to cook up against the Colts as a receiver, runner, and ... thrower. But even in a bad game for Miami's pass offense, he was serviceable enough for 30 yards on three receptions, with four fewer targets than Douglas.
Surprisingly, it's his ability to run the ball that might be something Bobby Slowik and the offense should look into moving forward. Any way to get him the ball more is welcome, especially when the rookies struggle in games like this against a tough defense, and teams like Denver and Chicago are still to come.

title: Five Instant Overreactions to the Dolphins-Bills Matchup
full_text:
Miami's defense put up a valiant effort, but it wasn't enough, as the Dolphins ultimately fell to the Bills by a score of 26-9.
Let's overreact to some key developments, both positive and negative, from this Week 11 matchup.
The Miami Dolphins offense was abysmal, and many of the struggles came from underwhelming individual performances.
Caleb Douglas, who had previously dropped a pass in each of the last two games, dropped another three throws Sunday, and only caught two of his 11 targets. Fellow rookie Chris Bell also had a deep pass bounce off his fingertips.
Miami’s weapons couldn’t create separation on key downs, and the offensive line, particularly along the right side, struggled once again. Jonah Savaiinaea and Austin Jackson are difficult to ignore and easy for opposing defenses to key in on. Their consistent one-on-one losses and need for help not only hamstring the Dolphins from a game plan perspective, but also take away potential support for Patrick Paul and Kadyn Proctor, who gave up timely pressure.
The struggles from the Dolphins’ youth, while inevitable, are extremely difficult to overcome with this little to rely on in terms of veteran presence. Miami's offense badly needs an influx of talent in the 2027 offseason.
Chop Robinson's resurgence after an underwhelming second season is a very positive development for this Dolphins team, and he once again looked strong against Buffalo.
Robinson’s conversion rate of speed to power has vastly improved this season with his added weight, and when he attacks from the wide-nine alignment, he can eliminate the space between him and the tackle in a hurry. He did so multiple times in this game, pressuring Josh Allen and moving him off his spot.
There were also several instances of Robinson moving bodies in the run game, caving in offensive linemen and tight ends to make it easier for his teammates to make plays.  Robinson's play has become more consistent, and if he continues to develop, he could be a foundational piece of Miami's defense moving forward.
Outside of a long, game-clinching drive following a Miami turnover on downs, the Dolphins’ defense did more than enough to keep them in the game. More importantly, they did it with a drastic talent discrepancy.
Even with the late success, James Cook only averaged 4 yards per carry, and Josh Allen finished 27/45 with two interceptions.
The film will tell the full story, but for Josh Allen, a quarterback who has historically torched the Dolphins with his legs, to not record a carry is impressive work from Miami's defensive players and staff. Their pressure and back-end coverage appeared to frustrate him, and forced him into bad throws on multiple occasions. Once again, against a stellar offense, Hafley's group puts up a performance to be proud of.
The well-chronicled Miami Dolphins special teams struggles have been nothing short of embarrassing, and this game was yet another prominent example of that. Buffalo not only converted a fourth down with a fake punt but also lined up for an onside kick up two scores, only to take a delay-of-game before kicking off regularly.
Daniel Carlson looked solid, making three field goals, including two from 50+ yards. However, the kick return team was undisciplined, with Kaytron Allen committing a 15-yard unnecessary roughness penalty.
Chris Tabor's unit has been the worst on a team that is bereft of talent. While on offense and defense, there have been instances of the sum playing better than their individual parts; that hasn't happened in the kicking game.
Malik Washington's ability as a runner and receiver have been on display this year. A week after throwing a touchdown and making an impressive catch, Washington had a nice carry where he lined up as a running back, and in another instance, made a crucial one-handed snag on fourth down.
Washington should be Miami's solution for easy offense. For someone who consistently makes the first defender miss, the Dolphins haven't done nearly a good enough job getting him designed touches. He's easily their most explosive and consistent weapon right now (given Caleb Douglas' struggles catching the football) and should see his opportunities match his ability.
Tyler DeSena is currently a journalism student at the University of Central Florida. Prior to joining Dolphins On SI in 2026, DeSena worked with dolphinstalk.com, and created independent social media content on X, YouTube and TikTok.

title: Dolphins Sunday Mailbag: Douglas, Uche, Brewer, and More
full_text:
Part 2 of the pre-Bills game Miami Dolphins On SI mailbag:
Does Bell or Kevin Coleman get in the end zone against Buffalo? Put on your sports betting hat! (Assuming Bell plays)
Bell indeed will play, but I don’t bet and don’t make recommendations. Purely for enjoyment purposes, I certainly wouldn’t count on either player scoring a touchdown if I’m being honest.
Some talk of re-signing Uche has surfaced in recent weeks. What would a fair contract for both parties look like and if the Dolphins do re-sign him, should they envision him in his current role or should their sights be on adding someone else and having him serve more as a rotational/backup piece?
Hey Dana, Uche is making about $1.3 million this season, which is a very low salary for a starter and I don’t know if you could bring him back for less than something like $4 million. In an ideal world, Uche would be part of a rotation on the edge with Chop Robinson and maybe one or two other players.
Another recent position group that got hit really hard was offensive tackle in 2022. Austin Jackson was supposed to be the starter at RT, but he missed a bunch of the season, came back, and got hurt again. Armstead only played 65% of the snaps. Shell and Little played a lot, and Kendall Lamm came in late in the season and was almost immediately injured and missed the rest of the year. Another fun part of this is the salary cap. The Dolphins are well known at this point for paying a lot to players who are no longer on the team. But now they also are top heavy in injuries. The five highest cap hits (per OTC) this year that are actually with the Dolphins are Sieler, Jackson, Brooks, Willis and Brewer. So three of their top five cap hits that are on the team are not playing right now. So their top 8 cap hits are either dead money or on IR (Sieler is the 6th highest). We know all the big ones, but how scary is it that only six players on the active roster have a higher cap hit than Zach Wilson?
Editor’s note: This message came before it appears as though Brewer would play against the Bills, but the point remains. And, yes, the Zach Wilson cap money from 2026 is just not good.
If you end up with the No. 1 pick, do you take the wide receiver Smith or do you look for a decent haul in a trade? And then you can pick an edge in the top 10.
Hey Frank, I’ve said time and time again on the All Dolphins Podcast and the Dolphins Collective and have written that I never would take a wide receiver with the first overall pick unless the gap between that player and everybody else in the draft was insane — and, I’m sorry, that’s not the case with Jeremiah Smith, as good as he is. I’m a big proponent of positional value and I think a quarterback, pass rusher or cornerback can have a bigger and more immediate impact than a wide receiver. So if the Dolphins get the No. 1 pick, the move should be taking Drew Mestemaker if they have a conviction he can be an elite QB or try to trade down to pick up additional assets.
Hey Poup! I know it's only 9 games, but what trade is looking better 9 games in? Caleb Downs for Proctor, Coleman and Traore? Or Waddle (including subsequent 49ers trade) for Johnson, Chris Bell, Trey Moore and Kyle Louis?
Hey Luis, this is a very interesting question and there are two factors not mentioned here, first the fact that Downs was a prospect with no NFL experience and then there’s the cap hit taken with the Waddle trade in 2026 but the money/cap saved in future years. All that said, I like the Waddle package better, but those look like great trades right now.
Hi Alain, it seems there are several groin injuries plaguing the Dolphins. Do you think this could have anything to do with their extended stretching protocols?
Hey Luke, I’m not a medical expert, but I think more stretching actually would help prevent groin injuries, not create them. I also think the data would support that notion. Sometimes there’s just bad luck involved that we have to accept.
Alain, will we see a fade route in the end zone to Douglas in the future when we get into the red zone with his high-point catch ability? I know opportunities have been limited but seems like he would do well with that as well in other situations before the red zone.
Hey Jeff, I like your thinking and the only question I would have is whether Douglas’ high-pointing ability would translate into the end zone where it’s more quick jumping as opposed to have a lot of time to judge a pass downfield, which is what we’ve seen so far. But I would like to see them try (as long as they don’t overdo it). It’s certainly preferable to calling it on a regular basis with Tyreek Hill.
I have not seen an update on Trey Moore since September, he was listed as a starter had a good camp and then the Dolphins had us think he was just nicked up. Any word on his return and what his injury is?
Hey Marc, no, this has been well documented, Moore sustained a not-insignificant ankle injury in the preseason opener against Washington. Head coach Jeff Hafley said in the aftermath of the injury he was “hopeful” that Moore could be back at some point in the 2026 season. I’ve thought along that it’s 50-50 at best we’ll see Moore at all this season.

title: To Win or Not To Win? That Seems To Be a Question for Miami Dolphins Fans?
full_text:
The Miami Dolphins will look to pull off a gigantic upset and win a game at Buffalo on Sunday for the first time since 2016, and sadly a question that some — maybe even many — fans will be asking is: Would that even be a good thing?
This is the reality of a team still in the early stages of a rebuilding project that's gotten off to a promising start but still has some steps to go. One of those is continuing to acquire high-end talent, and what better way than to be picking at the very top of the draft?
And this is where wins can become losses.
The Dolphins, who will be eliminated from the race for the AFC East title if they lose at Buffalo on Sunday, currently hold the third overall position in the 2027 draft order — though they're tied with the Tennessee Titans and Los Angeles Chargers for the worst record in the league at 1-8.
After the injuries that had defensive tackles Zach Sieler, Jordan Phillilps and Zeek Biggers and quarterback Malik Willis join De'Von Achane on injured reserve — with only Willis having a chance to return this season — the idea that the Dolphins might finish with something like a 2-15 or even 1-16 record isn't necessarily farfetched.
In an ideal world, the Dolphins would experience some success in the second half of the season with some wins mixed in here and there and still land the top pick in the 2027 draft.
Except it doesn't work that way.
Each win could cost the Dolphins the shot at the No. 1 overall pick and the chance to take quarterback Drew Mestemaker or wide receiver Jeremiah Smith or try to parlay that pick into additional draft capital with a team looking to make the move up for the top selection.
So, again, the question becomes whether a gigantic Dolphins upset win over the Bills on Sunday would be preferable to another loss if it gets them closer to that No. 1 overall pick.
The Dolphins, of course, were in this situation seven years ago in Brian Flores' first year as head coach after they started 0-7 and were outscored by an average of 40-6 over the first four games.
The Dolphins, though, never once held the top spot in the 2020 draft at any point during that 2019 season because Cincinnati started the season 0-11 before finally getting a win. The popular story goes that the Dolphins lost their shot at the No. 1 overall pick when they defeated the Bengals in overtime in Week 15 that year, but that's fiction and even had they lost that game and wound up tied with 13-3 records, Washington then would have had the top pick, not Miami.
So the notion that the Dolphins lost Joe Burrow because they defeated the Bengals in late December 2019 is simply not true. That chance was lost basically when the Dolphins defeated the playoff-bound Philadelphia Eagles earlier in the month in a game that featured the famous "Mountaineer Shot."
As it was, the Dolphins ended with the fifth pick as fans know too well and selected QB Tua Tagovailoa with their first of three first-round picks that year.
The Dolphins then went 10-6  in 2020 to start a string of four consecutive winning seasons. So did it work out better for the Dolphins that they enjoyed some success toward the end of Flores' first year with the wins against the Eagles and at New England in the season finale or would it have been better had they gone, say, 1-15 and ensured getting Joe Burrow?
Given the season Burrow is having, it's easy to look back and, say, sure the Dolphins would have been better off losing all those games in 2019, but didn't the Dolphins establish a mentality, a mind-set during the second half of that 2020 season instead of tanking?
The argument for tanking in 2019 also seemed stronger than it does this year because Burrow was such a great prospect coming out of LSU, though that didn't become apparent until maybe midway through that season.
We've already seen comparisons made of Mestemaker to the QB the Dolphins will face Sunday, Josh Allen, and if the Dolphins scouts see it, then it becomes a lot easier to cheer for losses because he would become an absolute no-brainer at the top of the 2027 draft.
But there are no guarantees.
The other question is whether Dolphins fans would feel better about head coach Jeff Hafley and the whole organization if the team ended up winning, say, two or three more games this season as opposed to finishing 1-16, which would become the worst record in franchise history.
It's a tough balance to strike because fans should want the team to do well every time out, but looking out for the long-term benefits of the franchise also makes sense.
The Dolphins have had either the first or second pick in the draft twice in their history, but they didn't take a quarterback either time.
In 2005, the Dolphins selected Auburn running back Ronnie Brown at number 2 in Nick Saban's first year as head coach and went with veteran journeyman Gus Frerotte as their starting QB. Looking back, it's pretty obvious they messed and should have taken Aaron Rodgers, though he wasn't selected until pick 24.
In 2008, the Dolphins had the top pick and bypassed the chance to take Matt Ryan by selecting tackle Jake Long, a decision that's easy to criticize after the fact because Ryan had a long and successful (though maybe not great) career with Atlanta that included one Super Bowl trip and Long   basically had six good years before injuries derailed his career.
The Dolphins did need a quarterback that year, but they waited until the second round to select Chad Henne, who had a long career in the NFL but almost exclusively as a backup.
So in hindsight, sure, the Dolphins probably should have taken Ryan.
But it says here that Long was on a Hall of Fame track before his injuries and we also need to point out that Ryan wasn't a slam dunk because it wasn't just the Dolphins who passed on him but also the St. Louis Rams picking second overall and taking defensive end Chris Long despite also having a need at quarterback.
For historical reference, three quarterbacks taken first overall went on to win the Super Bowl with the team that drafted them — Peyton Manning, Troy Aikman and Terry Bradshaw. John Elway, Eli Manning and Matthew Stafford also won the Super Bowl as first overall picks, but each with their second team.
This all brings us back to the original question of whether it's better for the Dolphins to get some wins down the stretch this season or whether the more losses, the better.
The reality is there might not be a correct answer because either choice isn't ideal.
But it's where the Dolphins find themselves in 2026.
And the hope is they're not in that position again anytime soon. However that gets accomplished.

title: Vikings Need Bigger Chuck Demmings Sample Size After Week 11 Loss vs. 49ers
full_text:
Last week's Sunday Night Football game against the San Francisco 49ers was a disaster for the Minnesota Vikings. Nothing seemed to go well for the Purple and Gold in Mexico City, and the 35-10 loss still leaves a bad taste in fans' mouths.
Perhaps the most disappointing part of the Vikings' prime-time struggle was that players didn't rise to the occasion against tough competition. Although Minnesota had injuries to account for, which kept a few players out of action, the next man up didn't always shine.
With starting cornerback Isaiah Rodgers out, most people assumed pressure would fall on Charles "Chuck" Demmings and Zemiah Vaughn to pick up the slack. However, those two young defensive backs didn't see much time on defense, as Demmings only played 14 defensive snaps and Vaughn was in for six,
Demmings, a fifth-round pick of the Vikings who stood out during training camp , played two defensive snaps for Minnesota before last Sunday night's game. Head coach Kevin O'Connell and defensive coordinator Brian Flores seem to be easing him into action, leaving him unprepared to take on a bigger role against the 49ers.
The Vikings looked to their struggling safeties to pick up the slack against San Francisco. In fact, James Pierre and Byron Murphy Jr. were the only two cornerbacks to play more than 14 snaps, which left 49ers pass-catchers like Mike Evans and George Kittle often matched up against Harrison Smith, Josh Metellus, or Theo Jackson.
Despite his limited playing time this season , Demmings has an above-average Pro Football Focus grade. His 66.3 overall defensive grade isn't spectacular, but it is solid. However, that grade is only based on his 16 defensive snaps.
To get a more accurate idea of his potential, he needs more time on the field. Although last week's game was a good opportunity, Minnesota decided against putting the 23-year-old defender in that position.
The Vikings aren't a team that uses their cornerbacks a lot on defense. In fact, out of Minnesota's 617 possible defensive snaps, only three players at the position have played more than 20 reps this season. Here is the snap breakdown through Week 11:
While it is disappointing that Demmings isn't more involved in the Vikings' defense, it doesn't reflect on him as a player. It seems Flores' schemes for Minnesota don't rely heavily on cornerbacks, and the rookie's limited playing time was planned.
Hopefully, the Vikings' coaching staff can figure out a way to get Demmings more experience during his rookie season, so they can properly evaluate him and prepare him for a bigger role in Minnesota's defense in the future.

title: The Vikings May Be Facing a Difficult Justin Jefferson Decision Soon
full_text:
The Minnesota Vikings have a long history of elite offensive talent. Fran Tarkenton basically invented the mobile quarterback role; Hall of Famers Cris Carter and Randy Moss formed one of the greatest receiving duos in NFL history; and Adrian Peterson was one of the greatest running backs the game has ever seen. Sadly, none of them ultimately led Minnesota to the championship they’ve chased for over six decades. Now, the team may be approaching a crossroads with another elite offensive talent in Justin Jefferson.
The seventh-year wideout has been one of the league’s top talents since the Vikings selected him 22nd overall in 2020 (thanks, Philly). But Minnesota’s lack of playoff success during that time and some concerning patterns in his performances are worth acknowledging. With so much uncertainty on the horizon and serious questions about the Vikings’ championship readiness , it may be time to have some very difficult discussions.
Make no mistake, this isn't a hit piece; it’s mainly an acknowledgment that Jefferson has largely lacked the infrastructure needed to thrive at the level he’s always been capable of. His career-best season in 2022 earned him Offensive Player of the Year honors after a 1,809-yard performance, and his 1,533-yard, 10-touchdown season in 2024 was a major reason for Minnesota’s 14-3 record. Still, neither led to even a single playoff victory.
A revolving door of mostly bad QB play has grounded “Jettas” the last two seasons, even though he miraculously managed to break 1,000 receiving yards in 2025. But so far, 2026 is pacing to be his worst year yet, even with Kirk Cousins back in the building.
Jefferson has averaged only 61.4 receiving yards per game through nine appearances this season. However, it should be noted that he left Week 3’s matchup against Tampa Bay early in the first quarter, but previous injuries haven’t seemed to slow his output much.
He is currently pacing for a career-low 983 yards, assuming he plays in 16 total games. He netted 1,074 yards in 2023 (10 games). He's also surpassed his career high in fumbles with two in 2026. Last Sunday night’s turnover against the 49ers was especially concerning, as he seemed to make a pointless cutback on a likely scoring play while displaying some of the worst ball security imaginable.
The all-22 of Justin Jefferson's explosive catch and fumble. What do you see? pic.twitter.com/UhQJahwGRi
The implication that Jefferson's skills are fading seems like a massive overreaction, but his continued decline in production should concern everyone involved. Luckily, winning may be the cure for everything.
It’s been over 2,500 days since the Vikings’ last playoff win, coming more than three months before Jefferson even entered the building. To say the postseason pressure is reaching a peak may be an understatement. At 7-3, ESPN’ s football power index gives the Vikings a 92.3% chance to make a postseason appearance . What they do with that playoff berth is another question.
The Vikings will have several key players set to hit free agency in March, including Andrew Van Ginkel, Blake Cashman, Isaiah Rodgers, and others. Spotrac currently projects the Vikings to have $27.8 million in 2027 cap space , and while that number will certainly change, the team may look very different going forward. With key players likely on their way out, continued QB dysfunction , and a projected cap hit of  $49,493,850 for their star receiver, general manager Nolan Teasley may have a tough task in his first full offseason.
It may be painful to admit, but if the Vikings do not make a playoff run, or at least get a single win, they may consider parting ways with the fan-favorite receiver. A pre-June 1 trade could save the Vikings $21,993,750 toward their salary cap in 2027, while trading him after June 1 could save $34 million. That’s not even mentioning the immense haul of draft picks Minnesota could acquire in a potential trade.
The Vikings still have seven regular season games and a probable playoff appearance in 2026. There is still a lot of football left , and things can shift quickly. But if the Vikings cannot get it done when it matters most this season, both the team and Jefferson could be better off long-term by parting ways this spring.
The good news? A return to form for one of the game's best weapons and a Minnesota playoff run can quickly put an end to this entire discussion. For now, it’s worth preparing for.

title: Vikings' Snap Count vs. 49ers: Biggest Winners, Losers & Role Changes in Week 11
full_text:
The Minnesota Vikings got beat down by the San Francisco 49ers on Sunday Night Football, and the Purple and Gold will need to re-evaluate everything and prepare for the remainder of the schedule for the 2026 NFL season.
The 35-10 loss showed Minnesota is extremely vulnerable to a patient quarterback with excellent offensive line play. The Vikings knew this game would be their toughest test of the year so far, but the team collapsed on the primetime stage.
It was interesting to see how Vikings head coach Kevin O'Connell used his players in Week 11. The snap count tells a lot of the story, but matching it with their performances reveals who the biggest winners and losers were in terms of playing time.
WR2 Jordan Addison missed another game with his thumb injury, forcing a depth chart adjustment. Tai Felton was the clear winner, playing 72 percent of Minnesota's offensive snaps.
Felton stepped into the WR3 role well, beating out fellow wide receiver Myles Price by 37 snaps. The 23-year-old pass catcher led all players with 12 targets. Although he caught six for 42 yards, the increased snap counts and targets are encouraging signs for the second-year pass-catcher.
Even though the Vikings abandoned the run early against the 49ers, Mason ran the ball 11 times in Minnesota's 21 rushing attempts. While that's a good sign for him as a runner, the Purple and Gold don't seem to like having him on the field if he isn't schemed to carry the ball.
The stats back up sidelining Mason. He had the second-worst Pro Football Focus run-blocking grade on the team (44.2), which opened the door for RB3 DeeJay Dallas to take 13 offensive snaps during the game.
Coming into this game, Charles "Chuck" Demmings had played only two defensive snaps this season, which came in Week 3 against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers. Fellow cornerback Isaiah Rodgers was ruled out for this game, opening the door for the fifth-round rookie to get more opportunities.
Demmings rewarded Minnesota's trust in him by posting a 64.9 PFF pass-coverage grade while continuing to be a special teams contributor. Getting the 23-year-old experience against a tough team will only help him get ready for the future.
It was obvious that T.J. Hockenson would return as the Vikings' TE1 upon returning from injury. But Gavin Bartholomew went from 53 offensive snaps in Week 10, where he caught three passes for 36 yards and a touchdown, to playing 18 snaps and catching one pass for five yards.
Earning the worst PFF offensive grade of any Vikings player (28.4), Minnesota might want to see even less of the second-year tight end on offense. His 16.1 PFF pass-blocking grade was also the worst of any player on the team against the 49ers, which is highly concerning.
Stepping into the WR2 role with Addison out felt good for Jauan Jennings. He played 77.6 percent of Minnesota's offensive snaps on Sunday and turned his opportunities into three catches for 20 yards. While that doesn't sound good on paper, Jennings had six catches this season heading into the game, so it was a significant improvement.
Although he didn't thrive in this new role, he didn't flounder either. Jennings will likely continue to be directly behind superstar Justin Jefferson on the wide receiver pecking order until Addison fully recovers from his thumb injury.

title: Joe Huber’s Breakout Has Likely Sealed One Vikings Veteran’s Offseason Fate
full_text:
Heading into the 2026 NFL season, the Minnesota Vikings liked Joe Huber a lot. The 2025 undrafted free agent was a backup guard, but head coach Kevin O'Connell threw him into the mix for the competition at center.
Although the starting center job eventually went to Blake Brandel, Huber is still making an impact this year. Starting left guard Donovan Jackson suffered a torn meniscus in Week 4 against the Miami Dolphins, creating an opening for Huber.
Huber has played in all nine games for the Vikings this season, but didn't play an offensive snap until Week 4. Heading into Week 11, he has played a total of 371 offensive snaps and 38 special teams snaps, giving him the seventh-most offensive snaps on the team.
Starting right guard Will Fries has a 59.9 Pro Football Focus grade this season, but he has allowed 18 total pressures in pass protection, which have resulted in three hits and four sacks. Not only that, but he has been flagged for four penalties this season.
Meanwhile, Huber has a 68.6 Pro Football Focus grade. This season, he has allowed six total pressures in pass protection, but has not surrendered a sack. He has allowed three quarterback hits and been flagged for two penalties.
Fries hasn't been terrible this season, but justifying his five-year, $87.72 million contract will be difficult based on his performance. An out in his contract after this season would result in $12 million in dead cap, and Minnesota will need to consider exercising that clause.
On the other hand, Huber is in the second year of a three-year, $2.975 million contract. Minnesota will be paying Huber $1.123334 million next season before he is scheduled to become a restricted free agent in 2028.
Moving on from Fries would save the Vikings about $9.5 million in cap space or $17.5 million with a post-June 1 release. Unless the sixth-year offensive lineman steps up in a big way soon, he is in danger of losing his spot to Huber.
On The Alec Lewis Show , The Athletic's Alec Lewis shared the possibility of Jackson returning from his meniscus surgery during the postseason . If that happens, Minnesota will have to decide who starts at right guard: Fries or Huber.
This will definitely be a position to watch for the remainder of the season and well into the offseason. Huber is giving the Vikings options on the interior of the offensive line, and it is putting pressure on other linemen, specifically Fries, to step up their game.

title: Jauan Jennings Nearing Point of No Return With Vikings After Week 11
full_text:
When the Minnesota Vikings signed Jauan Jennings, he seemed like a perfect addition to the team's wide receiver room. His proficiency in the red zone and success in San Francisco led to him earning a one-year, $8 million deal with the Purple and Gold.
Sadly, he hasn't lived up to the signing. Through seven games with the Vikings, he has been targeted on 16 passes and has nine receptions for 74 yards, giving him 10.7 yards per game during his first year in Minnesota.
Jennings had an opportunity to change the narrative on Sunday Night Football against his former team . With WR2 Jordan Addison out with a hand injury, the sixth-year veteran got to play 52 offensive snaps, which accounted for 77.6% of Minnesota's total offensive plays. He had six targets but caught only three, gaining 20 yards.
The worst thing for Jennings from Sunday night's embarrassing loss to the 49ers was that he was outproduced by not only tight end T.J. Hockenson (six catches for 55 yards) but by two wide receivers under him on the depth chart.
Tai Felton played four fewer offensive snaps than Jennings, but caught six passes for 42 yards on 12 targets. The surprising one was Myles Price, who caught both his targets for 26 yards despite playing only 11 offensive snaps.
Minnesota continues to hope that Jennings will have a game that breaks the stagnation of his play, but that hasn't happened this season, and there haven't been many signs that he is ready to have a breakout game.
It will be interesting to see what happens when Addison returns from his thumb injury and the offensive snaps need to be redistributed. Will head coach Kevin O'Connell continue to put faith in Jennings to turn things around, or will he give more opportunities to players like Felton and Price?
If Jennings continues to squander opportunities, there will eventually be a point where giving him snaps won't provide any value at all. Considering the team is entering Week 12 of the 2026 NFL season, the clock is ticking for him to change the narrative of his time in Minnesota and convince the team that believed in him to continue putting him on the field.

title: Glaring Kevin O’Connell Problem Can’t Be Masked After Vikings Fall to 49ers in Week 11
full_text:
Sunday night’s 35-10 loss to the 49ers is certainly not what Vikings fans, or the team itself, were hoping for with the eyes of the world on them in primetime. The brutal loss felt all too familiar despite the unique circumstances of the international stage. Unfortunately for Kevin O’Connell, concerning patterns have become too glaring to ignore on the biggest of stages.
The Vikings are 7-3 in 2026 and 50-28 overall since hiring O’Connell in 2022. Fans have witnessed a 13-win 2022 season, a 14-win 2024 season, an NFL Coach of the Year win, and two playoff appearances through four full seasons. Still, the Vikings and O’Connell may be approaching a fork in the road.
Disappointing primetime performances are nothing new for O’Connell and the Vikings, especially against the NFL's better teams. He is now 6-12 in primetime , including 1-7 in the regular season against teams who are .500 or better at kickoff. That also doesn't count his 0-2 record in the playoffs, including an upset home loss to the Giants that ended the 2022 season. Needless to say, the primetime lights have not been friendly to the Vikings in recent years.
The Vikings are 6-12 in primetime games under Kevin O'Connell. They're 2-6 since the calendar flipped to 2025, with losses by 22 (Lions), 18 (Rams), 16 (Falcons), 27 (Chargers), 17 (Bills), and 25 (49ers).
For a coach once labeled one of the league's best young minds, O’Connell’s offenses rarely show up ready for primetime. In two primetime games so far this season, the Vikings have totaled 16 points against the Bills and 49ers for a -42 point differential.
They’ll face the 5-5 Patriots for a Thursday night matchup in Foxborough on Dec. 10 before hosting the 8-2 Lions for Sunday Night Football on Dec. 20, hoping to put an end to the primetime narratives.
If the Vikings want to be seen as real contenders, they’ll need to seriously step up in their most important games, especially on offense.
Many fans across the NFL would list O’Connell as one of the league's better offensive play-callers, but do the numbers back it up? Let’s break down the stat that matters most for an offense: scoring.
The Vikings offense finished 7th in total points in 2022, 22nd in 2023, 9th in 2024, 26th in 2025, and currently ranks 29th in 2026. Obviously, inconsistent quarterback play is a major factor in at least three of those seasons, but that ultimately falls on an offense-minded head coach who has failed to find long-term stability at the position.
The Vikings' 16 touchdowns this season (offense/defense/ST) are the fewest they've had through 11 weeks since at least the 2000 season. Previous low: 17 in 2006. Highest: 37 in 2009.
For all of the positive leadership skills and locker room buy-in O’Connell may bring to the table, his early reputation as an offensive innovator may have been unearned. With serious doubts around the Vikings’ playoff readiness in 2026, O’Connell may be running out of chances to end the worrisome trends emerging throughout his tenure.
