title: Titans' Search for Help in Secondary Gets Desperate With New Signing — But it Still Isn't Enough
full_text:
Today, the Tennessee Titans signed CB Corey Thornton off the Carolina Panthers' practice squad. This comes one day after Tennessee signed offseason-regular DB Derrick Canteen to their own practice squad, signaling a mad rush to plug their game-losing gaps in the secondary.
Robert Saleh's defense has allowed 40+ points in three straight games. In all three, opposing QBs threw for more than 300 yards and downright picked on the Titans' CBs. With Cor'Dale Flott leaving this past week with a neck injury, a bad thing got even worse. This unit looks unplayable.
I'm not here to knock the front office for trying to find temporary solutions therein. Truth be told, I actually like Thornton as a pickup at this stage in the season. He logged an eye-popping interception with the Panthers earlier this month, and is just 25 years old and in his second NFL season.
He fits the bill in Tennessee, particularly regarding what this team is trying to become over the next few years. The younger the Titans get, the better. But a likable signing is not enough for a 1-9 football team that has no greater struggle than the one in the secondary. It's too little, far too late.
This past offseason, Tennessee went all out to sign Flott, as well as CBs Alontae Taylor and Joshua Williams. It was played off as an expensive effort to fast-track Saleh's defense to success. In retrospect, it's hard to stomach just how much money was apparently wasted.
Between the three defenders, Tennessee chunked out $111 million. Per PFF, both Taylor (107th) and Williams (101st) are in the bottom tier of 108 players at their position. Flott's overall grade is hardly better, ranking 80th. At least he has two picks this season.
Whether it comes in the draft or by way of cheaper, much more fortunate signings in the future, the Titans are going to have to chip away at the disastrous structure they've built downfield. This is an issue bound to persist for the rest of this season, at least.
I don't need to be the one to tell you that fringe additions heading into Week 12 won't completely fix this team's problems. However, even when Flott returns and if Taylor plays the rest of this season at nickel (his strong suit), you're looking at an incomplete puzzle.
The Titans got it wrong this past offseason as far as the secondary goes. I hope Thornton comes onto the scene and carves out a significant role. Even then, though, it would make the millions Tennessee spent on their current group look even worse.
Band-aids over broken bridges. This one is going to take time in Nashville.
Lane covers the Tennessee Titans, where he brings an evolving team's journey to fans on a daily basis. A longtime sports fanatic and recent baby blue jersey aficionado.

title: Why the Titans Will Beat the Jaguars in Week 12, Why They Won't, and a Prediction
full_text:
The Tennessee Titans winning on the road in Jacksonville in Week 12 would mark their least-likely win of the season. DraftKings Sportsbook has the line set at 14.5 in favor of the Jaguars; that's a whole two touchdowns. After the Titans' 51-30 loss last week, maybe they're not all that far off.
Tennessee's offense could do their part once again, only for Robert Saleh's defense to allow 40+ points and result in yet another loss for the Titans. Jacksonville at least looked beatable in Nashville two weeks ago, however, and that's enough to make this interesting.
That leads us to this week's will, won't, prediction. Here's one reason the Titans will beat the Jaguars, one reason they won't, and my own prediction.
The Titans offense has scored 23 or more points in five straight games, and more than 30 in two of their last three. Cam Ward's unit is operating at a season-best, and if Tennessee wins in Week 12, it'll be because they finally overcome their own defensive shortcomings.
This is a Titans vs. Titans scenario, but that's how it has been for Tennessee in recent weeks. It's a matter of getting out of their own way and, for once, trying to piece together a semi-complete game.
Jacksonville will have All-Pro S Jessie Bates this time around, after he missed the Titans' first meeting due to having just been traded to the Jaguars. It appears more likely now Ward has a good game than not, which is enough progress for the offense to be pinned as the Titans' winning factor.
This is a weirder reason, but something about the Jaguars' latest loss to the New York Giants and J.J. McCarthy tells me they won't be sprinting to repeat it. Great teams rarely lose back-to-back, especially not when the modern Titans are involved.
I just don't see a 7-3, Super-Bowl-contending Jacksonville team returning to their home field off that loss without some anger. The Jaguars' 18 points last Sunday was also the first time they'd scored less than 30 since October 11.
It's bad timing for a Tennessee team coming off their own defeat, but the motivation is different on either side. A loss for Jacksonville mars an ongoing playoff chase, while a loss for the Titans pushes them closer to the first overall pick.
From the outside looking in, it's the perfect storm for a nasty divisional game for the road team.
That leads us here. I try to balance the two perspectives in this series with my prediction, and the silver lining here is that the Titans' defense finally holds a team to less than 40 points. Elsewhere, though, don't expect any surprises.
Cam Ward puts on another promising, low-mistake performance. Tennessee's defense gets ripped by Lawrence and the Jags just enough to keep the Titans out of it most of the way through. Not necessarily a blowout (coming in right under the spread), but not a close contest, either.
These two teams were worlds apart in Week 10, and one game in two weeks isn't enough to change that. I've got the Jaguars coming out on top, but if Ward keeps climbing, Titans fans should happily pocket his improvement and press on regardless.

title: Titans' Snap Count Analysis in Week 11: Reserve WRs Show Out, While Secondary Takes Another Hit
full_text:
After losing 51-30 in blowout fashion to the Dallas Cowboys on the road, the lowly Tennessee Titans fall to 1-9 for the second consecutive season.
Currently, the Titans are in possession of the No. 1 pick in the NFL Draft, edging out fellow one-win teams the Los Angeles Chargers and the Miami Dolphins due to strength of schedule. Tennessee may consider losing more in order to lock in the coveted top pick.
It's time for the weekly breakdown of the decisions made by the Robert Saleh-led coaching staff, both the good and the bad, based on players' snaps. Unsurprisingly, the offense remains in the driver's seat. We'll touch on the fun stuff first.
Against the Cowboys, WR Chimere Dike was QB Cam Ward's favorite target, leading the Titans in receptions and receiving yards. Dike caught six of seven targets for 69 yards. This marks Dike's second game in three weeks with at least 60-plus receiving yards and five-plus receptions.
In the previous week, Dike recorded 54 snaps against Jacksonville, and he played 53 in Dallas. Not to mention his role as a returner on special teams, Dike had six returns for 127 yards, which totals more than 200 all-purpose yards on the day.
Already, in his second season, Dike has climbed to sixth all-time for the most kick return yards in franchise history with 2,700 yards.
Earlier in the season, the 23-year-old receiver had a limited role, only recording six receptions in the first seven weeks of the season. However, Dike has been entrusted with a larger role in the offense, especially with rookie standout WR Carnell Tate being sidelined for two games nursing an injury, and he's proven himself recently.
It's been an odd year for WR Calvin Ridley. Prior to playing the Cowboys, he only had six catches for 91 yards. The Titans were open about trying to deal the aging receiver ahead of the NFL trade deadline, but there were no takers. Against Jacksonville, Ridley only played four snaps, and it looked like the Titans were moving on from him in favor of the practice squad call-up Xavier Restrepo.
In Dallas, Ridley had took an unexpected leap and made an impact despite only playing 26 snaps. He caught five passes for 68 yards, including a touchdown on a miraculous play from Ward , who escaped Cowboys defenders to find Ridley in the back corner of the end zone on a fourth and long.
It was Ridley's first game of 60-plus receiving yards and a touchdown since Week 16 of 2024 , nearly two years ago.
Nearing age 32, Ridley's best days are more than likely behind him. To be fair, most of his touches in this contest came in garbage time. But he still played his best game of the season by recording season highs in receptions and receiving yards, as well as scoring his first touchdown of the year. Improvement is improvement for a player that had been obsolete.
After trading away two defensive pillars in DT Jeffery Simmons and S Amani Hooker ahead of the NFL trade deadline, the Titans' defense has taken a significant step backward. For the third week in a row, Tennessee has allowed 40-plus points.
Furthermore, the Titans' secondary has allowed at least one opposing receiver 100 or more yards in four straight games.
Against Dallas, CB Joshua Williams led the Titans with a team-high 11 tackles but allowed a game-high 92 receiving yards and eight catches on 10 targets, according to PFF . Williams was one of four Titans to play all 65 defensive snaps.
In the week prior against Jacksonville, Williams played all 74 defensive snaps and allowed 86 yards and six receptions. Playing a ton of snaps doesn't make a player a snap winner.
The Cowboys' duo of WR Ceedee Lamb and WR George Pickens combined for 18 catches, 234 receiving yards, and two touchdowns. Opposing receivers are continuing to find success against Williams, who hasn't recorded a pass breakup since his season debut in Week 6, which is extremely concerning for someone who, again, plays every snap.
Tennessee making a change seems like the obvious fix. But after Amani Hooker was traded at the deadline and Cor'Dale Flott left in Week 11 with a neck injury, this may just be a matter of waiting until the 2027 NFL Draft... at the earliest.

title: How Titans Wasted No Time Crowning a New WR2 After Wan'Dale Robinson's Move to IR
full_text:
No position group on the Tennessee Titans is as packed with young talent as the WR room. Cam Ward's climb in the latter half of this season is owed in large part to his varied cast of weapons that only seem to get better as the age decreases on the depth chart.
Carnell Tate is inarguably the team's WR1 at this point, taking the role almost as soon as he came onto the scene as a rookie this year. That left $70 million offseason pickup Wan'Dale Robinson in the team's WR2 slot, but his struggles and eventual move to IR opened that door wide.
The result in Week 11 was a decisive takeover from Florida product Chimere Dike. We made the case prior to kickoff that Dike should be heavily involved in the slot in place of Robinson, and that came to pass in an exciting way despite a loss to the Dallas Cowboys.
Dike's 54 snaps were second on the team only to Tate's 62. Elic Ayomanor trailed on the outside with 37, followed by Calvin Ridley (26) and Xavier Restrepo (17). Dike hit a season-high 60% slot rate without Robinson in rotation.
The clear separation lies with the Titans' fourth overall pick, and their only playmaker in the WR core to achieve Pro Bowl honors.
Those were for his impact on special teams, sure, but Dike stepping into a larger role as a pass-catcher in this offense is best-case scenario. The same speed and vision that make him an elite returner also mean he's a swift, effective route runner.
Dike is a Swiss Army knife, and the Titans should be using that to their full advantage now and in the future. His six receptions for 69 yards led the team vs. the Cowboys. Compared to Robinson, Dike has 209 yards to Robinson's 272, and that's on half of the latter's 38 receptions.
It's also necessary to point out that Dike has generated those numbers on far fewer snaps in the passing game, too; he wasn't even a play-to-play option in that way when the season began. This is a recent emergence, though it's great that Tennessee didn't waste time implementing Dike.
No matter what move the Titans make with their top pick in next year's draft or how Robinson performs when he returns, Dike is a proven fixture of this offense's success. He should be kept around, and further, pushed into the spotlight.
The dude has what it takes. All he needs are consistent chances to prove it, and zips from Cam Ward downfield.

title: Ranking 4 Top Prospects Titans Could Take With First Overall Pick in 2027 Draft
full_text:
If you're reading this, we don't have to tell you how important the 2027 NFL Draft is for the Tennessee Titans. Not only is it a crucial interval for HC Robert Saleh and GM Mike Borgonzi to prove their collective vision, but it's a window of opportunity for this rebuild to actually take the next step.
As of now, the 1-9 Titans hold the first overall pick next spring. That would be the second time in three years, and QB Cam Ward rapidly improving is starting to make that selection look like a great investment. Tennessee needs an even better, more immediately beneficial pick this time around.
Based on ESPN's big board - which is almost a consensus for teams not in the QB market - I'm ranking the four most realistic targets the Titans could spend their top pick on if they end up securing it by the end of the season.
If I were in Borgonzi's shoes, here's how I'd assess the ladder of candidates at the top of the list.
Jeremiah Smith is the biggest no-brainer to pass through the draft in years, and it'd be shocking if the Titans (or any team, for that matter) passed up on him.
Smith's 17 touchdowns and 1,482 yards are both good for the best in college football this season. The big-body receiver, and former teammate of Carnell Tate, is as elite a route runner as they come. He excels at outrunning defenders and going up for contested catches over them.
In short, Smith can do it all. The only drawback of this selection is the pitiful state of Saleh's defense after DT Jeffery Simmons and S Amani Hooker were traded, but with another first-rounder and two picks in the second, Tennessee could make up defensive ground after taking Smith if they wished.
Colin Simmons is my favorite defensive prospect in this draft, and is perhaps the most obvious "don't overthink it" prospect on the board. The Texas EDGE is a good ol' fashioned star.
In his junior year with the Longhorns, Simmons has amassed 10.5 sacks (good for fifth nationally), as well as 2 forced fumbles and 32 total tackles. He's a wrecking ball off the edge, exhibiting lighting speed and versatility at 6'3", 246 lbs.
Simmons has a great burst, shifty footwork, and all the makings of a long-term defensive cornerstone. This is his second straight season with 10+ sacks, and he had nine as a freshman. If the Titans don't go Smith, Simmons is my top option for a pivot.
If the Titans are after an EDGE and Colin Simmons isn't the choice, South Carolina's Dylan Stewart is essentially a lateral move to the same dominant end.
Stewart is taller and more trim than Simmons, at 6'5", 250 lbs, and not quite as outright explosive on the sack front - he has 2.5 on the season. But with three forced fumbles and 18 pressures, the Gamecock is a sleeping giant and one-on-one nightmare.
He overpowers linemen with ease and slips tackles with impressive, quick footwork. Stewart is agile, long, and another player that would be difficult for any GM in need of an explosive defender to overthink. I may prefer Simmons on the page, but the Titans would have a winner in either.
Finally, we'll pivot slightly to the CB position with Leonard Moore, out of Notre Dame. Moore has been widely considered the top CB in the 2027 class, and it's arguable that the Titans need more help in the secondary than anywhere else.
However, between the money Tennessee spent at CB this past offseason and the undeniable prowess of the three prospects above him, I'd rather see the Titans take a swing at this position later in the draft or in free agency than with their top selection.
In last year's College Football Playoff, Moore held the aforementioned Smith to one catch on two targets, and just seven receiving yards. This season, Moore has forced one fumble and defended seven passes. He's failed to produce an INT through 11 games after nabbing five last year.
Teams don't throw to Moore for a reason. He's a rock-solid prospect with the physical tools to go far in the NFL, and even if the Titans went a surprising route and chose him out of this batch, it would be far from the end of the world.
The 2027 pool of players is just that good, and the Titans are poised to have their pick of the lot. They'd almost have to try to mess this one up at first overall.

title: Titans Found a Role for WR Calvin Ridley vs. Cowboys — But Fans Shouldn't be Fooled by the Stats
full_text:
With Wan'Dale Robinson being put on IR ahead of Week 11, the Tennessee Titans' WR room was prepared for a youth-first shakeup. That's precisely what happened, with second-year playmaker Chimere Dike leading the team with six receptions for 69 yards. Rookie Carnell Tate scored a touchdown in his return from a two-week absence.
What may have surprised Titans fans on the surface was veteran Calvin Ridley's involvement. Ridley entered the contest with just six receptions on the season and posed as someone who barely survived the trade deadline. He finished with five catches vs. the Cowboys for 68 yards.
Ridley was also on the receiving end of Cam Ward's outrageous touchdown pass at the end of the game. This is a player who Tennessee has heralded again and again as a need-to-get-touches guy; someone who could play an important role as a veteran in this developing offense.
Based on the numbers alone, you may think that page was turned in Week 11. But don't be fooled, Titans fans. Ridley had just 26 snaps against Dallas, the only productive portion of which came on the final drive in garbage time. This game was not a breakthrough.
If anything, it's a sign that his ever-dwindling role is still trending in the same direction.
The question that grows week after week is: If Ridley was going to be used in such a limited capacity, what was the point of holding on to him in the face of even slight reported interest. He should've been a "sell at all costs," and was instead held to pick up late-game snaps from rookies and sophomores.
Ridley simply doesn't have a clear place on this roster moving forward. His restructured contract runs through next season, but if the Titans use the first pick they currently hold on WR Jeremiah Smith, Ridley's already reduced playing time could potentially fizzle out entirely.
For comparison, Ridley's aforementioned six snaps came in way under Tate's 62, Dike's 54, and Ayomanor's 37. When Robinson returns, we could even see Ridley's involvement dip down to the level of practice-squad regular Xavier Restrepo, who had 17 snaps in Week 11.
It was fun to see Ridley go off in tandem with Ward as the game wound down last Sunday; and again, that final pass and score will go down as a long-time highlight. However, Ridley's gasp for snaps right before the buzzer is the most telling blow to his place in this offense.
It's a whole lot of smoke and no fire, Titans fans, and it will stay that way for Ridley barring a change that hasn't come close to being made all season.

title: Why Robert Saleh Needs to Turn RB Nick Singleton's 'Chance' Into a Reality for Titans in Week 12
full_text:
The Titans' running game led by RB Tony Pollard has been one of the few bright spots in an otherwise miserable season. Pollard is on pace for his fifth consecutive 1,000-yard season and is someone Tennessee undoubtedly would love to have back after this season.
But what about the backs behind him? RB Tyjae Spears was supposed to provide an electric one-two punch in Tennessee’s backfield. Instead, it’s turned into a one-man show, primarily due to Spears’ inability to stay on the field.
HC Robert Saleh recently confirmed that Spears has only been operating at about 70%, so they’ve essentially shut him down to give him a chance at extending his career beyond this season (likely elsewhere).
With Spears sidelined, the team has turned to veteran RB Michael Carter whenever Pollard needs a breather. Carter’s reliability in pass protection has given him the nod over rookie Nick Singleton in most cases, but at some point, it would be wise for the team to start mixing in a few carries for the Penn State product.
At minimum, they should give him the carries that Carter occasionally gets. Last Sunday, he ran the ball four times for nine yards, and he has just 16 rushing yards on the season.
Meanwhile, Singleton hasn’t touched the ball since October 4th and only has seven carries on the year. Granted, he hasn’t done much with those limited opportunities (12 yards), but he’s also a rookie who would benefit from seeing himself on film and then being able to make corrections through those reps.
Saleh, in the same breath as he delivered the Spears news, said there's a "chance" we see Singleton. It's time to take that chance.
The Titans have made it clear they want Pollard back, and he’s at least publicly saying the interest is mutual. If the money is right, there’s a good chance he will be a part of their immediate future plans.
But with the team sitting at 1-9 and Spears heading to injured reserve, there’s no reason not to give Singleton more playing time than he’s recently gotten, especially when we already know what Carter is at this point in his eight-season career. Singleton could ultimately prove to be a non-factor going forward, but the only way we're really going to find out is by letting him play.
It doesn’t have to be an entire series or anything of that nature, but if you want to spell Pollard for a few plays, why not use Singleton on early downs and then go back to Pollard or Carter in obvious passing situations to help with protection?
There are ways to get the rookie on the field without sacrificing Pollard’s touches, and that’s something the Titans need to figure out starting next week on the road in Jacksonville.
Shaun is a longtime Titans fan who has years of experience in the field. He missed being on the team beat, and is here to change that. He also writes scripts for EA Sports' Madden games, where fans may have heard his work.

title: 2 Titans' Defensive Position Groups Begging for a Refresh This Offseason After Week 11
full_text:
For the first time in more than two years, the Tennessee Titans gave up 50-plus points to the Dallas Cowboys in a 51-30 romp on Sunday. Robert Saleh properly ripped them in the aftermath.
Prior to the NFL trade deadline, Tennessee's defense was holding opponents to an impressive 21.5 points per game through the first six weeks of the season. Since trading two franchise cornerstones, four-time DT Jeffery Simmons and defensive captain S Amani Hooker, the Titans' defense has been on a downward spiral.
Since Week 8, Tennessee's defense has allowed a league-worst 44.7 points per game by a wide margin, according to StatMuse . The second-worst is the New England Patriots, who allowed 33 points per game in that stretch.
This mid-season defensive regression has been untimely for the Titans because Tennessee's offense has scored an average of nearly 30 points per game since Week 8, which is the sixth highest in the league.
Unfortunately, the Titans' offense hasn't been able to muster enough points to earn a win, with the defense giving up 40 or more points in three straight games. Looking ahead to the offseason, Tennessee's front office must address glaring issues on the defense to avoid being a bottom-dweller in the standings for a fifth consecutive season.
The Titans' secondary has been grilled over the previous three weeks.
In Week 8 against the Cincinnati Bengals, WR Tee Higgins had 10 catches for 155 yards and two touchdowns to pair with teammate WR Ja'Marr Chase, who had 11 catches for 141 yards and a touchdown. Coming out of the bye, Tennessee's defense allowed seven catches for 152 yards and a touchdown to the Jaguars' WR Parker Washington.
This past Sunday in Dallas, Cowboys' WR Ceedee Lamb accumulated 11 receptions for 132 yards and a touchdown alongside teammate WR George Pickens, who had seven catches for 102 yards and a touchdown himself.
Trading away Hooker to the Buffalo Bills ahead of the deadline obviously would shake up the secondary. However, the trade has revealed a massive lack of discipline for a position group that has been absolutely decimated recently.
While Hooker was still a Titan when Higgins and Chase combined for almost 300 yards and three touchdowns, Hooker was a shining light because he intercepted three passes to keep Tennessee in the game. In free agency, the Titans' front office spent more than $675 million, which was second only to the Kansas City Chiefs, per Spotrac .
Three of the top nine highest-paid players were cornerbacks: Alontae Taylor, Cordale Flott and Joshua Williams. Since Week 8, Taylor has allowed 218 yards, Flott has allowed 213 yards and Williams has allowed 324 yards while forcing zero turnovers.
For perspective, the Titans have allowed an average of nearly 380 yards per game over the last three games. On average the combination of Taylor, Flott and Williams is responsible for 251.6 of all pass yards allowed. These numbers are especially damning when considering their combined salary is $38.3 million this season.
The Titans must address the glaring lack of production in the secondary over the offseason if this defense is going to show any sign of life next year.
The other major position group that was impacted by the trade deadline was plainly the defensive line. Simmons being dealt to the Chicago Bears wasn't a surprise given his name had been in the rumor mill for years. However, a true surprise was the Titans releasing DT Jordan Elliott midseason due to an incident in practice.
Signed in the 2026 offseason, Elliott inked a two-year deal worth up to $8.5 million; he was intended to fortify the defense line alongside Simmons. However, in the end, he only made five appearances for Tennessee. A shorthanded Titans defensive line hasn't been impressive without Elliott, and especially Simmons.
Fellow 2026 signee, DT John Franklin-Myers has been the most productive D-line man this season aside from Simmons. However, his 18 tackles and 1.5 sacks pale in comparison to Simmons' 38 tackles and four sacks despite Franklin-Myers playing three more games than Simmons as a member of the Titans.
Prior to arriving in Nashville, Franklin-Myers combined for 14.5 sacks and 42 tackles in his two seasons as a Bronco , where he was far more dominant. Outside of Simmons and Franklin-Myers, no other Titans' defensive lineman has recorded a sack this season. Something is missing.
Filling the shoes of a potential future Hall of Fame talent in Simmons is nearly impossible to do. Nevertheless, the Titans will have to find talent to bolster the interior of their defense ahead of the 2027 season. The front office has their work cut out for them.

title: How 1 Poor Pick in 2026 Draft Continues to Cast a Shadow Over the Titans' Rebuild
full_text:
It's impossible not to at least like what general manager Mike Borgonzi did with the 2026 draft class. The Titans have two rookies of the month in WR Carnell Tate and LB Anthony Hill Jr. RG Fernando Carmona Jr., before being sent to IR after Week 3, was an immediate-impact starter.
The only real reason you may not love the class (save for the suspicious absence of RB Nick Singleton), is EDGE Keldric Faulk. Tennessee traded up into the first round to take Faulk with the 31st pick, crowning the former Auburn Tiger as a pivotal young piece in Saleh's new defense.
Saleh's defense has obviously been miserable as of late, and Faulk, who wavers in and out of involvement, has failed to inspire any confidence in his progress. Saleh said last month that he'll bet Faulk will pan out as "one of the Titans' greatest."
Check out one stat from Faulk that says everything you need to know about where the rookie stands right now:
#Titans EDGE Keldric Faulk has played 230 snaps this season. He has recorded two pressures in 2026.
Not only is Faulk struggling to generate pressure, but a deeper look at his stats reveal a player that is showing no signs of life for Tennessee.
According to PFF metrics, Faulk's two pressures on the season are dead last among 111 players at his position. His overall grade, 43.6, is just two spots above the worst in the league at 109th. To top it all off, Faulk had zero pressures in yesterday's loss to the Dallas Cowboys.
Borgonzi doesn't have a perfect reputation, but he's clearly moving capable playmakers into pivotal roles and trending in the right direction. With as much say as the Titans have in the draft over the next two years, it's critical that Tennessee has someone who can get it right at multiple intervals.
That's why Faulk is particularly worrying. Tennessee only moved up four spots, basically trading a fourth-rounder for a fifth, but that's a first round grab speeding in the wrong direction. For reference, the Buffalo Bills took EDGE T.J. Parker with the 35th pick - given to them by the Titans for Faulk.
Parker has 13 pressures this season, as well as 3.5 sacks and a forced fumble. Not dominant, but night and day compared to Faulk.
As the Titans' defense moves toward a reset, punctuated by Saleh's rageful comments today, Faulk's path to development appears foggy. His shortcomings as a rookie are likely to limit his opportunities, making this pick look worse (and more worrying) by the week.

title: Robert Saleh Rips Titans Defense and Threatens Job Losses After Cowboys Disaster
full_text:
It's apparently "no more Mr. Nice Guy" in Nashville today. Robert Saleh took the podium for his day-after press conference following yesterday's 51-30 loss to the Dallas Cowboys, and for perhaps the first time this season, didn't show an ounce of restraint.
Saleh called the Titans' performance "disgusting" and "embarrassing" after the game on Sunday. Clearly, his frustrations didn't subside with a night to sleep on them. The head coach said today that Tennessee's defense didn't "reciprocate" the offense's success moving the ball.
What's more, when asked for positives regarding his defense, Saleh didn't hold back: "I'm not going to try and sugar-coat things ... It's been dog ----." Saleh went as far as to openly call jobs into question, adding of both players and coaches that those who get better will stay.
Those that don't? Well, they won't. Saleh also alluded to the hard conversations going on behind the scenes right now for Tennessee, though as expected, he won't reveal those details. This sounds like a dumpster fire, and on the field, it is.
But there's something refreshing about Saleh threatening to burn this thing to the ground. Saleh, alongside general manager Mike Borgonzi, are initiating the sort of purification process that this franchise has needed for years.
The Titans have allowed 45 points per game in the month of November. If that doesn't beg for a reset, I'm not sure what does. Saleh's own unit is broken, and the offense that Borgonzi has built through the draft isn't being allowed to fully flourish as a result.
Thankfully, the first step has already been taken. The Titans made some difficult trades and acquired the draft capital to see them through for the next two years. Borgonzi, coming off an inarguably solid draft that saw Carnell Tate and Anthony Hill Jr. join the ranks, appears equipped to keep building.
But Tennessee must fully tear down what is broken to build something sturdier in the same spot. Saleh's first year behind the wheel has been marred by the miscues of Brian Callahan before him, and Callahan's short-lived era was marred by Mike Vrabel's bitter end.
The cycle has to stop, and the slate must be wiped completely clean, at some point. That's why Saleh's comments should be a breath of fresh air for Titans fans. He's publicly furious at the brand of football this team is playing; finally, the usual "coach speak" has been entirely dropped.
Expect a flurry of moves across the board this offseason if things don't improve for Tennessee before the end of the year. At 1-9, I'm not sure what the next seven games could bring that will satisfy Saleh. If embarrassment is what it takes to spark change, then Tennessee must temporarily embrace it.
Lane covers the Tennessee Titans, where he brings an evolving team's journey to fans on a daily basis. A longtime sports fanatic and recent baby blue jersey aficionado.

title: Commanders Get Brandon Aiyuk’s First Visit. Monday Night Changed What Awaits Him
full_text:
According to a report by ESPN's Adam Schefter , the Washington Commanders will meet with free-agent wide receiver Brandon Aiyuk on Wednesday. Drew Rosenhaus, Aiyuk's agent, confirmed the visit to Schefter. Washington will be Aiyuk’s first stop, according to the Associated Press . Aiyuk cleared waivers Tuesday afternoon after no team claimed his San Francisco contract, leaving him free to sign anywhere.
Aiyuk last played an NFL game on Oct. 20, 2024, when he tore the ACL, MCL, and meniscus in his right knee. Rosenhaus has said Aiyuk passed a physical in San Francisco and has been running routes on his own. That’s encouraging. ESPN reports Aiyuk is expected to work out during Wednesday’s visit. Washington will get its own look at his movement and conditioning after more than two years away from NFL games. His last full season was 2023, when he earned second-team All-Pro honors. Washington has seven regular-season games left. Aiyuk would have to learn offensive coordinator David Blough’s offense, build timing with Daniels, his former Arizona State teammate ( the two recently spoke ), and get enough practice work to earn a role. That makes Wednesday’s meeting a calendar question, too.
Monday night made that question more interesting. Antonio Williams caught nine passes for 122 yards against the Bengals, including gains of 22 and 42 yards on the final drive that set up rookie kicker Drew Stevens’ winning field goal. Stefon Diggs caught four passes for 45 yards, and Treylon Burks caught two for 30. Williams played 57 of Washington’s 68 offensive snaps Monday . With McLaurin out, the Commanders have reason to examine another receiver, but Williams has already earned a substantial role. Aiyuk’s 2023 resume alone shouldn’t put him ahead of Williams, who has earned the snaps he’s getting.
Antonio Williams had his first career 100 yard game and came through when Washington needed him most. 9 REC, 122 REC YDS, 11 TGT vs Bengals. The third round rookie is starting to make some noise in the OROY conversation. https://t.co/ZMPIVSM2sV pic.twitter.com/ilQUrSPHdc
NFL Network's Ian Rapoport has suggested a practice-squad start , which would let Washington bring Aiyuk into the offense without immediately opening a spot on the 53-man roster. That remains a possibility, not an agreement. It also would not put a date on his first game. Wednesday’s workout could show Washington how close Aiyuk is to playing. Then the Commanders can decide whether to sign him and, if they do, where he starts. title: Commanders Daily: Washington Pulled Off a 45-Year NFL First Against Cincinnati. Why Did It Need a Walk-Off?
full_text:
The Washington Commanders did not hit the ground running on offense Monday night against the Cincinnati Bengals. In fact, the team stumbled, gaining only 27 yards on 15 plays across their first four possessions, all of which ended with Tress Way working his magic. After that, Washington scored on their next six possessions: one touchdown and five field goals. NFL Network said the Commanders are the first team in 45 seasons to finish a game with six straight scoring drives of at least 50 yards . That said, the real question here is: how did that much sustained offense still leave Washington behind in the final minute? Down 10-0, Washington drove 79 yards in 1:43 before halftime. Jayden Daniels scrambled for 10 yards on third-and-9, then found tight end Chig Okonkwo for 32 yards. On a play that Treylon Burks appeared headed for a touchdown, he instead drew pass interference in the end zone, and then Jacory "Bill" Croskey-Merritt scored from the one. That drive started it all. The Bengals won the opening toss and elected to receive, so Washington got the ball first in the second half, and Daniels' 47-yard run sparked another scoring drive. Later, Stefon Diggs added a nice 29-yard catch on second-and-20, extending the drive that gave Washington its first lead. The Commanders finished with 428 yards, 23 first downs, and 150 rushing yards on 26 carries. After converting 7-of-14 third downs against the Giants , Washington went just 2-of-10 against Cincinnati, doing most of its work on first and second down. All that yardage kept rookie kicker Drew Stevens busy. Washington reached the red zone four times and scored a touchdown once; the other three trips ended with field goals. Cincinnati had allowed touchdowns on just 40% of opponents’ red-zone trips coming into Monday, so the Bengals have been doing this most of the year. Still, Washington put together a 13-play, 73-yard drive that reached Cincinnati’s 7 and came away with a 25-yard kick. The late 41-yarder was a different decision. Facing fourth-and-1 at the Bengals’ 24, Commanders head coach Dan Quinn took the points, sending his special teams unit out for the field goal and a 19-17 lead with 2:26 left. He said he wanted Daniels to get another chance if Cincinnati answered: “And I didn't want him to not touch the ball again at the end of the game.” Joe Burrow did answer. Evan McPherson’s 56-yard field goal put Cincinnati ahead 20-19 with 46 seconds left. After the kickoff return, Daniels took over at his own 28 with 39 seconds and no timeouts. He found rookie Antonio Williams for 22 yards, spiked the ball, then went back to Williams for 42 more to the Bengals’ 8 on a play that even Peyton Manning said was perfect. Manning quoted Dan Marino on ESPN's ManningCast, saying, "There's no defense for a perfect throw. That was a perfect throw." Another spike gave Stevens time to make his fifth field goal, a 26-yarder as time expired. Washington won because Daniels and Williams covered 64 yards in two throws, and Stevens didn’t miss. Against Arizona on Sunday, the Commanders will need more of those long drives to end with someone other than their kicker scoring.
The entire final drive that sealed the @Commanders win, as seen on the ManningCast. pic.twitter.com/wIsF7V4TPN

title: Commanders Report Card: Daniels and Defense Delivered, but One Unit Nearly Cost Washington the Bengals Win
full_text:
The Washington Commanders' Week 11 result served as the team's most cathartic moment of the season, bar none. In fact, you'd have to go back a couple of years to their iconic 2024 campaign to locate a moment that meant as much for their tired fan base as this 22-20 win over the Cincinnati Bengals did, especially after the number of instances in which loyal viewers' hopes had been dashed in identical contexts.
Time and time again, the Commanders have come up short in last-second attempts at deciding games on their own terms. Their loss to the San Francisco 49ers , their most recent defeat at the hands of the briefly healthy Los Angeles Rams , and their infamous tie split with the New York Giants were each fraught with poorly composed drives in the clutch, gaffes that doubled as fleeting glimpses of hope just two seasons removed from Washington's 12-5 record.
Their matchup against the previously 7-2 Cincinnati gave the Commanders a chance to toss their helmet into the divisional race's ring, with their handling of a contender proving that they're talented enough to hang with the league's upper crust when they're executing as a united front. And this time, when they got the ball back down one in the game's final minute, they played it perfectly, connecting for big plays, hustling downfield, and knocking the go-ahead chip shot through.
Almost everyone played up to their level of competition as Washington collected its third win in four games. Here's which position groups made fans proud, and who'd be better off using this game as another learning opportunity:
Jayden Daniels got off to something of a slow start, a trend he's been no stranger to this fall, but it was hard to lay the hammer down on his inability to move the ball downfield. Despite the chances repeatedly handed to him by a defense that did similarly well to limit Joe Burrow and co., the Commanders quarterback couldn't find a way to escape the Bengals' defensive line.
He went down three times, each time to Cincinnati sack artist Boye Mafe, rarely leaving him time to diagnose the active downfield coverages he was seeing. It didn't help that he looked tentative in second-guessing his reads and eventually baited star wideout Stefon Diggs into the first sideline conniption of his homecoming D.C. stint.
Washington Commanders Stefon Diggs Throw the f***ing ball pic.twitter.com/vttRPNvfw7
Fortunately for the Landover crowd, Daniels eventually strung together long enough drives to continue keeping up after the pre-halftime rushing touchdown. Washington settled for field goals on each of Washington's five second-half drives thanks to his favorite targets, pass-catchers who enabled the quarterback to finish with 289 passing yards alongside a team-high 55 on the ground.
When he's alternating between dynamic scrambling and pinpoint-accurate passing, few distributors can hang with Daniels in a competitive matchup, and he finally got to prove it in a nationally viewed spot.
Daniels' reworked receiving corps of Diggs, Antonio Williams, Treylon Burks , and Chig Okonkwo may sound like a skeleton crew considering the number of injured options Washington's lost along the way, but optimistic outsiders would see it as the team's way of whittling the position group down to the dependable rotation of playmakers.
As sorely missed as Terry McLaurin is, Williams has stepped up as the new difference-maker , catching nine of 11 targets for 122 yards. Williams caught 22- and 42-yard passes on Washington’s final possession, moving the ball to the Bengals’ 8 to set up Drew Stevens’ winning 26-yard field goal.
Antonio Williams had his first career 100 yard game and came through when Washington needed him most. 9 REC, 122 REC YDS, 11 TGT vs Bengals. The third round rookie is starting to make some noise in the OROY conversation. https://t.co/ZMPIVSM2sV pic.twitter.com/ilQUrSPHdc
Diggs, too, deserves credit for continuing to produce after getting initially blanked over the less-than-productive opening half. Burks generally did his job as the deep threat, while Okonkwo kept punishing matchups as a runner, surprising defenders with his raw combination of size and athleticism. Had it not been for Van Jefferson's tough drop on their attempt at a flea flicker, this would have felt like a spotless outing from a group that had little to work with over the night's early goings.
The Commanders’ backfield hierarchy remains unsettled, but it was nice to see Jacory "Bill" Croskey-Merritt welcomed back into the rushing rotation after a lengthy absence. He hadn't seen action since that disastrous Giants draw, but his presence was felt immediately with a touchdown to put Washington on the board.
He was also handy as a short-yardage option, collecting as many receptions (two) as fellow running back Austin Ekeler, the veteran with whom Croskey-Merritt had never enjoyed a lengthy team-up thanks to injuries suffered by the rushing options over the last two years. They were needed this time around given Rachaad White's limited usage, a less-than-shocking deployment decision given the questionable tag he spent much of last week draped with.
As exhilarating as Daniels was on the go, he should still be getting more than 50-odd yards from one of his backs regularly, but the Commanders still seem to be hunting for a clearer look at this positional hierarchy. Until then, we'll just have to be thankful for every time the backs escape the dogpiles in their relentless attempts at extending drives on the ground.
While some of the scorers managed to put their best feet forward at the opportune moment, Daniels' unit of blockers and protectors continued struggling to avoid the same mistakes they always seem saddled with. Josh Conerly Jr. false-started in the first quarter, and Chris Paul did so in the third, with Brandon Coleman particularly succumbing to Mafe on the Bengals' career night.
Lucas Patrick, too, didn't exactly wow the masses with several high snaps that frequently put Daniels at a slight disadvantage, and it's not often that someone of Dexter Lawrence's mass leaves someone in the dust, as he did on one of Daniels' wrap-ups.
Dexter Lawrence... sheesh! pic.twitter.com/oPPZOukNY6
Still, they gave Daniels enough time to deal down the gridiron, and that's more than we can say after a few other choice losses from earlier in the season. The same pile-up of jumpy infractions will have to be assessed eventually, though, as it remains unclear why the same Commanders struggle so mightily with the pre-snap penalties.
The Bengals getting shut out to start the game sounds like a much bigger shock than whatever reaction the Commanders' own slow start elicited, and for good reason. Burrow's armed with one of the game's best one-two receiver combinations in Ja'Marr Chase and Tee Higgins, and they hadn't scored fewer than 31 points in each of their five straight wins heading into Monday Night Football.
He's too good a pocket passer to be allowed to do his job uninterrupted, prompting the Commanders' aggressive blitz attack to disrupt his flow. And that they did; even though he reached 300 passing yards, he still looked considerably less comfortable, repeatedly resorting to last-second finds that only the best of the best can regularly hit.
It helped his case that several would-be picks were dropped by opposing defensive backs, and he still took as many sacks as Daniels while watching his offensive line occasionally crumple. They stuffed the Bengals' run game in the trenches; Chase Brown gained six yards on six carries, and Cincinnati finished with 31 rushing yards. Luvu also stopped Burrow on fourth-and-one at Cincinnati’s 45 in the first quarter, giving Washington a possession in Bengals territory. They did all they could to ensure the offense got their chances to flip stops into points.
THE COMMANDERS DEFENSE DENIES JOE BURROW ON 4TH DOWN pic.twitter.com/6kdFktlq37

title: Commanders Free Agent Dream Signing on Verge of Becoming Reality
full_text:
The San Francisco 49ers are releasing Brandon Aiyuk , ESPN’s Adam Schefter reported Monday, clearing the final hurdle for a pairing Commanders fans have wanted since 2024. Washington is already back in the conversation, though the first step might not be a spot on the 53-man roster. NFL Network’s Ian Rapoport called Washington Aiyuk’s “most likely landing spot” and said the Commanders could offer him a place on their practice squad. The development finally moves this story forward after months of questions. Last week’s report that Aiyuk had repaired his relationship with Jayden Daniels suggests any bad blood between the two is behind them. Now that San Francisco has made its decision, Washington still has one to make.
The expected outcome, all eyes now shift to the #Commanders , who could offer Brandon Aiyuk a spot on their practice squad. It's his most likely landing spot, especially now on the same page as Jayden Daniels. https://t.co/Ld8ZVPKlRk
Because the 49ers are releasing Aiyuk after the trade deadline, he must first pass through waivers. A team claiming him would have to take on the remaining terms of the four-year, $120 million extension he signed in 2024, making it far more likely he clears waivers Tuesday at 4 p.m. ET and negotiates a new deal as a free agent. The move comes as Aiyuk’s two-game roster exemption expires Monday following his November 9 reinstatement from the reserve/left squad list. Aiyuk has not played in an NFL game since tearing the ACL, MCL, and meniscus in his right knee on October 20, 2024. He passed a physical last week, and his agent, Drew Rosenhaus, says he is healthy and willing to work out for interested teams. That still leaves Washington to judge how close Aiyuk is to handling game snaps after more than two years away. The practice squad would give the Commanders a way to bring him into the building and evaluate him in their offense without immediately opening an active roster spot. It would not guarantee a promotion or establish when he might play.
Daniels played with Aiyuk at Arizona State. General manager Adam Peters was in San Francisco’s front office when the 49ers drafted him in 2020, and Wes Welker coached Aiyuk there before joining Washington’s staff. With Terry McLaurin out for the season and Stefon Diggs, Treylon Burks, and Antonio Williams carrying the workload, the Commanders have reason to examine their receiver options. A practice squad deal also protects the locker room. If the fit or conditioning isn't there, Washington can move on cleanly without disrupting the active roster. Aiyuk caught 75 passes for 1,342 yards and seven touchdowns in his 2023 All-Pro season. The connections can open a conversation. They can't answer what he can give Washington right now. title: 10 Commanders Quotes on Stopping Joe Burrow and Keeping NFC East Hopes Alive
full_text:
The Washington Commanders beat the Giants 24–21 with a touchdown drive between two late defensive stops. Dan Quinn liked the finish. He also wants to know whether his team can do it again. The Bengals have scored at least 30 points in five straight games , and Washington is still working through its problems in pass coverage . Offensive coordinator David Blough said his group has not reached its standard, either. Monday night gives both sides another chance to show where they stand. From Quinn’s review of the Giants game through Saturday’s final practice, these 10 quotes tell the story of Washington’s week before facing Cincinnati.
Question: If Hartman can bring people from his life onto The Bachelor, would he bring anyone from the Commanders? “I’d bring the whole team if I could. I think maybe, I know towards the end you get to do, like, a home or they kind of meet the family thing. I think maybe I’ll just bring the whole team because that is my family right now. They probably know me the best in the world. So I think that would be a good barometer for her and myself to kind of see what I’m about and what she’s about.”
Question: Is there anything about Ja’Marr Chase’s game that Williams would like to bring into his own? “Definitely. I think one of the things that really makes him special is his ability just to make guys miss and run through tackles after the catch. But this year I’ve actually had the opportunity to watch, like, a lot of the top guys that we’ve gone against. So I always, you know, watch them from the sideline and see what they’re doing on the field in person.”
Question: Burrow likes to step up through the B gaps when he escapes pressure. How can Washington take that away? “As a defensive line, we have to cage the quarterback. So when we do have pressure, make sure there’s no holes or leaky gaps that he can run through and gain 15 yards plus.”
Question: In the 2024 Bengals game , how did Daniels decide to throw to Terry McLaurin in single coverage with a free rusher coming at him? “I think it was more so like I’m going to throw the ball to Terry and whatever happens, I got to pick myself up, somebody else pick me up off the ground. You know, at that moment, but it was worth it.”
Question: Why is Burrow so good against the blitz ? “He knows where the hot is. He can see it. Like I said, elite processing. He sees the hot and he’s right now to it. And those guys are great run after catch. So he just gets the ball in their hands quick and then lets them go and make plays. When you got two dudes like that on the outside and you got a running back like [Chase] Brown and you got a tight end, you just want to get the ball to those guys’ hands and let them be playmakers like they are.” Brown entered Week 11 leading all NFL running backs with 47 receptions , giving Burrow a reliable outlet underneath when teams bring pressure.
Question: What did Quinn like about Washington’s no-huddle sequence against the Giants, and why did the offense wait until the fourth quarter to use it again? “We did make that decision just to, one, have that as part of the game plan. To say, this would be something we think that we wanted to get to, to move quickly. And so we’ll have that available in the games moving forward when we want to choose to use it. But I do think it’s a weapon worth doing. Sometimes it’s even by a personnel group, just to stay in this group to get going. And so having, I don’t know how to say this, more guys, just I felt like the last couple weeks, we found a better rhythm of people not in and out. And so I think that plays into it too, to stay in this group and get them going for a while.”
Question: What techniques must Washington’s cornerbacks keep in mind against Cincinnati’s receivers? “Where’s his split? What leverage am I playing? And then when I have my leverage, I have to own my leverage. ... And then you gotta be tight enough to contest the catch. You gotta compete. That’s gonna be huge. ... But we can’t make it a seven-on-seven pitch and catch all over the field and can’t have that. We gotta be tighter in coverage.”
Question: How has Washington’s defense helped the offense during games? “I think for our players specifically, they feel the confidence of that. You feel like our defense is running off after a sack or a turnover and you’re like, ‘Man, these guys, if we score seven tonight, if we score 10 tonight, we score 13 or 14, whatever it may be, we got a chance to win this game.’ But, at the same point, we wanna live up to our standard of execution and things like that. And we really haven’t reached it as an offensive unit yet. So it’s being able to run the ball efficiently; it’s being able to be explosive in the passing game. We have done a good job taking care of the football, but we gotta be better on third down. And then I think when we can kind of piece a full game together, it’ll really help our defense out as well.” Entering Week 11, Washington’s offense ranked 30th on third down, and Cincinnati’s 30th-ranked third-down defense gives Blough’s unit an opening to extend drives and address its red-zone issues .
Question: Does Cosmi see a path for Washington to go on a run after the Giants win? “For sure. I mean, I think we could compete with anybody coming down this pipe. So we got to keep stacking them and getting wins and putting wins in the win column. From that standpoint, the division is very much accessible to us. So we just got to win ball games here. It’s that simple. Execute and we got a shot for sure.”
Question: How much did the Giants win change Washington’s opportunities in the second half of the season? “You take advantage of an opportunity. And when you miss them, there’s regret. And when you take advantage of them, I think it does provide something of proof to say, ‘This is how you can operate and do that.’ And so the proof is in, can you do it again? Can you do it again? And so that’s the response with the group. And that’s what I’m looking for.”

title: Commanders News: Jayden Daniels Wants No Punts in Joe Burrow Rematch | Burgundy Roundup
full_text:
In today's Burgundy Roundup, Washington has backfield decisions to make before facing a Bengals defense that has been getting to quarterbacks. Cincinnati has questions along its offensive line, but its second-quarter scoring surge leaves the Commanders little room to waste a possession. The last time the Washington Commanders and Cincinnati Bengals played, neither punter saw any action beyond holding on field goals in a 38-33 thriller that Washington won. Of the 13 possessions in that game that didn't end in kneel-downs, only Cincinnati's missed field goal didn't produce points. Commanders quarterback Jayden Daniels let his opinion be known on Friday : "We go out there, and hopefully we don’t punt." - Some of the team's plans for Monday Night Football were known on Saturday: Lucas Patrick will be the team's starting center , while others still need attention, i.e., Jacory "Bill" Croskey-Merritt. For Bill to play, the team still needs to activate him from injured reserve. Washington also still has decisions to make on running back Rachaad White and cornerback Amik Robertson. - The pressure numbers point to a tougher test for Daniels. Cincinnati has pressured opposing quarterbacks on 37.2% of their dropbacks this season and got to Aaron Rodgers on 46.9% in Week 10. New York pressured Daniels on 20.5% of his dropbacks against the Giants. Bengals head coach Zac Taylor knows Daniels well: "Every play is alive for a big play with him, whether it's using his feet or his arm talent."
Sack Saturday featuring Jonathan Allen, Myles Murphy, and Boye Mafe🔥 Almost hunting time again.. 🤧 #Bengals #WhoDey pic.twitter.com/OZddJM1AIb
- Getting to third-and-short won’t make things easy for Washington. Against Pittsburgh, Cincinnati showed two deep safeties on second-and-4 before Bryan Cook came down to help hold Jaylen Warren to three yards. Jordan Battle dropped Warren for a loss on the next play. Bengals safeties coach Jordan Kovacs said Cook’s play was “not a blitz” — he was fitting the run from deep. Daniels will have to account for where those safeties can go after the snap, not just where they start.
Bryan Cook stuffing the Warren run pic.twitter.com/GC58ukCSVm
- Washington has an opening on the other side of the ball, although Cincinnati has ways to protect it. Starting right guard Dalton Risner is out, and left guard Dylan Fairchild is questionable . Bengals center Ted Karras called right tackle Amarius Mims “a star,” whose work allows the line to “allocate resources elsewhere.” If Cincinnati can trust Mims alone on the edge, it may be able to give its guards more help. Washington still has to find a way through to Burrow. - Getting ahead of Cincinnati hasn’t been the problem for its recent opponents. During the Bengals’ five-game winning streak, they’ve been outscored 37–17 in the first quarter. They’ve outscored those same opponents 66–9 in the second. Washington could win the start and still be chasing Burrow by halftime. - Austin Ekeler put another part of the job plainly: “You can’t make mistakes; that’s what it takes.” Washington carries a plus-seven turnover margin into the game, compared with Cincinnati’s plus-two. Neither defense took the ball away in the 2024 meeting. If the Commanders get that extra possession tonight, they have to do something with it. - Northwest Stadium will have a few extras in store for fans on Monday, starting with "Hail Raiser" rally towels handed out at the gates. Go-go band Rare Essence will also perform live at Legends Plaza, and former linebacker Brian Orakpo will be honored as this week's Legend of the Game. - Even a win would still leave Washington third in the NFC East behind Dallas (5-6) after all three division rivals won Sunday. It would cut the gap to the first-place Giants (6-3-1) to two games. - Kickoff is set for 8:15 p.m. ET at Northwest Stadium, with national television coverage on ESPN and local broadcast coverage on FOX 5 DC. Full TV, streaming, and radio details are available in our How to Watch Commanders vs. Bengals guide .
The Washington Commanders released their final Week 11 injury report on Saturday afternoon. The biggest news is that Jacory “Bill” Croskey-Merritt (groin), Lucas Patrick (concussion), Amik Robertson (ankle), and Rachaad White (heel) are all questionable. Three pieces of vital information are still to be determined, as Robertson was injured on the final sequence Friday, didn't practice Saturday, and while the team did not rule him out, they're going to wait to decide. Commanders head coach Dan Quinn named Patrick the starting center for Monday's game despite his game designation, and Rachaad White's heel is something to watch.
The no-huddle was part of Washington’s plan early against the Giants. The Commanders kept the same personnel on the field, which Dan Quinn said helped the offense find a rhythm. “I do think it's a weapon worth doing,” Quinn said Saturday. If Jayden Daniels gets the offense moving Monday night, that tempo could keep Cincinnati from changing personnel between snaps. Quinn didn't say how often Washington might use it.
“But one thing I can always say is I always give that city my all, gave that team my all, and when fans come out to watch us play, they knew that 93 was gonna show up and give everything he had," Allen said. "At the end of the day, the things that I did wrong, I apologize and move on.”
Brown ranks third on the Bengals in receptions, behind Chase and Higgins. His 47 catches have produced 246 yards and two touchdowns, an average of 5.2 yards per reception. He also leads Cincinnati with 441 rushing yards. Washington has to account for him whether Burrow hands him the ball or drops back to pass.
